articles.title: Serbia Bank Owner Arrested Following Licence Revocation
articles.body: Alta Bank HQ in Belgrade. Photo: Wikimedia/Andrei Romanenko The owner of Serbia’s Alta Bank, Davor Macura, was arrested on Monday, three days after the National Bank revoked the bank’s licence. Macura was arrested on suspicion of abuse of office for withdrawing money from Alta Bank’s treasury and obtaining a financial gain of 45 billion dinars (nearly 385 million euros). In addition to Macura, G.M., director of the Bank’s Treasury and Cash Management Department, and I.P., an employee responsible for treasury operations, were also arrested on the orders of the Public Prosecutor’s Office for Organised Crime. They are suspected of assisting Macura in committing the alleged criminal offence. The prosecution suspects that Macura exceeded the limits of his authority up until October 31. G.M. and I.P., who were responsible for the direct handling of assets held in Alta Bank’s treasury, allegedly provided Macura with “access cards or used their own cards and were physically present to enable unauthorised entry into the bank’s treasury”. “During these unauthorised entries, D.M. [Macura] allegedly removed money from the vault, thereby obtaining an illicit financial gain amounting to approximately 45 billion dinars,” the prosecution said. The National Bank of Serbia, NBS, revoked Alta Bank’s operating licence on October 31 citing a significant deterioration in its finances and concerns over its liquidity. “The Executive Board noted that the revocation of the licence was preceded by supervisory measures aimed at ensuring that the bank increased its liquidity levels,” the NBS said, adding that the interests of the bank’s depositors had been put at risk. Alta Bank expanded its operations during the Serbian Progressive Party’s time in power under former President Aleksandar Vucic. In 2025, for example, Serbia’s state-owned electricity company, Elektroprivreda Srbije, EPS, changed its payment arrangements, directing Belgrade residents to pay their electricity bills into Alta Bank accounts. Shortly before calling parliamentary elections, former President Vucic launched a podcast on his YouTube channel with Alta Bank among its main sponsors, featuring advertisements for it displayed in the studio. Vucic’s list in the October 25 parliamentary elections lost power after 14 years of rule to the Student List, which has won an absolute majority. North Macedonia Bank takes control of Alta subsidiary Meanwhile, in neighbouring North Macedonia, the central bank has placed Alta Bank AD Bitola under temporary administration, taking control of its assets following the collapse of its majority shareholder, Alta Bank AD Belgrade, in Serbia. The measure on Sunday was intended to protect the bank’s assets and depositors amid a sharp withdrawal of funds, North Macedonia’s Central Bank governor, Trajko Slaveski, told a press conference. Slaveski said around 2 million euros had been withdrawn from the Bitola-based bank within days, prompting the intervention. He stressed that the North Macedonian bank remained liquid and had a sound loan portfolio. The Serbian bank’s exposure to its North Macedonia counterpart was relatively small, he added, at around 1 million euros, and did not threaten its liquidity. Under the temporary administration, which can last up to three months, central bank-appointed administrators will assume management responsibilities, while the Serbian-majority shareholder will lose its voting rights. Customers will be meanwhile allowed to withdraw no more than 10,000 denars [around 160 euros] per week through payment cards issued by the bank. The bank said its branches will temporarily stop serving customers from Monday until further notice. Slaveski also said potential buyers may acquire the Serbian shareholder’s stake in the bank as a potential long-term solution.

articles.title: Romania and Moldova Seal First Joint Defence Procurement Deal
articles.body:
Romania and Moldova signed a military cooperation agreement on Monday, paving the way for the latter to access the European Union’s Security Action for Europe SAFE programme to finance the purchase of military vehicles.

The agreement marks the first joint defence procurement arrangement between the two countries and represents another step towards strengthening their military cooperation, officials said.

“This is a major opportunity for both countries to strengthen their cooperation in the fields of economy and security … and also a good way to protect our territories and our citizens,” Romanian Prime Minister Luca Niculescu said.

He added that SAFE funding would allow both countries to modernise their defence capabilities while supporting the development of Europe’s defence-industrial base through joint procurement.

Although Moldova is not an EU member and its constitution enshrines a policy of neutrality, it can participate in the programme through a partnership with an EU member state, in this case Romania.

Under the agreement, Moldova may join an existing procurement framework between Romania and Italian manufacturer IDV, Iveco Defence Vehicles, allowing it to acquire 62 multipurpose IVECO military trucks.

The vehicles, which will be produced at an IVECO plant in Romania, are intended to replace ageing Soviet-era trucks still in service with Moldova’s armed forces.

Moldovan Defence Minister Anatolie Nosatii said the acquisition would improve the army’s logistical and operational capabilities, while helping align military standards and strengthen interoperability with Romania.

Officials also indicated that Bucharest and Chisinau could extend their cooperation under SAFE to include air-defence and anti-drone technologies.

Both countries face growing security challenges stemming from Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Moldova, which borders Ukraine and lies close to the war-affected Black Sea region, has become concerned about the risks posed by Russian military activity and hybrid operations.

Although constitutionally neutral, Moldova has stepped up efforts to modernise its armed forces and strengthen cooperation with Western partners. Romania, an EU and NATO member sharing a border with Moldova, has been one of its strongest supporters, providing political, economic and security assistance as Chisinau pursues closer integration with the European Union.

The SAFE programme, adopted by the EU in 2025, provides up to €150 billion in loans to member states for joint defence procurement. It is designed to accelerate military investment, strengthen Europe’s defence industry and reduce reliance on non-European suppliers.

The framework also allows eligible non-EU partner countries, including Moldova, to participate in certain joint procurement arrangements.

articles.title: Poland’s Rule-of-Law Crisis Deepens as Rival Judges Claim Control of Top Court
articles.body:
A decade-long dispute over who controls Poland’s highest court escalated over the weekend, when a group of judges sought to remove its leadership, police were deployed to the building, and President Karol Nawrocki cut short a foreign trip to intervene.

The next flashpoint is seen on Tuesday, November 3, when Anna Korwin-Piotrowska – one of the five judges elected by the current parliamentary majority but prevented from taking up their duties by the country’s president – has called a general assembly of Constitutional Tribunal judges to approve the court’s proposed budget for 2027. With the existing leadership, led by the court’s president Bogdan Swieczkowski, continuing to dispute her authority, it remains unclear whether the meeting can proceed as planned.

The battle over the makeup of the Constitutional Tribunal, which has the power to overturn laws that violate Poland’s constitution and should act as an independent check on government and parliament, dates back to 2015, when both the outgoing centrist government and its right-wing successor made contested appointments to it. During Law and Justice’s (PiS) subsequent eight years in power, major reforms to the judiciary raised concerns over political interference and brought Poland into prolonged conflict with European institutions over the state of the rule of law in the country.

Reversing those reforms was among Donald Tusk’s central campaign promises before his coalition took office in 2023 and his pro-European government has made restoring the court’s independence an essential part of repairing the country’s democratic institutions. The Tusk-led government has since refused to recognise the Tribunal’s legitimacy in its current form, but attempts to change the system through legislation have been blocked by opposition-aligned presidents.

The immediate deadlock concerns five judges elected by the current parliament whom Nawrocki has refused to swear in. These judges subsequently took their oaths without him, but the Tribunal’s leadership prevented them from hearing cases. In October, the Venice Commission, the Council of Europe’s constitutional advisory body, concluded that the president could not use his role in the appointment process to obstruct duly elected judges from taking office.

However, PiS and President Nawrocki accuse Tusk of using unlawful methods to replace the court’s leadership with judges sympathetic to his government.

The competing claims came to a head on Friday, when the five judges attempted to assert their authority over the Tribunal. Korwin-Piotrowska announced the suspension of its president, Swieczkowski, and his deputy, and declared herself the court’s acting head. The existing leadership rejected the move, leaving the institution with rival claims to authority.

Separately, Justice Minister Waldemar Zurek sought to have Swieczkowski and his deputy, Bartlomiej Sochanski, stripped of judicial immunity, potentially paving the way for criminal charges over their alleged obstruction of the Tribunal’s work.

The announcement brought more protesters to the Tribunal’s grounds in Warsaw, where supporters of the opposition had already been demonstrating for weeks against attempts by the newly elected judges to take up their posts. Senior PiS politicians joined the crowd, while police increased their presence around the building.

Meanwhile, President Nawrocki cut short a state visit to Senegal, ordering his plane to turn around over Spain and return to Warsaw. He arrived at the Tribunal in the early hours of Saturday, challenged the authority of the judges seeking to take control, and helped the court’s deputy president enter the building.

“Last night, Poland’s constitutional order was violated, and a constitutional state institution was forcibly taken over,” Nawrocki said in a statement issued shortly after 05:00 on Saturday morning. He demanded that police withdraw from the premises and announced emergency consultations with parliamentary party leaders.

In a televised address on Saturday evening, Prime Minister Tusk defended the intervention, accusing PiS and the PiS-aligned presidents Andrzej Duda and his successor Nawrocki of perpetuating the crisis. “Nobody had any doubt that the Tribunal, in the form imposed by PiS, was not a real court,” he said, arguing that repeated attempts to resolve the dispute through legislation had been blocked.

Tusk compared the situation to a thief who steals an elderly woman’s handbag, then complains of violence when caught, while bystanders suggest dividing the stolen money between the thief and the victim. “On certain matters, there can be no compromise,” he said.

A constitutional reset to end an undignified row?

Poland’s Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights, a leading civil liberties organisation, questioned whether Friday’s intervention by the government would help restore the Tribunal’s authority, calling the escalation “extremely harmful”.

“The confrontations between judges and the President of the Republic of Poland outside the entrance to the Tribunal building undermine the dignity and authority of state institutions,” the organisation said in a statement.

The European Commission weighed in on Saturday, backing the Polish parliament’s authority to appoint Tribunal judges. Meanwhile, US Ambassador Tom Rose warned that crowds outside the court risked worsening an already volatile situation. “The last thing Poland needs is a confrontation that spirals out of control,” he wrote on X, while stressing that Washington did not intend to interfere in Poland’s domestic affairs.

With parliamentary elections scheduled for 2027, Tusk’s coalition faces pressure to deliver on its promise to restore judicial independence, while the opposition has made resistance to the government’s intervention a central issue. In August, Tusk announced that he was determined to ensure the newly elected judges could take up their posts at the Tribunal by September, even if the process was not particularly elegant. Speaking at the Campus Polska Przyszlosci event, he said he needed to be certain that “our judges will enter that building”.

On Saturday afternoon, Nawrocki held meetings with parliamentary party leaders to discuss possible solutions. Among the proposals put forward by parties as far apart as the left-wing Razem and the far-right Confederation was a constitutional reset of the Tribunal, involving the replacement of all its sitting judges with a new bench appointed through a cross-party agreement.

articles.title: Bulgaria’s Presidential Election Winner Pledges Reset with Russia
articles.body:
Bulgaria’s acting President, Iliana Iotova, cemented a five-year mandate after winning the runoff election on Sunday. Backed by the Progressive Bulgaria government and her former Bulgarian Socialist Party, BSP, Iotova won 57.6 per cent of votes cast against the pro-EU opposition candidate, Andrey Gyurov, on 39.5 per cent. Turnout was low at 29.1 per cent, but higher than the all-time low of 22.98 per cent registered in the first round on October 25.

“People believed in our way of politics, which pledged dialogue, conversations, searching for decisions, coordination,” Iotova said on Sunday evening in a briefing that Prime Minister Rumen Radev also attended and where he answered most of the questions.

“Bulgarians chose the future instead of the past, they chose peace, stability, normalcy”, said Radev, both of them dodging questions on the low turnout.

Iotova built her campaign as “the President of peace”: she has pledged to offer a more balanced attitude towards Russia and be skeptical about further military aid to Ukraine. She has also called for Bulgaria to be less obedient to the EU.

“If you say yes to everything, which was Bulgaria’s case for decades, you are voiceless … but things have changed a lot, times have changed in the EU, too”, Iotova said in a TV debate with Andrey Gyurov.

In an interview on October 30 on YouTube with two pro-Russian commentators, she said: “I don’t see Russia as an enemy state … I hope Russia will take part in Europe’s future security architecture.”

During her campaign, Iotova was criticised, along with Prime Minister and Progressive Bulgaria leader Rumen Radev, for remaining elusive about drone attacks in the Black Sea, including in Bulgaria’s zone, and for a lack of preparedness.

Her Vice will be Kiril Valchev, Director of the Bulgarian News Agency, the country’s official newswire, his nomination raising questions about Bulgaria’s media freedom and political ties.

After her victory on Sunday, Iotova said all the criticism from the opposition had been a form of aggressive political attacking, adding: “But we didn’t allow ourselves this speech of hate.”

Iotova was born in 1964 in Sofia. She worked as a TV presenter and news editor at Bulgarian National Television in the 1990s. Her time there is remembered for a controversy from 1995, when, on air, she prioritized coverage of then-Socialist Prime Minister Zhan Videnov doing a traditional dance, or horo, at a public event instead of covering the death of 14 soldiers during an accident – the case became colloquially known as “the blood horo”.

Iotova’s involvement with the Moscow-aligned Bulgarian Socialist Party started in 1997, first as a head of the party’s press office. She joined the party аs Bulgaria was going through an economic crisis and was pressured by mass protests aimed at Socialist-led cabinets.

Iotova became an MP in 2005, when the BSP clung to power through a coalition with the NDSV, the National Movement for Stability and Progress, the now faded party of former monarch Simeon Saxe-Coburg-Gotha.

She became a Member of the European Parliament in 2007 and again in 2014.

In 2016, she resigned from the EP to become a Vice President when Rumen Radev won his first term.

She remained in position until January 2026 when, following months of speculation, Radev resigned from the Presidency to form his own party, Progressive Bulgaria, which won the April elections. This made Iotova acting President, while Radev became the first politician to have served both as President and Prime Minister.

articles.title: ‘Life on Hold’: Poland’s Immigrants Face Years Waiting for Residence Permits
articles.body:
For seven years, Necati has called Poland home. The Turkish software engineer works for an international company in Gdansk, pays taxes and plans to build his future in the country. He applied for long-term EU residency in December 2024, submitting a complete set of documents. Almost two years later, he is still waiting for a decision.

"Since my EU Blue Card expired in February 2026, my life has been on hold," he tells BIRN. "I cannot travel abroad for client business, visit my family, or make standard cross-border financial transactions."

Necati is one of hundreds of thousands of foreigners caught up in Poland's increasingly overwhelmed immigration system. Over the past decade, the country has quietly undergone a profound transformation: once a place people largely left in search of better opportunities, it has become a destination for workers, entrepreneurs and refugees from across the world. Foreigners now pay 21.5 billion zloty (5.5 billion euros) a year into the pension system, 6.2 per cent of all contributions. But while immigration has become part of everyday life, the institutions meant to manage it have struggled to keep up.

The country's voivodeship offices, however, are far from idle. In the first half of 2026, they granted 190,900 temporary residence permits, a record pace, according to data from the Office for Foreigners compiled by Glos Migranta (Migrant’s Voice), a civic initiative of foreigners in Poland.

Yet applications are outpacing the people processing them. The law generally provides for a 60-day decision period for temporary residence once procedural requirements are met, but the average processing time ranges from 242 days in Malopolska to 658 in Silesia. In Mazovia, which includes Warsaw, the average wait now exceeds a year. And the official figures count only completed cases, excluding those still pending.

When millions of Ukrainians crossed into Poland after Russia’s full-scale invasion, the voivodeship offices were given breathing room. From April 2022, deadlines in certain residence proceedings were suspended, along with the usual legal consequences of administrative delays. That provision, now Article 100d of the special act on assistance to Ukrainian citizens, however, applies to foreigners of every nationality. Initially intended to expire at the end of 2022, it was introduced under the previous Law and Justice government and repeatedly extended under Donald Tusk’s coalition. It now runs until March 4, 2027.

It is precisely this provision that migrant rights campaigners are now challenging. They acknowledge the solution was indispensable in 2022, but argue that almost five years later it has become part of the problem.

“It was meant to be a temporary measure to help the system cope,” says Vladimir Medvedev, co-founder of Glos Migranta. “It should have been lifted two years ago, yet here we are in 2026, and nothing has changed. The system is still not working.”

Under ordinary administrative rules, foreigners can formally challenge delays. Article 100d, however, suspends the deadlines and restricts those remedies, allowing offices to argue that no deadline has technically been breached even after months or years of waiting.

In May 2025, the Supreme Administrative Court refused to apply the provision to the period after June 2024, finding it incompatible with the constitutional right to a fair hearing. The law nevertheless remains in force. In June 2026, the Interior Ministry acknowledged in a letter to Poland’s Ombudsman that courts would likely decline to apply it in similar cases, but maintained that administrative offices must continue enforcing it.

“The Ministry understands the problem and its causes, but in our view, it is not doing enough to resolve it,” Marcin Kusy, director of its Migrants’ Rights Team at the Ombudsman’s Office, tells BIRN.

Since April 2022, the office has received 1,161 complaints concerning the legalisation of residence, and lengthy proceedings are among the most common problems raised by migrants.

“Unfortunately, we’re not talking about months of waiting, but years,” Kusy says. “The uncertainty alone takes a toll on people’s sense of security.”

There are practical consequences, too. Banks often require foreigners to produce valid residence documents before granting access to services, while proof of a pending application may not be enough. For migrants running businesses, being unable to open a bank account can make it impossible to operate.

“I’ve heard of cases where people’s existing accounts were blocked simply because they didn’t receive their new residence permit in time,” Medvedev says. Some, he adds, have resorted to paying taxes and bills in cash at the post office.

International travel presents another obstacle. A pending residence application may allow someone to remain legally in Poland, but without a valid residence card or visa, leaving the country can mean being unable to return, stuck between countries.

For Medvedev, the problem is personal. A software engineer from Minsk, he moved to Poland in 2021 and has since become a Polish citizen. His wife, also Belarusian, has been waiting for a temporary residence permit since October 2025, despite an initial decision deadline of January 2026.

In August, Medvedev built a website and began posting information in Telegram groups. What started as an attempt to understand his wife’s predicament quickly developed into the Glos Migranta (Migrant’s Voice) campaign.

On August 24, around 300 people, mostly Belarusians and Ukrainians but also other migrants and Poles, gathered outside the Mazovian Voivodeship Office in Warsaw to demand shorter waiting times and the restoration of legal safeguards. Getting them there proved difficult. Some prospective participants feared deportation or confrontation with far-right groups, despite the demonstration being legal and protected by police. Others carried fears shaped by life in countries where joining a protest can lead to arrest or worse.

“One of the biggest obstacles was psychological,” Medvedev says. “For people who come from countries where protesting can be physically and legally dangerous, taking to the streets is not an easy decision.”

Beyond repealing Article 100d, the campaign is calling for more staff in immigration offices and reliable public information on application backlogs and processing times.

For some migrants, seeking legal redress has become another lengthy journey.

Necati challenged the Pomeranian voivode’s inaction before the administrative court in Gdansk – and won. But his residence application remains unresolved. The voivode appealed the ruling to the Supreme Administrative Court, which is due to hear the case in December. The appeal, Necati believes, will prolong his wait by at least another year. When he approached the office directly, he said officials advised him to apply for another EU Blue Card, placing him in a second queue that could take 14 to 15 months.

The authorities, meanwhile, point to the sheer scale of the workload. In a written response to BIRN, the Mazovian Voivodeship Office said its foreigners’ department was handling more than 200,000 cases, with an estimated workload of over 3,500 per employee.

The office cited rising application numbers, additional responsibilities without corresponding increases in staff, lengthy recruitment procedures and the complexity of individual cases. Reassigning employees and organising Saturday information sessions had temporarily reduced some backlogs, spokesperson Luiza Jurgiel-Zyla said in the statement, but were “not sufficient to solve the problem”.

“The numerous inquiries, letters and complaints submitted by foreigners, institutions and legal representatives add to our workload,” Jurgiel-Zyla wrote. “Complaints filed with the administrative court require staff to prepare responses, gather documents, correspond with the court and carry out tasks arising from its rulings. The same staff are also responsible for processing residence permit applications.”

Kusy confirmed that foreigners challenging delays are sometimes told they are only adding to the administration’s workload.

The tension extends to requests for public information. When Glos Migranta sought data on immigration proceedings, the Lublin voivode described repeated requests as “harassment of the authority”, while the Pomeranian office accused the applicant of attempting to divert staff from their duties. The Kuyavian-Pomeranian office, asked for comparable figures, responded with two numbers: 43 employees and 21,741 pending cases.

With Poland heading towards the 2027 parliamentary election, migration has become an increasingly contentious political issue. For some of those caught up in the residence permit backlog, the delays have also raised questions about how the Polish state treats foreigners.

“We are just a tool in this big game,” Medvedev says. “Some politicians are for us, some are against us, and they play with that to get more votes.”

The complaints reaching the Ombudsman’s Office reveal what Kusy describes as “a profound sense of disillusionment with the Polish state”.

“These are people who have lived here for years, sometimes decades. They pay taxes, have families and businesses here. Poland is the centre of their lives, yet this is how they are treated,” he says, arguing that foreigners should not have to bear the consequences of the state’s failure to make that system work.

Still, he sees the delays primarily as an organisational failure rather than evidence of deliberate discrimination. “The authorities are well aware of the problem and the pressures behind it,” he says.

“I love Poland and want to build my future here,” Necati admits. “But living in continuous legal limbo, and having to fight the very system I loyally contribute to, has taken a severe toll on my mental wellbeing. I ask for no special privileges, only fair, timely treatment in accordance with Polish and EU law.”

Medvedev worries that experiences like these could erode migrants’ trust in democratic institutions. “Many people fled dictatorships and came to Poland specifically because it is a democratic European country where human rights should be respected. But in reality, we are facing systemic discrimination at the state level,” he says.

Yet Medvedev draws a distinction between the failures of Poland’s immigration system and a failure of democracy itself: “We are fighting this failure using legal, democratic tools. We want to fix and improve a system we believe in, not tear it down.”

articles.title: Exhibition in Kosovo Capital Asks What Antifascism Means Today
articles.body: This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp At the entrance to a former prison in Pristina, a flag bearing three arrows is the first clue to what awaits visitors inside. The symbol, long associated with antifascism, has been reimagined by Kosovar visual artist Kemil Bekteshi - the arrows’ peaks depict the mountains of Kosovo, and there’s the beak of a black bird in reference to the double-headed eagle symbol cherished by Albanians across the Balkans. “This is a very old anti-fascist symbol,” said Julian Rieken. “It comes from the dismantling of the swastika and reframing it into a leftist symbol and they are trying to reactivate it but in the context of what is happening now.” Rieken is Transnational Curator of Antifascism: Now, a decentralised network of exhibitions that begin and end in Germany but with a particular focus on Eastern and Southeastern Europe and the former Yugoslavia. The exhibitions began this year and will end in 2029, unfolding across 13 different locations and bringing together artists, curators, journalists and researchers in exploring how political violence is remembered, how authoritarian narratives take hold and how resistance can be reimagined. The Pristina chapter, A Bird with a Stone Wing, is being hosted in the Kosovo’s capital’s Prison of Ideals Museum and BIRN’s Reporting House. In the former prison, the old cells contain stories of political repression, socialist memory, women’s resistance, far-right networks and the consequences of war. The exhibition and accompanying research project poses the question: what does anti-fascism mean today? “This place carries so many different and complex histories that can speak a lot about resistance, about oppressed groups, groups that are only oppressed if a certain regime is in place,” Kalas Liebfried, Initiator and Artistic Director. For Rieken, the exhibition is not only about revisiting the past, but an attempt to understand how authoritarianism can reappear under different conditions. “We see a lot of the term fascism, a lot of fascist sort of resurgencies, but there’s very little definition of what it is now,” he told BIRN. “The question is not: ‘Is there fascism?’ But ‘How much fascism is there?’ ‘Where is it?’ and ‘How can we work against it?’” Pristina prison-turned-museum. Photo: BIRN Antifascism: Now began in Munich, a city that was central to the rise of Nazism. Pristina is the first leg outside Germany, and part of a region synonymous with antifascism during World War Two and the emergence of the Non-Aligned Movement during the Cold War that followed. This history fed into the wars of the 1990s when federal Yugoslavia fell apart, and is still argued over today. “Pristina is a challenging place to begin the international programme,” Rieken said. The Prison of Ideals Museum was once a site of political detention and violence, during the socialist period and after, when Kosovo was ruled from Belgrade under Slobodan Milosevic. It ceased to exist as a prison in 2015. In what was once the prison shaving room is now an installation by Italian artist Stefano Romano, called Songs for the Present Tense, a performance co-written by current women inmates of the correctional centre in Lipjan/Lipljan, some 25 kilometres south of Pristina. “If you listen to the performance, they all speak about freedom, guilt, paying the price of their actions,” said Romano. Another cell contains paintings by artist Vigan Nimani depicting, among others, Yugoslav leader Josip Broz Tito, while filmmaker Blerta Haziraj highlights the Antifascist Front of Women, known as AFZ, and the history of women partisans in Kosovo. The exhibition also looks at violence suffered by LGBTQ+ communities, including a video installation by Igor Grubic revisiting anti-LGBTQ+ in Serbia in 2001. A different kind of confrontation appears in work by Jonas Hoschl, created in collaboration with the recherche-nord collective and Rashad. Played on a TV placed in one of the prison cells, it shows journalists’ encounters with far-right networks at a pub in a small German town popular with local extremists. Xheve Krasniqi Lladrovci’s wedding dress displayed at Reporting House in Pristina along letters to her husband during his jail term. photo: BIRN At the Reporting House Museum, the exhibition moves from the architecture of imprisonment to the ways journalism and personal testimony shape historical memory. The question of who holds the camera and who is seen through its lens is addressed. It features a painting of a photograph of Albanian migrants arriving in Italy by ship during the exodus that followed the fall of communism in Albania in the early 1990s. The photograph captures an unusual reversal: an Albanian migrant, Armando Lulaj, photographed journalists as they photographed the arriving migrants. Those who were the subjects of the image turned the lens on the people documenting them. The painting was commissioned by Lulaj, who asked artist Zef Shoshi from the Manifesto Collective to produce what Lulaj described as his “last socialist painting”. It is displayed above a real human skull, bringing together migration, artistic memory and the physical traces of human life. “I am glad we made this part of the museum, as the first documentation of the exodus in Albania we have in the museum,” said BIRN Kosovo executive director Jeta Xharra. Also in Reporting House, ‘A Wall Divides Us’ presents dozens of letters exchanged by Kosovo Albanian activists Xheva Krasniqi-Lladrovci and Fehmi Lladrovci between 1985 and 1990, coinciding with Milosevic’s rise to power in Serbia, growing repression of Kosovo Albanians, and the twilight of federal Yugoslavia. Lladrovci was imprisoned in the former Yugoslavia for his agitation for Albanian rights. He and Krasniqi-Lladrovci had been engaged for just over a month when he was imprisoned. Their communication continued throughout his detention. Xharra said it was “rare to find this much passion and political energy within the same letters”, presented publicly for the first time in almost 40 years, “It particularly impressed me how Xheva was teaching the elderly generation how to read and write [in order to write to their dissident sons in jail] and arguing for more education for young Kosovo Albanian girls who were abandoning school when Milosevic closed Kosovo public schools in 1990.” Alongside letters, the exhibition includes the red outfit Krasniqi-Lladrovci wore when she got engaged, and the ammunition vest she was in when she was killed in 1998 alongside Lladrovci while fighting Serbian security forces. ‘Antifascism: Now’ exhibition. photo: BIRN Also in BIRN’s Reporting House, The Camp Guard is an award winning, 40-minute interview with Esad Landzo, a former guard at the Celebici prison camp in Bosnia and Herzegovina during the 1992-95 war. Landzo was convicted by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, ICTY, for crimes against prisoners, including murder, torture and the infliction of severe suffering. After serving his sentence, he moved to Helsinki, Finland. “This country gave me a second chance at life and I’ll forever be grateful,” Landzo tells Croatian journalist Barbara Matejcic. The audio interview follows his journey from denial to remorse. “This is the only war criminal in former Yugoslavia who actually showed remorse for his victims, admitting guilt,” said Matejcic. “I found no other war criminal indicted ever showed remorse.” For Gazmend Ejupi, curator of the Reporting House museum, the project’s ambition extends beyond the individual artworks. “For me, it’s not just an exhibition,” he said. “It’s a project with the potential to be an art movement.” That ambition is reflected in the structure of A Bird with a Stone Wing, which evokes the image of a bird trying to fly while weighed down by history. It inhabits the contradiction of moving forward with histories that cannot simply be left behind. The exhibition in Pristina runs until November 28.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: Russia planning new large-scale attack on Ukraine targeting energy and logistics infrastructure
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said, citing intelligence reports, that Russia is preparing to carry out a new large-scale attack on Ukraine.

Source: Zelenskyy in his evening address on 2 November

Quote: "We have intel that Russia is preparing a new massive attack on our country – primarily targeting energy and logistics."

Details: Zelenskyy said the Russians are counting on the world's attention being focused on "the American midterms, and what is happening here in Ukraine, along with our difficulties with air defence and Patriot missiles, will be overlooked".

"We need signals from the world to Russia that will make them feel that terror is no good, that it will bring no gains, and that as long as this war continues, their oil will burn, and they will not be able to make money doing business with the world," the president noted.

Zelenskyy stressed that "we must not play games" when it comes to Russia's oil and gas revenues. Russia must be put under such pressure that it has no alternative but to end the war.

Quote: "America can do this, the world can do this. These Russian killings must be stopped. And we in Ukraine are quite rightly responding to every Russian attack on our people and our cities."

articles.title: Polish security forces prepare for possible sabotage on border with Russia's Kaliningrad Oblast
articles.body:
Polish police, working alongside the armed forces, the border guard and the security services, have established a special operations headquarters for a preventive security operation in the Warmian-Masurian and Podlaskie voivodeships.

Source: Marek Boroń, Commander-in-Chief of the Polish National Police, on Polish radio station RMF FM, as reported by European Pravda

Details: Preventive measures are being taken in response to reports that acts of sabotage may be carried out on the border with Kaliningrad Oblast in the coming days.

"This is directly related to the situation in our country today, namely acts of diversion and sabotage, this hybrid crime and the activities of Eastern secret services," Boroń explained.

The operation is being conducted by the police. Its command centre is located at the National Police Headquarters. The regional police headquarters in Olsztyn and Białystok are also involved.

The authorities were warned last week by military intelligence and allied intelligence services that sabotage could take place on the border with Russia, including incursions by armed groups.

Quote: "The police are ensuring security in the Królewiec district in case of possible incidents that could lead to acts of sabotage.

To this end, reinforcements from police departments in several voivodeships have arrived in the border area. This follows information we have also received from external services. We must ensure the safety of citizens living there, as well as protecting facilities and responding to any situations that could pose a threat to the public."

Details: Boroń denied any connection between the police mobilisation and the political crisis surrounding Poland's Constitutional Tribunal, where a dispute over the court's leadership has sparked protests and a confrontation between the government and the opposition.

Support Ukrainska Pravda on Patreon to help us keep reporting!

articles.title: Russia has attacked Ukraine with 171 drones during the day
articles.body:
Russian forces attacked Ukraine with 171 drones during the day on 2 November. Ukrainian air defence downed 139 of the drones.

Quote: "During the day on 2 November (from 06:30 to 19:00), the enemy attacked Ukraine with 171 attack drones (103 jet-powered), Gerbera UAVs and drones of other types, as well as 10 S8000 Banderol/Dan-Ts.

Early reports indicate that during this period, air defence shot down or jammed 139 UAVs (78 jet-powered) and eight S8000 Banderol/Dan-Ts."

Details: The Air Force added that around 20 attack drones are still in Ukrainian airspace.

Your support on Patreon helps us keep the news free and accessible.

articles.title: From Cannes to the presidency: France's new right-wing contender
articles.body:
In less than a month, David Lisnard has gained more than 300,000 followers on social media. His political movement, Nouvelle Énergie, claims to have surpassed 81,000 members, compared with around 55,000 a week earlier.

Until recently, the 57-year-old mayor of Cannes was relatively unknown outside French political circles. Now, he is attracting national attention ahead of the 2027 presidential election.

The electoral picture is more restrained. His online expansion has been remarkable, but it has yet to produce comparable levels of electoral support.

A survey conducted on 17–19 October gave Lisnard between 5.5% and 7% of first-round voting intentions,

depending on the candidates included

What makes Lisnard particularly interesting is the programme accompanying his sudden popularity. At a time when France's traditional right is struggling to distinguish itself from Emmanuel Macron's centrism and the nationalist right, Lisnard is defending an ambitious programme of economic liberalisation, drastic public-spending cuts and decentralisation. He couples these proposals with conservative positions on immigration, security and national authority.

For a country where economic liberalism has rarely inspired mass electoral enthusiasm, Lisnard's sudden popularity is striking. Whether voters are embracing his economic ideas or simply the man promoting them is far less certain.

Lisnard is hardly a newcomer to politics. He began his career in local government, became mayor of Cannes in 2014 and was elected president of the Association of French Mayors (AMF) in 2021.

He developed Nouvelle Énergie from a local political initiative into a national movement before leaving Les Républicains (LR) in March 2026 to pursue his presidential ambitions independently.

Lisnard has built his political reputation in Cannes, where he was re-elected for a third term in March with more than 81% of votes cast. His list won 45 of the 49 council seats, although fewer than half of registered voters participated.

Lisnard presents Cannes as evidence that public administration can be made more efficient without sacrificing investment. According to the municipality's 2025 accounts, the city's debt has fallen by nearly €82 million since 2014, while €72.5 million was invested during 2025 alone.

An independent audit by the regional chamber of accounts confirmed that Cannes had maintained sound finances and improved its management. It also found that transfers of responsibilities to the intermunicipal authority contributed to reductions in municipal expenditure.

Cannes's substantial tourism-related revenues further distinguish it from most French municipalities.

These qualifications do not negate Lisnard's record, but they complicate his argument that the same methods could be applied to France as a whole. A municipality benefiting from international tourism and major commercial events operates under very different financial and institutional constraints from the French state.

Nevertheless, his experience gives him an established political base.

Unlike a candidate whose notoriety originates entirely online, Lisnard had spent decades building relationships with elected officials before acquiring a much larger national audience.

The speed of that expansion has surprised even experienced political observers. According to Le Monde, he gained more than 300,000 social-media followers from late September to mid-October, with much of the increase concentrated on Instagram. His slogan, "something is happening" spread rapidly across social platforms.

Nouvelle Énergie, meanwhile, claimed 81,547 registered members and a database of 1,830 elected officials on 24 October.

Neither figure has been independently audited, and the latter does not necessarily represent politicians affiliated exclusively with the movement. Whatever the explanation for the rapid increase in visibility, Lisnard has succeeded in drawing attention to a political project that had previously received limited national exposure.

At the centre of Lisnard's programme is a severe diagnosis of the French economic model. He argues that decades of expanding public expenditure, taxation and regulation have weakened competitiveness, discouraged enterprise and left France dependent on borrowing to sustain a state it can no longer afford.

His proposed remedy is extensive. Lisnard wants to reduce annual public expenditure by €80 billion during his first year in office and by at least €200 billion by the end of the presidential term. His longer-term ambition reaches €300 billion.

His argument is that France taxes employment and production too heavily,

making companies less competitive while preventing employees from receiving a sufficient share of what their work costs employers. Lower contributions, he believes, would improve purchasing power and encourage employment without relying on further borrowing.

The programme extends well beyond taxation. Lisnard advocates greater labour-market flexibility, the elimination or consolidation of public agencies, a reduction in administrative staffing and a transfer of responsibilities away from central government.

On pensions, he supports raising the legal retirement age to 65 and introducing a compulsory funded component alongside the existing pay-as-you-go system.

The scale of these proposals deserves attention. Cutting €200 billion from annual public expenditure would require changes extending far beyond administrative efficiency.

France's social insurance, pensions, healthcare and public services account for a substantial proportion of government spending. Decisions about their financing inevitably affect the distribution of resources between citizens, businesses and generations.

There is also a difference between reducing public expenditure and reducing the fiscal deficit. Lisnard proposes returning most of the savings to workers and companies through lower contributions and taxation. Under his stated allocation, only €40 billion of the €200 billion would go directly towards debt reduction.

His campaign maintains that the necessary savings have been identified. Their feasibility, timing and effects on public services require independent examination.

French voters have repeatedly demonstrated their attachment to public services and social protection, including when supporting parties that favour greater economic freedom.

Lisnard nevertheless sees the existing welfare-state model as exhausted. In a recent interview, he argued that France needed to develop a new system rather than continue financing an increasingly expensive one through debt.

His liberalism also has clear limits.

On security, Lisnard advocates tougher criminal penalties, greater police authority and stronger measures against drug trafficking.

His immigration programme proposes substantially reducing residence permits, tightening access to certain benefits and asserting greater national control over migration policy, even where that would involve confrontation with European judicial institutions.

In education, he proposes giving schools considerably more autonomy, including greater freedom over admissions and organisation, while reinforcing academic standards.

These positions reflect his understanding of the state's proper role. He wants government to withdraw from areas where he believes individuals, businesses and local authorities can act more effectively, while strengthening its authority over security, justice, education and defence.

His programme therefore combines a substantial reduction in economic intervention with a demanding conception of public order and national sovereignty. Its political coherence depends partly on whether those stronger sovereign functions can be financed alongside the tax and spending reductions he proposes.

Lisnard's sudden visibility comes amid a prolonged struggle over the identity of France's traditional right.

The emergence of Macron's centrist movement weakened Les Républicains by attracting part of its moderate and economically liberal electorate.

At the same time, the Rassemblement National (RN) expanded its support among voters who might previously have identified with the conservative right, particularly on immigration, security and questions of national identity. Lisnard is seeking to establish a position within those divisions.

His relationship with Bruno Retailleau illustrates the difficulties. The two men share conservative positions on immigration, public order and national authority, alongside commitments to controlling public expenditure.

But Lisnard places economic liberalisation at the centre of his programme and has openly challenged the strategy of LR, which Retailleau leads.

Their disagreement is institutional as well as ideological. Lisnard left LR in March after the party rejected his preferred approach to an open presidential primary.

He subsequently called for a broader selection process capable of bringing together competing currents of the right.

Lisnard shares some of its positions on immigration and security, but his economic programme differs substantially from the nationalist party's more interventionist approach, particularly concerning social protection, industrial policy and the role of the state in protecting purchasing power. He also rejects withdrawal from the European Union, advocating cooperation between sovereign European states while opposing further political centralisation.

His growing influence has nevertheless begun to affect relations within the traditional right. On 21 October, Lisnard met Retailleau again to discuss the possibility of avoiding competing presidential candidacies, including through a primary. No agreement was reached.

From online popularity to political power

His foreign-policy positions also deserve attention, particularly in Ukraine.

Lisnard has repeatedly supported Ukraine against Russia's invasion and advocated strengthening European defence production. He has personal experience of cooperation with Ukrainian authorities: Cannes established a partnership with Lviv in 2022, followed by a medical cooperation agreement with the UNBROKEN rehabilitation network in March 2024.

He favours stronger European defence capabilities while maintaining that political sovereignty should remain principally with individual states. He has also argued for restoring structured diplomatic dialogue with Russia after the war.

His positions on Ukraine's eventual EU accession and specific post-war security guarantees remain less clearly defined.

For now, the most striking feature of Lisnard's candidacy is the speed with which a long-established local politician has acquired a national audience. His political organisation and economic convictions existed well before the recent surge in attention. What has changed is the number of people his speech reaches.

Whether that enthusiasm represents a growing constituency for economic liberalism remains uncertain. France's traditional right has long struggled to reconcile its commitment to lower public expenditure with an electorate that continues to value extensive social protection.

Lisnard has demonstrated his ability to govern a city and, more recently, to attract a national audience.

Governing France would involve a different test. His proposed reforms would require a parliamentary majority willing to reshape public expenditure on a scale rarely attempted in modern French politics.

articles.title: Zelenskyy's defence tech adviser announces protective "dome" over Kyiv that interferes with Shahed radio communications – photos
articles.body:
Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, an adviser to the Ukrainian president on defence technologies, has said a protective "dome" has been created over Kyiv that disrupts the radio communications used by Shahed drones.

Details: Beskrestnov explained that Russian drone operators use mesh radio communications to control Shahed loitering munitions remotely, so a protective dome had to be established over Kyiv to interfere with these signals.

Quote: "The task was large-scale and ambitious: a huge amount of work had to be completed across the entire city in just a few weeks.

All the major manufacturers of electronic warfare equipment were involved in the process, working around the clock to produce and install the equipment. The General Staff, the Ministry of Defence, the Ministry of Internal Affairs, the National Security and Defence Council, the President's Office and other units of the Armed Forces of Ukraine worked on the operation. The president supervised the operation throughout."

Details: Beskrestnov said the operation was complex both technically and organisationally.

Quote: "We are talking about many hundreds of locations across the city for antennas and equipment. This operation has forced the enemy to pause, upgrade their Shaheds and look for other solutions."

Your support on Patreon helps us keep the news free and accessible.

articles.title: Twenty-six killed in Russian aerial bomb attack on school used to distribute humanitarian aid in Zaporizhzhia Oblast – photos, video
articles.body:
Russian forces have bombed a school used to distribute humanitarian aid in Komyshuvakha, Zaporizhzhia Oblast. Twenty-six people, including police officers and first responders, are known to have been killed, five injured and 27 reported missing.

Source: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on X (Twitter); Mykhailo Semikin, Head of Zaporizhzhia Oblast Military Administration; Ukraine's State Emergency Service

Quote from Zelenskyy: "An utterly horrific Russian attack on the settlement of Komyshuvakha in the Zaporizhzhia region. Since this morning, the settlement has been hit several times by aerial bombs. The strikes targeted a school used for humanitarian purposes – people were receiving humanitarian aid there."

Details: Zelenskyy said that after the initial aerial bomb strike, the Russians launched a repeat attack with nine more bombs, hitting the shelter where people were taking cover.

"Tragically, 18 people have already been reported killed. My condolences to their families and loved ones. Five people have been injured. A rescue operation is underway at the site, and the search for people continues. It is extremely difficult. Military forces, first responders, and special services are involved," the president reported.

Zelenskyy said the Russian forces could not have been unaware that humanitarian aid was distributed at the school every week to local residents who had remained in Komyshuvakha.

Quote from Zelenskyy: "And this is further proof that Russia wants no de-escalation and no real justice. After the humanitarian operation in Oleshky, there was a moment when the next steps could have shown that progress towards peace was possible. With these killings, Russia is sending an entirely opposite signal: Russia is counting on more killings.

There must be a response to this – a response from the world. A strong and tough response. A response to Russia. And support for Ukraine. We must protect lives."

Update: Semikin reported that Russian forces struck the centre of the village with at least nine FAB-3000 guided aerial bombs.

"Eighteen people have been killed, including a police officer and two State Emergency Service personnel. Five people have been injured. A further 27 people are still missing," he wrote.

Search and rescue operations are ongoing at the scene.

The State Emergency Service reported that the death toll from the Russian airstrike had risen to 24, including two emergency workers and four police officers. A further five people have been reported injured, including two first responders.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in his evening address that 26 people are known to have been killed.
