articles.title: (Not) PTSD: The Ukrainian experience
articles.body:
In late September, headlines around the world carried a striking claim: "Nearly one in three Ukrainian civilians has PTSD or complex PTSD." It came from a new study by British and Ukrainian researchers, published in the European Journal of Psychotraumatology.

We treat war trauma in soldiers and civilians, in Ukraine and in the United States. We have no doubt that this war is causing enormous psychological harm. But I disagree with how that number has been presented. A natural response to a real and ongoing threat is not, by itself, a mental disorder. Calling a normal reaction to abnormal circumstances an illness does harm. So does downplaying what war does to people. Both mistakes get in the way of what matters most: understanding what each person actually needs, and making sure they get that kind of help.

The researchers surveyed more than 2,500 adults by phone in May 2024. By their count, 25% showed signs of probable PTSD, and another 6% of probable complex PTSD. It is careful work, done under difficult conditions. The problem lies in a single word: "post."

Post-traumatic stress disorder describes what happens after. The danger has passed, yet the body and mind keep reacting as if it were still close. Memories break into the present. The body stays braced for an attack that is no longer coming. The fire is long out, and the alarm keeps ringing.

The questionnaire the researchers used is built on that logic. It asks people to pick one event from the past and rate how it still affects them. That works for a veteran who has come home, or for a survivor years after a disaster. It works far less well for someone who will hear an air-raid siren again tonight.

Ukrainians are living inside a trauma that is still unfolding, day after day. Drones and missiles reach cities hundreds of miles from the front line. In those conditions, sleeping lightly, flinching at loud noises and staying on guard mean the alarm system is doing its job, because the danger is real. A woman in Kharkiv who wakes at every siren is reading her surroundings correctly.

Psychologists have a name for this: continuous traumatic stress. It was first described in places where the threat never went away. In Sderot, an Israeli town that lived under rocket fire for years, researchers found that residents' anxiety was tied to daily danger, not to a single past event, and that it eased when people moved out of range. An alarm that switches off once the danger is gone is an alarm that works.

The study's authors acknowledge this themselves. They write that in today's Ukraine, hyperarousal should be seen as an accurate signal of real threat rather than a "false alarm." They also warn that a tool designed for life after trauma may overcount PTSD among people who are still in danger. The lead author, Dr. Emma Facer-Irwin, noted that people's responses to an ongoing war do not always fit models developed for post-conflict settings. I agree. And when the tool does not fit the situation, the number it produces should not become the headline.

A phone survey is also no substitute for a conversation with a clinician. Questionnaires deliberately cast a wide net so that no one is missed, which is why they usually find more cases than a clinical assessment later confirms.

Read past the headline, and the study tells a different story about Ukrainians. More than 70% of respondents had lived through shelling near their homes. Half have a loved one on the front line. A third were forced to leave home. Yet only 6% showed signs of complex PTSD, the more severe form that can develop after prolonged trauma. That is lower than some earlier studies found. Among the possible reasons, the authors point to a strong sense of national identity, close community ties and mutual support.

Anyone who has spent time in Ukraine has seen this up close. It is the neighbor who sweeps up broken glass the morning after a strike and opens her shop on time. It is the teacher who holds class in a bomb shelter. It is the volunteers who arrive with tea and a generator before the smoke has cleared. These people live and work every day in conditions that are hard to imagine for anyone who has not been through them.

Labels matter. Tell a third of a country that it is sick, and those words can start to come true. People who believe they are broken begin to act broken, and normal reactions to danger start to look like illness.

At the same time, many Ukrainians still find it hard to see a psychologist or psychiatrist because of stigma. So the other half of the message matters just as much. If someone does come in for help, they are genuinely struggling, and that deserves to be taken seriously. Some people will do well after a few sessions; others, soldiers and civilians alike, will need long and intensive therapy. That call belongs to a trained professional who has actually talked with the person, not to a questionnaire or a headline. According to the WHO Mental Health Atlas, Ukraine has about 34 mental health workers per 100,000 people, compared with a European median of 53. That makes it all the more important for each person to get the kind of help they actually need.

None of this means ordinary reactions should simply be endured. A normal reaction can still be exhausting. Scientists call this cost allostatic load: the wear and tear the body pays for months and years in survival mode. Poor sleep, tension, irritability and fatigue are part of that price. When constant alertness keeps you from sleeping, working or simply being present with your family, it deserves attention. And you do not need a diagnosis to get help.

The good news is that an overworked alarm can be turned down, and much of what helps is simple. Slow breathing with long exhales calms the body. Insomnia is treatable, and even apps based on cognitive behavioral therapy help people sleep better. Regular physical activity reduces anxiety. Short group programs, led by trained people without a psychology degree, help those who have lived through war and displacement.

Psychologists who work after mass disasters name five things that help people recover: a sense of safety, calm, belief in one's own and the community's ability to cope, connection with others, and hope. While the war goes on, full safety is out of reach. That makes the other four matter even more, and they are built in kitchens, classrooms and bomb shelters as much as in doctors' offices.

For people whose alarm gets "stuck" and will not switch off, treatments that act directly on the nervous system are also being studied. One of them, stellate ganglion block, an injection that calms a cluster of nerves in the neck, reduced PTSD symptoms more than a placebo procedure in a trial with U.S. soldiers. The Weatherman Foundation offers this treatment to Ukrainian service members.

The study's own conclusions point the way forward. For most people, the authors recommend strengthening community and group support. For those whose symptoms persist, early treatment should target the sense of threat, avoidance and an alarm that will not shut off. That kind of care works, in Ukraine too: in a trial with Ukrainian veterans and displaced people, a structured form of psychotherapy significantly reduced PTSD symptoms. Finding the people who need specialist care will take conversations with clinicians, follow-up over time and tools built for a war that is still being fought.

Ukrainians are not broken. They fall asleep to sirens and get up the next morning to go to work, to school, to the volunteer center. There is strength in that worth recognizing, and exhaustion worth helping with. The way we measure their pain should respect both.

I sincerely thank my colleagues at the Weatherman Foundation for their help in preparing this material:

Meaghan Mobbs, PhD, CEO and President of the Weatherman Foundation. A former U.S. Army officer with a doctorate in clinical psychology from Columbia University, where she specialized in trauma.

Valerii Androsov, Director of the Psychophysiological Rehabilitation Program for the National Police at the Weatherman Foundation. A psychologist in Kyiv since 2017, postgraduate researcher and lecturer at NTU "KhPI".

Lauren Guillaume, Director of the Weatherman Foundation in Ukraine. Holds a Master's degree in Global Policy Studies from the LBJ School of Public Affairs (University of Texas at Austin).

articles.title: Putin has ordered private data centres to allocate capacity for state, says Reuters
articles.body:
Russian owners of non-state data centres will be obliged to reserve 10% of their capacity to ensure the uninterrupted operation of Russia's IT infrastructure under a decree signed by Russian leader Vladimir Putin on Monday.

Details: Putin has instructed the Russian Ministry of Digital Development to compile an inventory of available capacity and space in private data centres across Russia.

A special government commission, to be established under this decree, will be empowered to demand the release of reserved capacities, and operators will be required to provide access within 24 hours of such a decision.

The decree also allows for the temporary use of data centres located abroad, provided that permission is obtained from the Federal Security Service (FSB).

In recent weeks, Russian data centres have become targets of Ukrainian drone attacks: in October, facilities operated by Yandex and Sberbank were hit.

articles.title: No one would dare exclude Ukraine from World Championship elite division, former ice hockey official says
articles.body:
Kalervo Kummola, former vice president of the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF), is confident that Ukraine will not be pushed out of the elite division of the 2027 World Ice Hockey Championship to make room for Russia.

Source: Finnish newspaper Iltalehti

Details: Kummola said he had discussed the issue with the new IIHF president. He stressed that it had been made clear that any decision to exclude Ukraine and replace it with Russia would be impossible to implement, adding that no one would dare to make such a decision.

articles.title: Two boys, 4 and 10, injured in Russian artillery strike on Nikopol
articles.body:
Russian forces have attacked the city of Nikopol with artillery, injuring two brothers aged four and ten.

Source: Oleksandr Hanzha, Head of Dnipropetrovsk Oblast Military Administration

Quote: "Two children have been injured due to a Russian artillery strike on Nikopol."

Details: The four-year-old boy was hospitalised. Medics provided treatment to his ten-year-old brother at the scene, and he will receive treatment at home.

A house was damaged as a result of the attack.

Background: Six people were injured as a result of Russian attacks on Dnipropetrovsk Oblast throughout 1 November.

Support Ukrainska Pravda on Patreon to help us keep reporting!

articles.title: Slovakia joins coalition for return of Ukrainian children abducted by Russia
articles.body:
Slovakia is joining the International Coalition for the Return of Ukrainian Children.

Source: Marek Eštok, Slovak State Secretary for EU Affairs, on X (Twitter), as reported by European Pravda

Details: Eštok said that he met with the ambassadors of Ukraine and Canada on 2 November to formally hand over a diplomatic note confirming Slovakia's accession to the International Coalition for the Return of Ukrainian Children.

Quote: "By joining, Slovakia is contributing to international efforts to ensure the safe return of Ukrainian children who have been unlawfully deported or forcibly transferred during the war."

Details: Eštok stressed that his country's support for Ukrainian children extends beyond this initiative.

Quote: "Slovakia has helped renovate school shelters in Ukraine, organised stays in Slovakia for children of Ukrainian emergency workers and police officers, and welcomed thousands of Ukrainian children into our education system. Our shared goal is to see these children safely reunited with their families and back home."

articles.title: "He devoted many years to saving animals": Veterinarian Serhii Huzenkov killed in Russian attack on Kyiv on 30 October
articles.body:
Serhii Huzenkov, a vet who worked at the Kyiv City Veterinary Medicine Hospital in the Podilskyi district, was killed in a Russian attack on Kyiv on 30 October.

Source: Department of Environmental Protection and Climate Change Adaptation on Facebook

Quote: "Serhii Volodymyrovych devoted many years of his life to veterinary medicine and saving animals at the clinic on Yaroslavska Street, where every day, through his work, knowledge and compassion, he helped those who cannot ask for help in words.

For his colleagues, he was part of a large team, a person who devoted himself to an important cause – preserving animals' lives and health."

Details: In the comments on the post, Serhii is remembered as a kind and friendly person and a true professional.

"Serhii Volodymyrovych treated our Liova. We would have been seeing him for a consultation tomorrow. He was such a kind-hearted and compassionate man. May he rest in peace," Vita Boiko wrote.

"I cannot believe this… On 28 October, Serhii Volodymyrovych neutered two of our dogs. I've been bringing animals to him to be neutered for years. This is horrific," Halyna Holosovska wrote.

The Happy Shore Animal Protection Society, which set up a temporary animal shelter in the Holosiivskyi district, said that right from the start Serhii had cared for the animals and treated every one of them with compassion. He joined the volunteers in walking the dogs and helping in every way.

Background: From the evening of 29 October until the morning of 30 October, Russian forces attacked Kyiv with ballistic missiles and drones. The strikes damaged apartment buildings, cars, a petrol station, a restaurant, a medical facility and a warehouse.

Support Ukrainska Pravda on Patreon to help us keep reporting!

articles.title: Cooperation with Trump and end to military aid for Ukraine: Germany's AfD unveils policy papers
articles.body:
Foreign policy representatives of Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party have presented two position papers calling for closer cooperation with the Trump administration, an end to military aid for Ukraine and a rapprochement with Russia.

Source: European Pravda, citing German newspaper Welt

Details: Markus Frohnmaier, the AfD parliamentary group's foreign affairs spokesperson and deputy leader, fellow deputy leader Stefan Keuter, and Gerold Otten, deputy head of the group's foreign affairs working group, reportedly presented the two position papers in Berlin.

The papers note that the US and Europe are inextricably linked by a shared culture and history. They also mention millions of descendants of German immigrants, adding that figures such as Donald Trump embody this German heritage.

The AfD's foreign policy experts are seeking mutually beneficial, pragmatic transatlantic cooperation and welcome certain aspects of the Trump administration's shift in foreign policy. They support a possible reduction in US troop numbers in Germany and plans not to deploy US missiles there.

In its paper on German-Russian relations, the AfD reiterates its calls to restart the Nord Stream gas pipeline, lift economic sanctions against Russia and end military aid to Ukraine.

The paper does not repeat the condemnation of Russia's invasion of Ukraine issued by the AfD parliamentary group after the full-scale invasion began in 2022. The AfD's foreign policy representatives describe the war in Ukraine as a tragedy that should end as soon as possible. They call for a peace settlement that takes into account the security interests of all parties to the conflict.

They argue that Ukraine should be neither a NATO nor an EU member and should become a neutral state again. Russia, they say, must recognise Ukraine's sovereignty. However, the paper also states that it is unrealistic for Ukraine to regain all its territory, including Crimea. The politicians propose that Ukraine's existence as a state and the territory it retains after a ceasefire or peace agreement should be secured by guarantor countries, preferably those not involved in the current war.

articles.title: Russia steps up use of electronic warfare systems to disrupt Starlink in Crimea and on front line
articles.body:
Russian troops are deploying more electronic warfare (EW) systems to jam Starlink communications.

Source: Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, an adviser to Ukraine's president and a radio technology expert

Quote: "This type of system provides EW coverage for individual sites over an area of approximately 25 sq km. The Russians have deployed these systems to protect almost all key facilities in Crimea and are increasingly using them along the front line."

Details: Beskrestnov noted that these systems previously consisted of six trailers parked side by side at a single site, but Russian forces are now trying to conceal the equipment by spreading it across a wider area.

The systems are built around prime-focus satellite dish antennas approximately one metre in diameter.

Quote: "Regardless of the camouflage used, the systems must have an unobstructed view towards the zenith, which limits the options for concealing them."

Details: Beskrestnov said Russian forces could hide the systems among lorries and also use small car trailers.

He added that EW systems could operate under canopies made of polycarbonate or plastic film. The expert also identified opaque greenhouses as possible places to conceal the equipment. He also considers camouflage nets unlikely to be used in rear areas because they attract attention.

The systems do not necessarily have to be located near electrical substations, as they can also run on generators. According to Beskrestnov, they operate in the 14-14.5 GHz frequency range.

articles.title: Ukrainian human rights chief on talks with Russian counterpart: "I know no other way to bring back our citizens"
articles.body:
Ukrainian Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets has explained that his role requires him to keep his emotions in check in order to ensure productive negotiations with his Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova. He said the two officials have been discussing a possible humanitarian mission covering six settlements in Kherson Oblast.

Source: Lubinets at a press conference on 2 November

Details: Lubinets was asked about his diplomatic attitude towards Lantratova.

Quote: "I don't know of any way to bring back our citizens other than through direct negotiations with the Russian side. In my view, if you adhere to diplomatic etiquette, you automatically have a better chance of a positive outcome.

The first meeting I held with Lantratova was five days after she was appointed. I raised the issue of Oleshky straight away.

When you see results, when your Russian counterpart calls you Dmytro Valeriiovych [using his patronymic, a respectful form of address – ed.], I see no problem whatsoever in calling her Yana Valerievna."

Details: Lubinets stressed that he is doing this for Ukrainian citizens, even though his personal feelings towards Russia are the same as most Ukrainians'.

He pointed out that if he allowed his emotions to affect his work, it would undermine the outcome of the negotiations.

He also said the Russian occupation forces did not subject the evacuees to filtration procedures in the course of the humanitarian mission in Oleshky.

Lubinets said he and Lantratova have also discussed possible humanitarian missions in the Oleshky hromada.

He expressed hope that the two sides will be able to apply the experience gained to other areas in the future.

Lubinets added that he and Lantratova have developed joint proposals and initiatives on humanitarian issues.

articles.title: Russia, accused of mass torture, withdraws from convention against torture
articles.body:
Russia has officially withdrawn from the European Convention for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment.

Source: press service for the Council of Europe, as reported by European Pravda

Details: The decision on Russia's withdrawal from the Convention entered into force on 1 November.

Russia notified the Council of Europe of its decision on 30 October 2025, and its denunciation of the Convention took effect one year after the date of notification.

Alan Mitchell, President of the Committee for the Prevention of Torture (CPT), said: "The withdrawal of the Russian Federation marks the end of the CPT's monitoring mandate in the country. It also marks the end of any independent monitoring of places of deprivation of liberty inside the Russian Federation."

Details: Russia had been a party to the Convention since 1998. Between 1998 and 2021, the CPT carried out 30 visits to Russia, during which it visited more than 450 places of deprivation of liberty. However, Russia was the only state party to the Convention that refused to authorise publication of the committee's visit reports and responses to them. Consequently, the Council of Europe was able to publish only four reports on visits to Russian places of deprivation of liberty.

The unpublished reports concern periodic and ad hoc visits, including 10 visits to Chechnya and the North Caucasus between 2000 and 2017.

Since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the CPT has received numerous reports of alleged acts of torture and ill-treatment in detention facilities by Russian officials not only in the occupied territories of Ukraine but also on Russian territory. However, due to the Russian authorities' refusal to cooperate, it has been unable to conduct a visit to independently assess the situation.

The Council of Europe emphasised the contrast between Russia's approach and that of the Ukrainian authorities, which continue to allow the CPT to visit any places of deprivation of liberty on their territory at any time.

Your support on Patreon helps us keep the news free and accessible.

articles.title: Ukraine's human rights commissioner explains why people were not evacuated from Oleshky directly to Kherson
articles.body:
Ukrainian Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets has said that a direct route across the river to Kherson was never considered for the evacuation from temporarily occupied Oleshky, as the front line passes through there and weakening Ukraine's defences would be unacceptable.

Source: Lubinets at a press conference on 2 November

Details: Lubinets noted that the plan for evacuating people was developed in close cooperation with Ukrainian forces.

Quote: "The logistical route was developed taking information from the Armed Forces of Ukraine into account… Nobody ever even suggested [a different route]. On the contrary, I was warned: don't even think about supporting the [Russian] proposal to clear the mines and make it possible to go from Oleshky straight to Kherson. This is the front line, we will not agree to this, we will definitely not do anything that would weaken the defence of Ukraine. That's why that route was never considered."

Details: Lubinets added that the evacuation route was developed with involvement from the Security Service of Ukraine, military intelligence, and testimony from Ukrainians who had previously escaped the occupied city on their own.

"This logistical route was developed taking two main criteria into account: first, the safety of the people, and second, speed," he emphasised.

The commissioner also noted that Ukraine and Russia are in communication regarding regular deliveries of humanitarian supplies to those who have decided to stay in Oleshky.

Quote: "We discussed the possibility of making the delivery of humanitarian aid systematic. We agreed on this directly. Discussions are currently underway on how to do this at least once a month. This is necessary for the survival of citizens who have made the decision to stay in Oleshky, so that they have at least some basic items."

Details: Lubinets said that some residents had chosen to stay in Oleshky, although he did not disclose how many. He stressed that they had personally confirmed to him that they had made the decision of their own free will. Food, water, medicines, fuel for generators and specialised equipment were delivered to support those remaining in the town and its hospital, which is still operating.

articles.title: US delivery of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine will span 3 years starting in 2030
articles.body:
Ukraine will be able to receive the 500 Patriot Advanced Capability-3 (PAC-3) interceptor missiles for its Patriot air defence systems between the fourth quarter of 2030 and the fourth quarter of 2033. Their sale has been approved by the US State Department.

Source: European Pravda, citing an unnamed US State Department official

Quote: "The estimated delivery timeframe for the PAC-3 missiles under the proposed arms sale to Ukraine, announced on 30 October, is from the fourth quarter of 2030 to the fourth quarter of 2033."

Details: The State Department also explained that the conclusion of the corresponding PAC-3 procurement agreement is to take place after it is approved by the US Congress, a process for which 30 days are allocated.

Quote: "Foreign Military Sales agreements are concluded through the signing of a Letter of Offer and Acceptance (LOA). The parties can agree on an LOA after the conclusion of the 30-day US congressional review period."

Support Ukrainska Pravda on Patreon to help us keep reporting!

articles.title: Ukrainian human rights chief says Russian equipment seen in video was used for mine clearance
articles.body:
Ukrainian Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets has said that Russian military equipment seen moving in Sky News footage filmed during the ceasefire in Oleshky was being used for mine clearance under Ukrainian supervision.

Source: Lubinets at a press conference on 2 November

Details: Asked about reports that Russian forces were using the ceasefire in Oleshky to build up troops and equipment, as well as footage showing their movements, Lubinets said the agreements reached with the Russian side explicitly prohibited such activities.

Quote: "We didn't just discuss this. We explicitly stipulated it in the document. The buildup of forces and movement of equipment are prohibited."

Details: Lubinets added that each side had appointed a representative responsible for monitoring compliance with the agreements. The parties initially agreed to check compliance every two hours and provide periodic public updates on the findings.

Lubinets said that before the ceasefire ended, he had met with Ukraine's designated representative and members of the defence forces. Following checks, both sides confirmed that no violations had been recorded.

He added that on 2 November, after seeing reports of alleged violations, he personally reviewed the footage, contacted Ukraine's designated representative and held a meeting.

Quote: "The video clearly shows Russian military equipment marked with red crosses. It was used for mine clearance under strict Ukrainian supervision. Once the mines had been cleared, the equipment returned to its original location.

I won't venture to make any judgements. I'm speaking about what happened under my supervision. The video can be interpreted in different ways."

Previously: Earlier on 2 November, British television news channel Sky News released a report on how Russian forces moved heavy equipment and ammunition in Oleshky under cover of the ceasefire. The journalists were granted exclusive access to the command centre at the headquarters of Ukraine's 34th Marine Brigade, where troops were monitoring Russian movements.

Dmytro Pulinets, commander of the brigade, told Sky News that during the ceasefire, Russian forces had repaired or replaced artillery systems, retaken previously lost positions, rotated troops, brought in reinforcements and equipment, and strengthened their aerial reconnaissance capabilities and fuel supplies.

Ukraine's General Staff also reported that the Russians had used the ceasefire to rotate units, fortify positions, strengthen anti-drone protection on roads and build up logistics.

articles.title: Ukrainian human rights chief says he and Russian counterpart have agreed to present joint proposal to Melania Trump
articles.body:
Ukrainian Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets says he and his Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova, have agreed to approach US First Lady Melania Trump with a proposal to extend the humanitarian mission in Oleshky to other settlements where the situation is dire.

Source: Lubinets at a press conference on 2 November

Quote: "I know that the Russian side, Ombudswoman Lantratova, also held a press conference today and formally approached Melania Trump with a proposal to organise similar humanitarian missions in other settlements.

I now want to do exactly the same. This is a proposal we have developed together. We are both approaching Melania Trump to extend this successful practice to other settlements, not just those in Kherson Oblast."

Your support on Patreon helps us keep the news free and accessible.

articles.title: Geladze Leaves Deputy Interior Minister Post, Joins Oil And Gas Corporation Board
articles.body:
Former Interior Minister and State Security Service Chief Geka Geladze has left his latest position as Deputy Interior Minister and reportedly joined the three-member supervisory board of the Georgian Oil and Gas Corporation (GOGC), a state-run company managing national energy systems.

Georgian Dream Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze issued a corresponding order on November 2, while pro-government media sources reported that Geladze has been appointed as a member of the GOGC board. The board’s other members are Chairman Vazha Khidasheli and Deputy Chairman Giorgi Chachibaia, according to the agency’s official website.

Geladze was appointed deputy interior minister on September 15, 2026, a day after he stepped down as head of the State Security Service of Georgia (SSSG), becoming the fourth SSSG head to leave the post in less than two years. At the time, he did not specify the reason for his resignation but said he would continue working “in another agency” following “consultations with the political team.”

Geladze, a former GD Interior Minister, became the fifth head of SSSG since its establishment in 2015, when he took office in April, replacing Mamuka Mdinaradze.

Before heading the SSSG, Geladze served as GD Interior Minister from May 2025. His earlier positions included deputy education minister (2023-2024), head of the Education Ministry’s Human Resources Service (2018-2023), head of the Interior Ministry’s Central Criminal Police Department (2016-2018) and deputy head of the National Probation Agency (2012-2016). He also held other positions at the Interior and Justice ministries and worked in the private sector.

articles.title: Testing finds widespread contamination of dairy products in Armenia
articles.body:
A consumer rights organisation in Armenia says laboratory tests found microbiological irregularities in dairy products from 11 domestic producers, including coliform bacteria in milk, sour cream, and cheese. The findings, which authorities have not confirmed, come three months after a Russian ban on Armenian dairy imports.

Although the consumer group’s findings, published on 30 October concern domestic food safety, the results emerge against a politically charged backdrop of Russia’s ban on Armenian dairy imports from 27 July. Russia’s Service for Veterinary and Phytosanitary Surveillance (Rosselkhoznadzor) banned the imports, citing alleged ‘milk from infected livestock’. Rosselkhoznadzor also claimed that Armenia lacks a system to confirm the origin and safety of dairy raw materials and fails to monitor agricultural producers.

The dairy ban followed Russian restrictions on Armenian alcohol, flowers, fruit, vegetables, mineral water, and fish. They began before the June parliamentary elections in Armenia. Russian Deputy Prime Minister Aleksei Overchuk has denied introducing any restrictions, calling it ‘usual normal work’.

Babken Pipoyan, the chair of the NGO Informed and Protected Consumer, presented the results in a press briefing. The tests were part of Inclusive Public Control, an initiative the organisation launched to examine the dairy market.

According to Pipoyan, samples came from local dairy producers in Marianna, Ashtarak Kat, Eremyan Products, Tamara and Ani, Marila, Milkin, Bonilat, Biokat, Chanakh, Arzni Katnamterk, and Igit. Most were sampled for milk, sour cream, and cottage cheese.

The samples went to three laboratories that the organisation describes as ‘internationally accredited’: the State Laboratory Services Centre, a state non-commercial organisation within the Food Safety Inspectorate, plus the private FDA Laboratory and Standard Dialog Laboratory.

The test found coliform bacteria, an indicator group commonly used to flag hygiene problems, in 3.2% fat milk from Ashtarak Kat, sour cream from Eremyan Products (25% fat), Arzni Katnamterk (20%), and Bonilat (17%), cottage cheese from nine producers: Tamara and Ani (7%), Marianna (9%), Ashtarak Kat (7%), Eremyan Products (12%), Milkin (9%), Bonilat (9%), Biokat (12%), Chanakh (7%), and Arzni Katnamterk (9%) and Igit’s chechil cheese sticks in 240-gram packs.

Cottage cheese samples also showed deviations in other indicators. Yeast and mould levels were abnormal in products from Bonilat, Tamara and Ani, Arzni Katnamterk, Chanakh, Marila, and Biokat. Lactic acid bacteria levels deviated in samples from Marianna, Chanakh, Marila, and Milkin.

Neither the inspectorate nor the named companies have commented. OC Media has not independently verified the findings.

Ani is an Armenian journalist with a background in multimedia reporting, podcast production and documentary filmmaking. She has a Master´s degree in Media Studies and is interested in stories about migration and post-conflict transformation. Outside of work, she enjoys film festivals, cycling, photography, and baking.

articles.title: Military personnel in Chechnya accused of faking soldiers’ war injuries for compensation
articles.body:
The Grozny Garrison Military Court is hearing a criminal case involving alleged fraud committed by a group of soldiers, who are accused of faking injuries in order to obtain payments under false pretenses. The total amount of damages incurred by the scheme reached ₽90 million ($1.1 million), the court said.

According to investigators, between December 2022 and February 2024, a group arranged for fake injury certificates to be issued to soldiers from a Defence Ministry military unit stationed in the Chechen village of Sernovodskoye. As a result, 30 soldiers received ₽3 million ($37,000) each in compensation for injuries they had not actually sustained. The prosecution alleges that under the scheme the soldiers gave half of each payment to the group running the scheme, the Russian newspaper Kommersant wrote on Sunday.

According to Kommersant’s reporting, the defendants are Aleksandr Stepanchenko, a former senior assistant to the military prosecutor of the town of Shali and a current major in the justice service, Ahmed Kagirov, a Chechen resident, and Rakhman Ganaev, a former Rosgvardia (Russian National Guard) officer. All three have been charged with organised fraud and face up to ten years in prison.

According to investigators, Kagirov and Ganaev used two soldiers from the unit, Zaurbek Viskhanov and Shamkhan Musaev, to find others willing to pass their passport details to Husein Magomadov from Grozny. Magomadov would then produce fake injury certificates in the name of a branch of the 412th Military Hospital in Khankala.

The documents were passed to Stepanchenko, who, according to the prosecution, arranged for them to be checked and forwarded them to the unit’s personnel officer, Ramzan Muzigov. Muzigov issued payment orders and submitted the documents to the financial authorities.

Magomadov has been placed on the wanted list and arrested in absentia. Viskhanov and Musaev were killed in the war, and proceedings against them were discontinued. Muzigov entered into a pre-trial cooperation agreement with the prosecutor's office, and his case was separated into a distinct set of proceedings.

During the preliminary investigation, the three defendants admitted their guilt but later retracted their statements in court. They said they had confessed after an investigator promised to suspend the criminal proceedings against them if they signed contracts with the Defence Ministry to be sent to the war. Stepanchenko was subsequently refused a contract.

Stepanchenko’s defence argues that the case materials contain inconsistencies, particularly regarding the dates on which documents were handed over and money distributed. His lawyer also said that bank statements showed transfers totalling ₽15 million ($185,000) to other individuals whom Kagirov identified as the actual organisers of the scheme. According to the lawyer, these included a former investigator from the military investigative department for the Ussuriysk Garrison. However, the investigator remains a witness in the case. He said he had been helping an acquaintance from his home region by purchasing three foreign-made cars in South Korea at Kagirov’s request, which were subsequently transported to Chechnya.

Kagirov also claimed that the investigator had threatened him and asked him to give false evidence against Stepanchenko. According to the lawyer, the court refused to admit video recordings in which Kagirov spoke about these allegations. The defence intends to seek the return of the case to the prosecutor for further investigation.

None of the 30 soldiers who received the disputed payments have been charged. They remain witnesses in a separate case, which has been suspended. According to Kommersant, the damage caused to the state has not been compensated.

Liza was born and raised in Vladikavkaz and now lives in Prague. She has previously worked for RFE/RL, ASTRA, Belsat, and others. She is currently completing her PhD in German and Slavic Studies at Charles University in Prague, specialising in the study of military and inter-ethnic conflicts in the North Caucasus. In her free time, Liza shoots feature films, writes about cinema, and travels — she has visited exactly 50 countries and is not going to stop there.

articles.title: Taliban Concerned Amid Reports Of US Deportation Of Afghans Via Pakistan
articles.body:
Afghanistan has asked the US government to "act responsibly" amid reports that it plans to deport dozens of Afghans via Pakistan, possibly in the coming days.

The US State Department did not confirm the reported deportation of Afghans, with a spokesman adding in a statement to RFE/RL that "we affirm our position that all countries must be able to manage their borders and immigration processes in a manner that ensures the safety, security, and prosperity of their citizens."

Pakistani officials have remained tight-lipped about the reports. The country's Foreign Ministry did not respond to multiple attempts via direct telephone calls and e-mails for comment.

The California-based nongovernmental organization AfghanEvac said the US government is preparing to deport more than 150 Afghans on a charter flight out of Louisiana, reportedly "as soon as November 2."

Shawn VanDiver, president of the organization, said the flight carrying the Afghans -- including two women -- would land in Islamabad, and that he "does not know what agreement has been reached between Washington and Islamabad on the matter."

In a November 2 statement, Afghanistan's Taliban-led Foreign Ministry urged the United States to respect the "rights and legitimate aspirations" of Afghans facing deportation.

It added that the Taliban authorities were ready to "engage constructively" with Washington, taking into account the "existing realities and legitimate concerns" of both sides.

Quoting three US officials, the New York Times reported on October 30 that the Afghan immigrants are currently being held in Louisiana. The AP also published similar reports, citing what it said were court documents.

Because it has no formal diplomatic relations with the Taliban, the United States cannot arrange for the deportation of the detainees to Afghanistan. They will instead be sent to Pakistan, which would then send them on to Afghanistan.

In an apparent reference to Pakistan, the Taliban said that "third countries should not bargain over the fate of another country's nationals in pursuit of temporary and limited concessions or other considerations."

Once allies for decades, Pakistan and the Afghan Taliban have been in a diplomatic deadlock amid sporadic bloody clashes along the border between the two countries since October 2025.

Pakistan accuses the Afghan Taliban of providing sanctuary to the Tehrik-e Taliban Pakistan (TTP), also known as the Pakistani Taliban, on Afghan soil. The Afghan Taliban rejects the allegations, saying it would not allow anyone to use Afghanistan's territory against another country.

Immigrants' rights organizations have expressed concerns about threats to the lives of those being deported to Afghanistan, saying the immigrants targeted include relatives of people who assisted US forces before the military withdrawal in 2021.

Refugees International (RI), a US-based humanitarian advocacy organization, has asked for a halt to "this and future flights," saying the immigrants face "targeted persecution" from the Taliban.

The group's director, Yael Schacher, said in a statement on November 1 that although "we lack details about the deal with Pakistan," it is known that the "plane will be landing in a country that has engaged in mass forced expulsions to Afghanistan."

In a sweeping deportation campaign, Pakistan has sent approximately 2.5 million Afghans back to their war-torn country since September 2023.

Tens of thousands of Afghans fled their country following the Taliban takeover of Kabul in August 2021, thousands of whom still reside in Pakistan as they await resettlement in third counties.

Tens of thousands of Afghan immigrants are said to be residing in Pakistan.

While many Afghans fled their country fearing retaliatory measures by the Taliban, others escaped to avoid the Taliban bans on civil liberties such as education, music, and freedom of expression. Afghanistan is frequently ranked among the world's worst countries for violations of human rights, and women's rights in particular.

The United Nations has repeatedly warned that the Taliban's ban on girls' education in Afghanistan is creating a "lost generation."

According to the UN figures presented to the Security Council in June, approximately 3.8 million Afghan girls between the ages of 7 and 18 remained out of schools in the country.

Daud Khattak is a senior international correspondent covering the Near East in RFE/RL’s Central Newsroom. He was previously the managing editor of RFE/RL's Radio Mashaal.

articles.title: Arrests, Resignations, Repainting: Here's What's Happening In Postelection Serbia
Trump Says Iran Wants A Deal ‘And It Could Happen’
Supreme Court rejects Trump bid to block 20,000 California ballots
articles.body:
The Trump administration had appealed to the Supreme Court over claims that a list of more than 20,000 ballots in California include non-US citizens.

On the eve of the US midterm elections, the administration of President Donald Trump made a last ditch attempt to sideline over 20,000 mail in ballots in California, claiming non-US citizens are attempting to vote.

The US Justice Department (DoJ), which is run by Trump's former personal attorney Todd Blanche, has claimed to have a list documenting non-US citizens on California's voter rolls.

In mid October, the federal government first filed a lawsuit based on the allegations, which was rejected by a California district court.

On Monday, the DoJ asked for a "limited injunction" directing the state of California to "stop commingling suspected illegal ballots with legal ones" pending the verification of voters' status.

However, hours after the appeal was filed, the Supreme Court said it would decline to stop California from counting the votes.

When the initial lawsuit was filed by the Trump administration earlier in October, Los Angeles District Judge David Carter had warned that singling out ballots would "wreak havoc" on the election process and harm voters' trust in the democratic process.

"If the executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger," Carter wrote in rejecting the initial suit.

Early voting has been underway in California for several weeks, with hundreds of thousands of ballots already processed.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The voter list had been compiled by the US Department of Homeland Security. In its response to the federal government's lawsuit, California defended its election integrity, and said the process used by the Trump administration to identify non-citizen voters was likely flawed and full of errors.

Last week, another federal judge ordered the DoJ to share its list with an immigrant rights group, and a voting rights watchdog based out of the University of California Los Angeles (UCLA).

A legal filing of the analysis found that thousands of US citizens on the list appear to be inexplicably flagged as ineligible to vote. US District Judge Carter said people recently flagged as noncitizens on voter rolls in other states have repeatedly turned out to be naturalised US citizens.

Trump has made unfounded claims of election fraud for years, despite multiple investigations finding such malfeasance is exceedingly rare.

For the current midterm election cycle, Trump has zeroed in on claiming non US citizens are trying to vote, despite these claims being repeatedly debunked by research and investigation.

"Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own ​constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the executive branch," US District Judge Carter wrote in October.

The most populous US state, California, leans heavily Democratic, and is not expected to be a competitive state for Trump's Republicans in the midterms.

California governor Gavin Newsom is an outspoken critic of Trump, and has warned the president's administration against trying to interfere in the state's voting process.

Ahead of the midterm voting on Tuesday, Newsom announced the deployment of election law experts, poll observers and a help line for voters to report any attempts of intimidation or interference at the polls.

articles.title: Ukraine: At least 26 killed in Russian strikes on aid center
articles.body:
At least 26 people were killed in Russian airstrikes on a school that was serving as an aid distribution center in Zaporizhzhia, a southern Ukrainian region. DW has more.

Here are the latest developments from Russia's war in Ukraine on Monday, November 2.

At least 26 people were killed and five more injured on Monday when the Russian air force launched repeated strikes on a school which was functioning as an aid distribution center in the southern Ukrainian region of Zaporizhzhia.

The multiple attacks, in which Russian planes reportedly launched more than 10 glide bombs, took place in the village of Komyshuvakha, about 35 kilometers (31 miles) east of the city of Zaporizhzhia and a dozen kilometers away from the frontline.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the attacks as "utterly horrific" and accused Russia of being well aware of the humanitarian purpose of the site.

"After the first aerial bomb strike, there was a double-tap strike with nine more bombs, specifically targeting the shelter where people were taking cover," he wrote on social media.

"The Russians could not have been unaware that every week, local residents who had remained in Komyshuvakha received humanitarian aid at that very location."

Ukrainian emergency services said two ‌members of ⁠a ⁠rescue crew were among the dead after falling victim to the so-called "double-tap" strike in which a location is targeted again with the aim of hitting first responders.

The attacks came less than 24 hours after a localized six-day humanitarian ceasefire in and around the town of Oleshky in the neighboring region of Kherson had expired.

Zelenskyy said the temporary truce could potentially have led to further steps toward a possible deal to end the ongoing Russian invasion, but said after Monday's strikes:

"This is yet further proof that Russia does not want any kind of ​de-escalation or any real justice... With these killings, Russia has sent a completely opposite signal; Russia is counting on further killings."

The Zaporizhzhia region has been targeted repeatedly for months by heavy Russian airstrikes.

Ukraine's General Staff on Monday blasted Russia's actions during a six-day humanitarian ceasefire in Oleshky, saying the Kremlin had used the break in fighting to rearm its forces and rotate troops in the front-line area.

In a social media post on X, the General Staff wrote: "Defense Forces of Ukraine ensured that the ceasefire was observed and acted exclusively within the framework of the agreements reached," adding, "The enemy, by contrast, used the humanitarian pause to improve its positions."

Residents in the Kherson region were warned to be vigilant and told to pay attention to air raid sirens, noting that an intensification of attacks was to be expected after Russia used the brief pause to "strengthen its capabilities."

In Moscow, the Kremlin brushed off the critique, saying Ukraine, "could have used the ceasefire to re-group as well," calling such activity, "normal practice."

Ukraine energy provider DTEK on Monday said that emergency power cuts had been initiated in Kyiv and the surrounding region at the request of national grid operator Ukrenergo.

The outages follow Russian attacks in central Ukraine that left over 200,000 Ukrainians in the area without power over the weekend.

DTEK had previously announced that, "equipment in the region has been seriously damaged due to enemy attacks," adding that energy workers were trying to "restore power to critical infrastructure facilities."

The attacks follow the Kremlin's playbook of seeking to destroy Ukraine's energy infrastructure, especially in cold months, in an attempt to break the will of Ukraine's citizens defending themselves against Russia's invasion by "weaponizing winter."

Ukraine's military has said that about 170 people were evacuated from the Kherson region (news agencies cite numbers ranging from 167 to 180) before a six-day ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky expired at midnight (Moscow time, 2100 GMT) on Sunday.

No resumption of hostilities was immediately reported after what was the longest pause in fighting since Russian forces invaded in 2022.

Kherson's regional governor on Sunday urged residents remaining behind to avoid "red zones" where he said the threat of Russian strikes "remains high, and the threat to life is extremely high."

Kherson has been subjected to drones attacks, shelling, glide bombs and airdropped mines for nearly five years.

In all, nearly 800 people were reportedly evacuated from the region during the temporary ceasefire, with residents shuttled to Russian-annexed Crimea, then to the Russia town of Anapa, before being flown to Belarus and then Ukraine.

Among those evacuated were 22 children and 21 individuals requiring mobility assistance said Ukraine's army.

US First Lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo XIV — both of whom were reportedly involved in securing the pause in fighting — praised cooperation between the sides, voicing hope that such work might lay the groundwork for a broader peace.

Before Russia launched its illegal invasion on February 24, 2022, and took control of 70% of Kherson, the area was home to more than one million people. Now it is estimated that about 140,000 remain.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Russia's forces struck a military facility in Ukraine's Odesa region, the Russian Defense Ministry said on Telegram on Monday.

The statement added that a cargo vessel, which the ministry claimed was used for military purposes, was also hit 58 kilometers (36 ‌ miles) south of ‌the Black ​Sea port city of Odesa.

Separately, news agency Reuters cited an official in Odesa as saying that four people had been injured in a Russian attack.

The United States is backing a ‌quick resumption ⁠of ⁠Russian natural gas ​exports to Europe ​via pipelines crossing ​Ukraine as part of talks ‌aimed at ‌securing ​an energy ceasefire before winter, the ​Wall Street Journal reported on ⁠Sunday, ​citing ​US, European ​and Ukrainian ‌officials.

The proposal involves selling Russian gas via a US intermediary to circumvent European sanctions, the report said, adding that it was mooted by US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff during trips to Moscow and Kyiv in September.

DW could not ​immediately ⁠verify the report.

Russia's share in European gas supply has declined to about 11% now from 45% on the eve of Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

The European Union currently aims to completely phase out Russian gas imports by the end of 2027. And EU leaders have said they don't want to go back to relying on Russia for energy supplies.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said that his country would stop hitting Russian oil refineries if Washington provided Kyiv with powerful Patriot interceptor missiles.

Speaking to US broadcaster Fox News, Zelenskyy said he had had "different and several" conversations with Trump and his team on the issue.

"We asked that we can't not respond after Russia's attack on our energy, after Russia is killing our people, attacks on our electricity, gas, refineries, on everything," he said.

"We said that if you want us not to attack Russia's refineries, they have not to attack our energy system. Another alternative, give us Patriot missiles, we will find money, not just aid," Zelenskyy added.

The Ukrainian leader said if Washington provided the missile systems for one month Kyiv would cease attacks on Russian refineries for the same period.

Asked if he was concerned that this would be seen as trying to "leverage" Trump, Zelenskyy said: "I don't have any concerns when I share the truth between partners."

Ukrainian authorities have been warning for weeks that their supplies of the Patriot interceptor missiles were dwindling.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Emergency alert apps in both Ukraine and Russia have been hacked, officials said.

Ukraine's air force said an air raid alert app was hacked late on Sunday, with fake alerts being sent to smartphones, warning people of nuclear and chemical threats.

SPRAVDI, Ukraine's Center for Strategic Communications, blamed Russia for the hack in a post on its X account.

Hours later, Moscow said the mobile app of the Russian Emergencies Ministry was hit by "a massive cyberattack."

"Attention! The mobile application of the Ministry of Emergencies of Russia has been subjected to a massive cyberattack, enabling attackers to send false information to the public," the Emergencies Ministry posted on Telegram.

It said authorities were working to fix the issue.

Hello and welcome to DW's coverage of the latest developments in Russia's war against Ukraine.

As a temporary ceasefire in Russian-occupied Ukrainian town Oleshky ended on Sunday night, Ukraine resumed attacks on Russian oil refineries.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his country would stop targeting Russian refineries if Washington provided Kyiv with powerful Patriot interceptor missiles to defend against Russian missile and drone strikes.

Meanwhile, Ukraine's air force said it suspected the country's aid raid alert system had been hacked.

Russia's Emergencies Ministry, for its part, said that a "massive cyberattack" hit its application that is designed to warn people of incoming drone attacks and other threats.

Stay tuned for the latest news and analysis from the ongoing war.

articles.title: US to drop South Africa, Rwanda from duty-free trade initiative
articles.body:
The Trump administration has said South Africa and Rwanda are breaking the rules of the AGOA free trade initiative, a centerpiece of US economic engagement with sub-Saharan Africa.

South Africa and Rwanda are set to be removed from a US trade initiative that has provided duty-free access to the US market for thousands of products from sub-Saharan African countries for 26 years.

On Monday, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said US President Donald Trump intends to "terminate" the two countries from the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) trade preference program starting in January 2027.

The program, which comes under regular review, was extended in February by Trump.

In a statement, Greer said that "the governments of Rwanda and South Africa are engaging in practices that are inconsistent with AGOA's eligibility criteria."

Greer said these practices include "barriers that undermine American trade and investment and practices that pose a threat to US national security and foreign policy interests in the region."

The statement did not provide any specific examples of the trade barriers or security and foreign policy issues in question.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

AGOA was introduced in 2000 by former US President Bill Clinton, and it has become a centerpiece of US economic engagement with sub-Saharan Africa.

Duty free access to the US market is seen as a critical economic boost for the more than 30 AGOA countries. Over 1,800 specific products are covered under AGOA.

Requirements for membership include eliminating barriers to US trade and investment, while maintaining an open market economy along with democratic principles like the rule of law, human rights and labor protections.

South Africa has been AGOA's largest beneficiary, with $1.7 billion (€1.5 billion) worth of goods like car parts, citrus fruit and wine, exported to the US under the program in 2025.

South Africa's Trade Ministry said last week that it was prepared for the decision, adding that AGOA exports comprise only about 10% of its ​total exports to the US and 1% of its total global exports.

"AGOA remains important to South Africa, but it does not constitute the totality of the economic relationship between South Africa and the ‌United States," it said in a statement.

In recent weeks, President Cyril Ramaphosa has also said South Africa must prepare for being excluded from AGOA by seeking new markets and trade deals with partners like China.

On Monday, the South Africa government said the US remains an important trade partner and it would provide support for affected sectors.

South Africa's export-dependent citrus industry warned that its entire value chain "on both sides of the Atlantic, is now under threat," and warned that jobs and the economic security of entire communities is now at stake.

The US has been putting economic pressure on Rwanda over its alleged support of the M23 rebel group in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

Washington sanctioned Rwanda's Defense Ministry last week, which denies any ties to M23, along with several individuals, institutions and a gold refinery.

Major Rwandan exports to the US include coffee and minerals.
