articles.title: FSB Claims Ukraine Sent Drone Goggles Rigged With Explosives to Russian Volunteers
articles.body:
Russia’s FSB security service said Monday that it thwarted a series of planned attacks against Russian drone operators after its agents uncovered a shipment of drone goggles rigged with explosives that were meant to be distributed to military personnel.

“During an X-ray examination, explosives specialists established that Ukrainian special services had embedded improvised explosive devices into the first-person view goggles where cooling fans are normally placed,” the FSB said in a statement.

The devices were allegedly wired to detonate immediately upon being turned on, killing or injuring the operators.

The FSB said a shipment of the tampered goggles was first discovered in the southern Volgograd region, after which law enforcement authorities intercepted larger batches shipped to various locations through Russia Post.

It did not disclose the exact number of seized devices.

A nearly six-minute video released by the FSB and shared with state media outlets showed a bomb disposal operation alongside interviews with an unidentified soldier and two female volunteers, who help distribute supplies to Russian servicemen.

One volunteer said FSB officers stopped her while trying to collect a shipment of three goggle kits sent by someone identified only as Daria. A second volunteer described receiving a separate shipment of goggles from another online contact who used the handle “Oleg Feniks.”

The FSB launched a criminal investigation into the illegal manufacture, acquisition and transportation of explosives, as well as attempted terrorism.

Officials warned volunteers working with the Russian army to inspect all incoming donations, claiming that Ukrainian intelligence services had previously masked explosives inside everyday items like power banks, Bluetooth speakers, car parts, heated shoe insoles and gift statuettes.

articles.title: Oleshky Ceasefire and Aid Operation End Without Any Violations, Lantratova Says
articles.body:
A ceasefire in and around the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine concluded this weekend without any violations being reported, Russia’s human rights chief said Monday, adding that discussions are under way to provide for regular humanitarian deliveries to civilians remaining in the area.

At the same time, Ukraine’s military accused Russian forces the six-day humanitarian ceasefire to strengthen their positions, while the Kremlin said it assumed Ukrainian troops had also used the pause to regroup.

The temporary pause in fighting, which began last Tuesday and ended Sunday, was organized to allow initial demining operations followed by the delivery of humanitarian relief to Oleshky’s residents, who faced acute shortages of food and medicine. Both Russia and Ukraine praised U.S. first lady Melania Trump for mediating the agreement.

“I want to emphasize that there were no incidents or violations of the ceasefire. Everything went according to plan,” Yana Lantratova, the Russian human rights commissioner, told reporters at a news conference in Moscow.

Her remarks contradict a statement issued on Saturday by Russia’s Foreign Ministry, which claimed that a Ukrainian drone strike on a vehicle in Oleshky had injured two civilians.

The Kremlin on Monday called the humanitarian operation in Oleshky a success, praising the “level of coordination achieved among participants from all sides,” though it noted there were no immediate plans for similar missions elsewhere.

Neither Lantratova nor the Kremlin have addressed the Foreign Ministry’s claim of a ceasefire violation. Ukraine has also not commented on the matter.

Russia seized Oleshky shortly after President Vladimir Putin ordered the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Lantratova said it was still unclear how many people ultimately left Oleshky during the six-day pause in fighting. While Russian authorities had prepared enough buses to evacuate up to 750 civilians, she acknowledged that many returned largely empty.

“A great deal of buses drove back empty,” she said. “Naturally, far fewer than 750 people left. To be completely honest with you, we simply had neither the time nor the opportunity to count people.”

Dismissing political scrutiny of the effort, Lantratova added, “I know there are attempts to politicize this. Unfortunately, all such attempts are petty and wrong, because our mission is not political, but humanitarian.”

Lantratova said she and her Ukrainian counterpart, Dmytro Lubinets, had agreed to seek regular, “at least monthly,” humanitarian missions to Oleshky. She asked Melania Trump to help mediate those future efforts.

“Moving forward, we will assess what other needs exist,” Lantratova said. “We are aware of the settlements near Oleshky, and we have already dispatched humanitarian aid to those areas.”

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky over the weekend called the Oleshky mission a success, expressing gratitude to those involved in negotiating the pause, including Melania Trump.

“When there is the attention of the world, there is the salvation of people,” Zelensky wrote in a post on Telegram.

Despite the praise of the humanitarian efforts, both Russia and Ukraine accused each other of using the ceasefire to rotate, regroup and supply their troops in the area around Oleshky. “This is standard practice in such situations. But I’m not familiar with the specifics,” Peskov told reporters on Monday.

articles.title: Kremlin Downplays Prospect of Resuming Gas Shipments to Europe via Ukraine
articles.body:
Russia is unlikely to resume natural gas deliveries to Europe via Ukrainian pipelines anytime soon, the Kremlin said Monday, downplaying reports that the option was being discussed as part of a proposed winter energy ceasefire.

The Wall Street Journal reported earlier that the Trump administration suggested the idea during talks in September as an incentive for Moscow to halt strikes on Ukraine’s energy grid. According to U.S. and European officials, advocates of the plan argued it would also allow Ukraine to collect transit fees while helping lower European heating costs.

Under the proposal, Russian gas would be sold through a U.S. intermediary to navigate European sanctions, with proceeds placed in an offshore escrow account to prevent Moscow from using the funds to finance its war effort.

“Frankly, the situation on the ground speaks all too clearly to the fact that those kinds of plans are impossible to implement right now,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters during a daily briefing. “But as for what the future holds, we’ll see.”

Peskov said any renewal of gas shipments through Ukraine would “depend on the willingness of buyers, the willingness of sellers and the capacity of sellers.”

He noted that, while the European energy market remains a “premium one,” countries in the Global South have demonstrated themselves as “centers of economic growth,” meaning that their consumption of oil and gas will only increase in the coming years, with Moscow poised to supply all of their energy needs.

Russian gas shipments to Europe by pipeline have largely stopped since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and Brussels has committed to ending all imports of Russian oil and gas by the end of 2027.

According to the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis, a U.S.-based think tank, the EU imported 6.9 billion cubic meters of Russian gas in the first three months of 2026, a 16% increase from the first quarter of last year and the highest volume since 2022.

Still, Russia now accounts for just 11% of Europe’s natural gas consumption, down from 45% on the eve of the 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

articles.title: Ukrainian Drones Hit Major Oil Transport Hub in Samara Region
articles.body:
Ukrainian drones struck one of Europe’s largest oil transport hubs in Russia’s Samara region, independent media reported Monday, as local authorities confirmed the overnight attack in the southern region without detailing any damage or casualties.

Samara region Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said early Monday that air defense systems were repelling an air barrage and urged residents not to post photos or videos online.

Samara’s Kurumoch International Airport temporarily suspended flights for two hours during the air raid alert.

The exiled news outlet Astra said it used eyewitness photos of a smoke cloud in Samara to identify at least one targeted facility as Transneft’s linear production and dispatch station. NASA satellite imagery also showed a large, black plume of smoke rising in the area where the site is located, directly southeast of the regional capital.

The Transneft station spans 216 hectares (534 acres) and has 71 storage tanks with a total capacity of 1.6 million cubic meters. It receives crude from Western Siberia, the republic of Tatarstan, the Orenburg region and Kazakhstan via four pipelines before routing it toward two refineries and the Druzhba export pipeline.

Monday’s attack marks the fifth drone strike on the Transneft production and dispatch station after reported strikes on Oct. 2, 7, 10 and 11.

It also came as Russia’s Emergency Situations Ministry said a major cyberattack targeted the app it uses to send people warnings about incoming air attacks. Ukraine reported a similar cyberattack on its air raid alert system earlier in the day, which it said sent out false messages about a radiation threat.

Russia’s Defense Ministry said it intercepted 212 Ukrainian drones across Russia and annexed Crimea between Sunday evening and Monday morning. Authorities in the Belgorod, Voronezh and Rostov regions reported minor damage and injuries.

In an interview with state TV channel Vesti on Sunday, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak, who oversees Russia’s energy sector, said Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries were adding to global fuel market imbalances and affecting prices.

That same day, Nizhny Novgorod region Governor Gleb Nikitin said a large-scale Ukrainian drone caused “significant damage” to an industrial facility. He did not identify the site that was hit. The region is home to the NORSI oil refinery, one of Russia’s largest.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky also said Sunday that his armed forces had hit the Kamensky plant in Russia’s Rostov region, which he said was involved in the manufacture of Russian missiles.

Despite U.S. attempts last month to introduce an energy ceasefire in the war, which is now approaching its fifth anniversary, Russia and Ukraine have continued to target power grid infrastructure, as well as oil refineries and other facilities.

In an interview with Fox News on Sunday, Zelensky reiterated his position that Ukraine will halt its attacks on Russian refineries if Moscow also puts an end to its strikes on the Ukrainian electrical grid.

articles.title: US midterms 2026: What polls reveal about Democratic, Republican voters
articles.body:
From the economy and cost of living to immigration, polls show where American voters agree and disagree.

US Midterms 2026: The country is about to get a new Congress. What do voters want? | This Is America

Americans will vote in the US midterm elections on Tuesday, with the economy, the cost of living, and immigration among the top issues. While Democrats and Republicans share concerns about the rising cost of living, recent surveys suggest differences in how they view the economy, President Donald Trump, and other key issues.

In an NBC poll released on Sunday, 75 percent of respondents said they were dissatisfied with the state of the US economy, and 51 percent said they were dissatisfied with their personal financial situation.

Other surveys conducted in October also offer a look into how voters from both parties felt about their finances and which issues mattered most.

The economy is the main concern for US voters, but Democrats and Republicans vary on the importance of issues like healthcare, immigration, and crime.

A Pew Research Centre survey, conducted between September 28 and October 4, suggested that 84 percent of registered voters considered the economy very important to their midterm vote. It was the top issue for 82 percent of respondents who prefer Republican candidates, and 88 percent for those who back Democrats.

However, the two groups differed on other issues.

About 85 percent of Democratic Party supporters considered the future of democracy very important, compared with 69 percent of Republicans. Healthcare was a priority for 82 percent of Democrats, compared with 53 percent of Republicans.

Republican supporters were more concerned about immigration, with 72 percent saying it was very important, compared with 53 percent of Democrats.

Violent crime was also more important to Republican supporters, at 64 percent, compared with 37 percent Democrats.

A KFF survey, conducted by the Kaiser Family Foundation, an independent nonprofit, from September 16 to 21, suggested 42 percent of registered voter respondents trusted Democrats more to handle healthcare costs, compared with 22 percent who trusted Republicans.

On the cost of living, 39 percent trusted Democrats more, while 25 percent preferred Republicans.

Views of President Trump and his economic policies remain divided along party lines.

In the Pew Research Centre survey, 91 percent of Democratic respondents and those who leaned Democratic believed Trump’s economic policies had made things worse.

Among Republican supporters, 39 percent said his policies had improved the economy, 35 percent said they made conditions worse, and 25 percent said they had little effect.

In the November 1 NBC News poll, 40 percent of registered-voter respondents approved of Trump’s overall job performance, compared with 60 percent who disapproved.

Americans are concerned about rising costs, but Democrats are more likely than Republicans to express negative feelings about economic conditions.

In an October Pew Research survey, 36 percent of Republicans rated the US economy as excellent or good, compared with just 9 percent of Democrats or Democrat-leaning voters.

However, the majority in both groups expressed concern about the cost of essential goods and services.

According to PEW, 82 percent of Democrats and Democratic leaners were concerned about food and consumer prices, compared with 62 percent of Republicans and Republican leaners.

Healthcare costs concerned 80 percent of Democrats and 57 percent of Republicans, while petrol and energy prices worried 81 percent of Democrats and 65 percent of Republicans.

A Fox News poll released on October 14 also had 74 percent of registered voter respondents rating the economy negatively, and 60 percent identified the cost of living as their biggest economic concern.

The November 1 NBC News poll found that 53 percent of Republican respondents were dissatisfied with the state of the economy.

The Pew Research Center also found that abortion and gun policy were less central to Democratic respondents in comparison with 2022. Among Republican voters, education policy and energy policy were less important than they were four years ago.

In the NBC poll, 51 percent of registered voters were dissatisfied with their personal financial situation, compared with 49 percent who were satisfied.

It was the first time in 30 years of NBC polling that dissatisfaction with personal finances outweighed satisfaction.

In an NPR/PBS News/Marist poll on October 19-20, 38 percent of likely voters said their finances had gotten worse over the past year, 44 percent said they had remained about the same, and 15 percent said they had improved.

A total of 51 percent of Democratic likely voters said their finances had deteriorated, compared with 21 percent of Republicans.

In a Reuters/Ipsos survey conducted from September 30 to October 5, 71 percent of Democrats and 57 percent of Republicans said their incomes had not kept pace with rising prices.

Eric Ham, a former Democratic congressional staffer and Senate national security adviser, said that Trump’s global tariffs and the US-Israel war on Iran had added to the financial pressure on American households.

“Americans are paying more not just in terms of self-inflicted wounds that President Donald Trump implemented through tariffs, but also if you look at this war of choice,” Ham told Al Jazeera.

Democratic voters reported higher enthusiasm about participating in the elections.

In the Marist poll, 91 percent of likely Democratic voters were enthusiastic or very enthusiastic, compared with 86 percent of Republicans and 76 percent of Independents.

John Fury, a former Republican congressional staffer, said the final days of campaigning were focused on turnout.

“This is not a persuasion election. This is a get-out-the base election,” Fury said.

In a KFF survey, Democratic candidate supporters were 25 percentage points more likely than Republican supporters to describe themselves as “more motivated” than usual to vote (63 percent versus 38 percent).

The November 1 NBC News poll also reported high interest in the elections, with 70 percent of registered voters rating their interest at nine or 10 on a 10-point scale.

Surveys conducted in the final weeks before the election suggested voters preferred Democratic candidates or Democratic control of Congress over Republicans.

An NBC poll conducted on October 28-30 and published on November 1 suggested that 52 percent of registered voters preferred Democratic control of Congress compared with 45 percent who preferred Republican control.

Similarly, the Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted from October 22 to October 26 suggested that 53 percent of likely voters would vote for or lean towards the Democratic candidates in their district, compared with 44 percent who supported Republicans.

These surveys measure voting sentiment, but they do not reflect the results of the individual races.

articles.title: US to suspend South Africa and Rwanda from duty-free trade access
articles.body:
South Africa loses duty-free access under AGOA, impacting $1.7bn worth of exports, including cars and farm products.

The United States has said it will suspend South Africa and Rwanda from duty-free trade benefits under the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA), effective January 1, 2027.

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Monday that both countries had failed to meet AGOA’s eligibility criteria. South Africa has been the largest beneficiary of the programme, exporting about $1.7bn worth of goods to the US under AGOA in 2025.

“President Trump found that the governments of Rwanda and South Africa are engaging in practices that are inconsistent with AGOA’s eligibility criteria,” Greer said in a statement.

There was no immediate response from either country.

AGOA beneficiaries are expected to meet eligibility requirements covering progress towards market-based economies, good governance and the elimination of barriers to US trade and investment, with Washington reviewing their eligibility annually.

Washington highlighted trade barriers, rule of law and human rights as issues it is deeply concerned about in Rwanda, which was also suspended in 2018.

With regard to South Africa, Washington said it was concerned by barriers to US trade and investment, corruption and threats to US national security and foreign policy interests.

President Donald Trump’s administration has cracked down on South Africa for what Trump says is its persecution of white people. South Africa’s government says this is a falsehood spread by fringe groups.

The US has also taken issue with South Africa’s foreign policy, in particular the genocide case it brought against Israel at the International Court of Justice. Israel denies genocide allegations.

South Africa’s Department of Trade, Industry and Competition said last week it was prepared for a negative outcome from the AGOA eligibility review and that it remained open to dialogue with the US. Exports under AGOA make up only about 10 percent of the country’s total exports to the US and 1 percent of its total global exports, it noted.

South African President Cyril Ramaphosa had also said in recent weeks that his country must prepare for being cut out of the programme, and that it was already seeking new markets and signing new trade deals with other partners such as China.

South Africa’s main exports to the US include precious stones and metals, motor vehicles, iron and steel. Its exports under AGOA are mainly motor vehicles and parts, as well as farm products and wine.

Rwanda’s main exports to the United States include coffee, tea and minerals.

articles.title: HRW calls on Zambia to halt post-election crackdown
articles.body:
Opposition figures arrested and disappeared since President Hakainde Hichilema claimed August victory.

Human Rights Watch (HRW) has called on Zambia’s authorities to halt the vicious clampdown on the political opposition that was launched following President Hakainde Hichilema’s victory in disputed elections in August.

The rights group demanded in a report released on Sunday that the authorities put a stop to the intensifying crackdown.

It accused Zambia’s government of silencing government critics, with several members of the opposition, as well as journalists and lawyers, arrested and some having disappeared in recent months.

“The post-election climate of intimidation, harassment, and repression has had a chilling effect on civic and political organizations, particularly on dissenting voices,” HRW said.

The group said that Zambian police and military “forcibly disappeared, arbitrarily detained, beat, and threatened opposition members and supporters as well as lawyers, journalists, and government critics in the days before and after general elections in August 2026”.

“Zambia’s government should break this dangerous cycle of repression,” added Ashwanee Budoo-Scholtz, deputy Africa director at HRW.

“The authorities should immediately halt the ongoing post-election crackdown, allow access to lawyers and provide medical care for those in detention, release everyone arbitrarily detained, and ensure accountability for abuses by security forces.”

Hichilema was sworn in for a second term as Zambia’s president following his victory in August. Critics have insisted that the election was marred by vote rigging.

As he was inaugurated at the National Heroes Stadium in the Zambian capital, Lusaka, his main rival Brian Mundubile was in detention, accused of treason after claiming the opposition had won the election.

Police raided Mundubile’s home the day after the August 13 elections. A former cabinet member, Mutotwe Kafwaya, was shot and killed during the operation.

HRW called on the Zambian authorities to institute an independent, impartial and thorough investigation into the matter.

About a dozen other opposition figures who have questioned the election results have been arrested.

Meanwhile, authorities suddenly closed the country’s courts two weeks after the election, a move that Zambian police stated was an “intelligence-led and preventive measure”, without providing details.

HRW noted that the closure prevents the opposition from filing legal challenges against the vote.

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy back in court seeking to have murder charges dismissed
articles.body:
Defence argues juror misconduct and judge’s questioning impacted Clancy’s trial for strangling of her three children.

Lindsay Clancy, the American mother facing murder charges for killing her three young children, has returned to court in a bid to get the charges dropped.

Clancy’s lawyers urged Judge William Sullivan on Monday to dismiss the first-degree murder charges against her in the state of Massachusetts in the United States, saying retrying her for killing her three young children would violate ⁠⁠her constitutional rights.

Prosecutors said they intend to retry Clancy if the case moves forward but have not decided if she would face the same first-degree murder charges.

Monday’s hearing was her second time in court since September, when jurors were unable to reach a verdict at her trial.

Clancy strangled her three children with exercise bands in 2023 at her home in Duxbury, a suburb of Boston in Massachusetts. Clancy then attempted to take her own life by cutting herself with a knife and was paralysed after jumping from a second-floor window.

At Monday’s hearing, defence lawyer Martin G Weinberg argued that the judge should have investigated further after the jury foreperson sent two notes indicating that a juror was not following the rules. Further questioning could have revealed grounds to remove the juror, identified as Michael Desronvil, and continue deliberations, he said.

After receiving the notes, Sullivan spoke with each juror, reminding them of their duties and explaining what constitutes reasonable doubt in a court case. He asked whether they could apply the law to the case, and all said yes.

But Weinberg argued that Sullivan had not gone far enough. A juror who said he could follow the law could have been lying, Weinberg said, and the situation warranted questioning the foreperson separately to learn more about what was happening during deliberations.

Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague argued there was no indication the holdout juror’s disagreement stemmed from personal bias or an inability to deliberate, rather than a different assessment of the evidence.

Sprague said the judge handled the ⁠⁠jury impasse appropriately, saying the fact that one juror dug in his heels did not mean Sullivan should risk interfering with the deliberations by questioning him.

“It is clear from the record this ⁠⁠juror did not refuse to deliberate,” Sprague said. “He refused to agree.”

Defence lawyer Kevin Reddington accused the lone holdout juror of using a mobile phone to research terms related to the case and questioned whether he had been truthful during jury selection.

Clancy has never disputed killing her three young children in 2023, but her lawyer has argued she had postpartum psychosis and was unable to control her behaviour. Prosecutors have acknowledged that Clancy, now 36, had mental health problems but said she acted deliberately and understood her actions were wrong.

Sullivan did not immediately rule on the motion to dismiss. He scheduled another hearing for November 16 and suggested a retrial could begin in March.

Another motion expected to be discussed is the state of Massachusetts’s request for a gag order barring lawyers and their supporters “from making extrajudicial statements to the media that would have a substantial likelihood of materially prejudicing the criminal proceeding”.

articles.title: Trump asks Supreme Court to block 20,000 California ballots before midterms
articles.body:
California says the move to block ballots from suspected noncitizens could disenfranchise eligible US voters.

The administration of United States President Donald Trump has asked the Supreme Court to stop California from counting mail-in ballots from more than 20,000 voters it claims are not US citizens.

The emergency request, filed on Monday, just one day before the US midterm elections, is the latest development in a legal battle between the administration and California, a Democratic stronghold and the most populous US state.

California says the move could disenfranchise thousands of eligible voters.

The Department of Justice wants the Supreme Court to step in immediately and force California to set aside ballots from voters on a list compiled by the Department of Homeland Security until after their citizenship status can be verified.

The department argues that once the ballots are mixed in with others, there would be no way to identify them and remove them if the voters were later found to be ineligible.

But California says the list is unreliable and could include thousands of US citizens.

Voting has been under way since early October, with ballots mailed to around 23 million registered voters and hundreds of thousands already processed. State officials say it would be nearly impossible to separate the ballots in question.

Last week, a federal judge rejected the administration’s request, raising concerns about the reliability of the data on the list.

“If the executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger,” Judge David Carter wrote.

The administration has turned to the Supreme Court after a federal appeals court also rejected the request on Friday.

It is not clear when the Supreme Court, which rejected an earlier effort to restrict mail-in voting in September, will rule. The case will be handled by Justice Elena Kagan, who hasn’t set a deadline yet for California to respond.

The dispute comes as Republicans fight to retain control of Congress in Tuesday’s elections.

Trump has repeatedly made false claims about widespread voter fraud, but studies and state audits have shown that ineligible voting, including by noncitizens, is rare.

articles.title: Iran pushing accelerated plan for ceasefire talks with US
articles.body:
Tehran says plan has been condensed and can be implemented within two days as it continues talks with mediators.

Iran has said it is trying to accelerate the ceasefire plan it has proposed to the United States, as the region braces for possible renewed fighting in the US-Israel war against the country.

Officials in Tehran said on Monday that the seven-step plan they put on the table last month remains the same, but could now be implemented more quickly. The proposal includes a swift reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and return to talks over Iran’s nuclear programme.

The statement comes as Iranian officials continue negotiations with Qatari mediators in the latest effort to find a diplomatic path out of the eight-month conflict.

US President Donald Trump has said the latest negotiations were “going fine” but has suggested several times that the United States could strike Iran after the November 3 US midterm elections.

The offer from Iran remains on the table but has now been “condensed and can be implemented within two days” instead of seven, Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said.

“If Iran’s demands are met, it is possible that both security will be restored to the Strait of Hormuz and the negotiation process will begin within a short period of time,” Baghaei said. “All of this depends on how the American side wants to proceed regarding the future of this process.”

Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has reportedly granted “powers” to the government to accelerate talks with the US to end the regional war, the state IRNA news agency said.

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi reiterated that Tehran is prepared for both diplomacy and military confrontation, as mediators ⁠Qatar and Pakistan continue to facilitate indirect talks.

“By accepting these conditions, the Strait of Hormuz will be opened and negotiations will resume,” Araghchi told IRNA in Ashgabat, Turkmenistan. “Otherwise, the current situation will continue and Iran will not bow down.”

Iran previously said the plan could be implemented within a week if the US met its conditions, which include lifting the naval blockade of its ports, the repeal of sanctions, and a guarantee of an end to strikes, and a complete regional ceasefire, especially in Lebanon.

Baghaei gave no indication that Tehran had changed its demands or that Washington had accepted its proposal.

Trump said the war on Iran will end “very soon one way or the other”, telling the Right Side Broadcasting Network (RSBN) on Sunday that Tehran would either “make a deal or we’ll just end it”.

articles.title: US petrol prices dip ahead of midterms as voters eye costs
articles.body:
Diesel prices ease to $6.29 per gallon, offering slight relief amid a global fuel demand squeeze.

Petrol prices have dipped amid renewed diplomatic efforts to end the US-Israel war on Iran, but remain high ahead of the United States midterm elections, as the cost of living remains a central issue for voters.

On Monday, the average price for a gallon (3.78 litres) of regular petrol was $4.17, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), which tracks daily petrol prices. That is down 12 cents from this time last week and 23 cents from a month ago.

By comparison, prices were $3.04 this time a year ago and $2.98 on February 28, when the US and Israel first struck Iran.

Diesel fuel prices remain high at $6.29 per gallon, but that is down 6 cents from this time last week. Diesel prices climbed above $6 a gallon for the first time in September before topping out at $6.53.

The average petrol price of President Donald Trump’s second term to date was set to exceed $3.46 a gallon on Monday, surpassing the previous record for a presidential administration set under former President Joe Biden, according to a Financial Times analysis of federal data.

Oil prices are continuing to fall, down 6 percent on Monday as diplomatic efforts to end the US-Israel war on Iran continued following in-person talks in Qatar over the weekend.

“Oil markets down significantly this morning after Trump signalled he favoured negotiations and not new attacks on Iran,” Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, said in a post on X. “Oil down [approximately] 5%, wholesale gasoline and diesel pointing to roughly 16 [cents per gallon] decline. The national average could fall under $4 a gallon in the next week barring a course change.”

Cost-of-living issues remain top of mind for US voters as they head to the polls. An Associated Press-NORC poll last month found that a majority of Americans believe addressing cost-of-living issues should be a priority for Congress, including 78 percent of Republicans and 89 percent of Democrats.

“Once this conflict comes to an end, gas prices will drop drastically, and the Iranian terrorist regime will not have a nuclear weapon,” White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers told Al Jazeera. “Protecting America’s national security from threats by a radical terrorist regime that has chanted ‘Death to America’ for 47 years was the right thing to do – and President Trump is the only president who has had the courage to do it.”

Rogers added, “Thanks to the exceptional work of the US military, more oil is now flowing out of the Persian Gulf than before the Iran conflict began.”

On Wall Street, oil and gas giant stocks were trending downward in midday trading. ConocoPhillips was down 3.7 percent, Chevron 2.3 percent and ExxonMobil 3.3 percent.

The major US indices more broadly were in positive territory. The Nasdaq was up 0.7 percent, the S&P 500 0.6 percent and the Dow Jones Industrial Average 1 percent.

articles.title: Russian bombing of Ukrainian aid centre kills 26 people
articles.body:
Ukraine’s president calls attack in Zaporizhia further proof that Russia does not want any ‌kind of de-escalation or justice.

A Russian ⁠bomb attack on an aid centre in Ukraine has killed 26 people, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said, two more than were reported earlier by Ukraine’s emergency services.

The strikes destroyed a school used as a humanitarian aid distribution centre in the village of Komyshuvakha in the southeastern region of Zaporizhia, Zelenskyy said on Monday. Five other people are reported to have been injured.

“After the first air strike, there was a repeat strike with nine more bombs, ⁠directly on the shelter ⁠where people were gathered,” Ukraine’s president wrote on Telegram.

“The Russians could not have been unaware that ⁠every week residents who have remained in ⁠Komyshuvakha were receiving assistance ⁠aid right there. This is yet further proof that Russia does not want any ‌kind of de-escalation, any real justice.”

Footage posted by Ukrainian emergency services showed a building reduced to piles of smouldering rubble. Rescuers were shown working at the site.

Among those killed were a police officer and two State Emergency Service rescuers, regional Governor Mykhailo Semikin reported on Telegram.

Efforts to rescue people on Monday evening were hindered as Russian drones launched additional attacks in the area that had been bombed, according to Mykhailo Semikin, a military official in Zaporizhia.

“After the humanitarian operation in Oleshky, there was a moment when the next steps could have shown that progress toward peace was possible,” Zelenskyy said on social media. “With these killings, Russia is sending an entirely opposite signal: Russia is counting on more killings.”

Elsewhere in Ukraine, emergency services reported that drone strikes injured 12 people in the eastern Kharkiv region and damaged a refrigeration facility, greenhouses and residential buildings.

Five people were also reported injured in the Black Sea port city of Odesa, where a warehouse was targeted and homes were damaged.

Russia’s Ministry of Defence said that it shot down 212 Ukrainian drones overnight, while the head of Russia’s Samara region, Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev, reported local air defences had repelled an aerial attack, without giving further details.

articles.title: Drone attacks extend campaign targeting Sudan’s power system
articles.body:
Attacks the latest to disrupt electricity supplies; army reports new defections from paramilitary RSF.

Drone strikes are reported to have hit three electricity substations in eastern and northern Sudan, the latest attacks in a concentrated campaign.

The attacks on Monday, which caused widespread power outages across parts of the country, brought the number of strikes reported to target Sudan’s electricity network to 18 over the past week.

Sudan’s military government has claimed that Ethiopia is aiding the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) – which it has been fighting since April 2023 – in carrying out the attacks.

Facilities in New Halfa and Aroma in eastern Kassala state were hit early on Monday, while the al-Ghazali substation in Sudan’s Northern State was also targeted, according to local media.

Videos circulating on social media appeared to show fires at the facilities, with civil defence teams trying to extinguish the fires. Al Jazeera was not able to immediately verify the footage and reports.

On Sunday, Sudan’s government said it had filed complaints against Ethiopia with the United Nations Security Council and the African Union’s Peace and Security Council, accusing Addis Ababa of involvement in the ongoing campaign of attacks on civilian infrastructure and power stations.

The Sudanese army also reported on Monday that a group of RSF members had defected by surrendering to its forces in Damazin, the capital of southeastern Blue Nile state.

The announcement follows a declaration, in video footage obtained exclusively by Al Jazeera, by senior RSF commander Siddiq Ander that he had defected.

In a statement, the army said that the development was the latest in increasing defections from the paramilitary group in Blue Nile state.

It added that the group’s commander had provided information concerning the management of military operations in Damazin, including “Ethiopian support” for the RSF.

articles.title: Trump, Vance campaign with candidates on last day before US midterms
articles.body:
Republicans and Democrats hold last rallies from Washington to Michigan and Texas as polls point to a tight race for Congress.

President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance have begun their final push ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, with Republican and Democratic candidates spreading out across the United States for a last day of campaigning.

On Monday afternoon in front of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in Washington, DC, Trump urged supporters to vote in Tuesday’s midterm election.

“If the people who voted for me and voted in the last election … if they go out and voted just a good portion of them, we will win in a landslide,” he said, before conceding that this could be an uphill battle.

“Now, that doesn’t happen because usually whoever is the sitting president, whether Republican or Democrat, good or bad, … for some reason the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms,” he added.

Trump also referred to the Senate race in Alaska as a “fraudulent election”.

“In Alaska, the Dumbocrats conspired to get a fake Dan Sullivan on the ballot to confuse voters,” he said.

The administration had renewed a legal push to bar Alaska from certifying its election results, alleging that Democrats conspired to recruit a “spoiler” candidate to divert votes from the Republican incumbent of the same name, Dan Sullivan, but US District Judge Sharon Gleason on Sunday dismissed the lawsuit, describing the request as “infeasible”.

Republicans are trying to hold their majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives despite Trump’s low approval ratings and polls predicting that the Iran war, high energy prices and the affordability crisis could mean a strong night for Democrats.

Closing the campaign at the Reflecting Pool was a departure from Trump’s recent strategy. The US president has staged more than 25 rallies in largely conservative areas over the past month, and wrote that Sunday’s rally in Kansas was the “last stop” of his 2026 midterm campaign tour.

The Reflecting Pool was also politically awkward. Trump’s renovation of the historic landmark ran nearly three months late and cost more than 10 times the initial budget. The “American flag blue” liner also began peeling after he declared the work complete, according to The Associated Press news agency.

In an interview on the New York Post’s Pod Force One podcast, Trump said that, if he had to work with a Democrat-led Congress, he would become “Mr Veto”.

“It wouldn’t be the first time [we] have a president and he doesn’t have the Senate. They set stuff up, you veto it. After a month or two of getting things vetoed, they come over, and you make a deal,” he said.

The president also indicated he would be willing to pardon people around him if he considered it necessary.

“I would if I needed to, sure,” Trump added.

Vance travelled to Rome, New York, early on Monday to boost Republican House of Representatives candidates Anthony Constantino and Kailee Buller at a rally that began at 9:15am ET (14:15 GMT).

Constantino is running to succeed longtime Republican Representative Elise Stefanik, who is not seeking re-election. A Siena Research Institute poll shows the race could be close despite a Republican registration advantage of about 80,000 voters.

“A new poll conducted by Siena Research […] shows that while voters in the district still favor Republicans more broadly, that sentiment does not necessarily translate to support for Constantino,” North Country Public Radio reported.

Buller is challenging Democratic Representative John Mannion in the neighbouring 22nd congressional district, which includes Rome.

Travelling back through Joint Base Andrews in Maryland, Vance spoke to reporters about the ongoing US-Israeli war against Iran. Trump had threatened renewed fighting after the midterm election.

Vance, however, suggested that “good conversations” with Iran were ongoing, and that new attacks were not a foregone conclusion.

“The president and I both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement. We’re going to keep on working at it,” Vance said.

“You never know, of course. The Iranians are always a little unpredictable, and as the president always says, he retains kinetic options. He retains non-kinetic options. But we’ve certainly made some progress. We’ll see if we can make some more.”

In Michigan, Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed spent the final day before the election campaigning alongside Michigan Democratic Representative Debbie Dingell and Massachusetts Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren.

He also urged supporters to vote as he rallied at Eastern Michigan University in Ypsilanti.

“If we’re nervous about where we’re going to go from here, go vote,” he said.

In Texas, Democrats James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa are making final pushes for the Senate and the governor’s race, respectively, with a joint rally in Austin at 6:30pm CT (00:30 GMT on Tuesday).

Talarico’s opponent, Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton, is scheduled to appear in Conroe at noon CT (18:00 GMT) and Allen at 6:30pm CT (00:30 GMT).

Polls show Talarico narrowly ahead of Paxton, while Governor Greg Abbott’s lead over Hinojosa has narrowed.

In Maine, Democratic Senate candidate Troy Jackson will make campaign stops in Yarmouth, Scarborough, South Portland and Portland, with events scheduled from 9am ET (14:00 GMT) to 6pm ET (23:00 GMT).

In Iowa, Democratic Senate candidate Josh Turek will be touring Harlan, Onawa, Le Mars and Sioux City to meet with voters, from 10am CT (16:00 GMT) to 6pm CT (00:00 GMT).

In Kansas, Democratic Senate candidate Adam Hamilton will be out from 7:30am CT (13:30 GMT) to 1pm CT (19:00 GMT), speaking to voters across Wichita, Topeka and Lawrence. The final event of the day has not yet been announced.

Separately, a federal judge in Washington is due to hear arguments early on Monday in a lawsuit over whether immigration agents can be present at polling places. Common Cause, UnidosUS, the League of United Latin American Citizens (LULAC) and the city and county of Denver are challenging the US administration’s position that armed agents from US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) may enter polling places for immigration enforcement.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in September that agents would not patrol polling sites but could enter to respond to threats or serve warrants on people. The plaintiffs argue that such operations would violate a federal restriction on armed personnel at voting places and could intimidate voters.

The Department of Homeland Security has said ICE is not planning operations targeting polling locations.

articles.title: Haley Stevens backs Mike Rogers. And, Gulf states brace for potential attack on Iran
articles.body:
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens stunned the political landscape by endorsing GOP Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers for Michigan's open Senate seat, breaking with her party less than 48 hours before Election Day. The surprise defection followed weeks of deteriorating relations with her former primary opponent, Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed. In her endorsement of Rogers, Stevens cited El-Sayed's ties to political streamer Hasan Piker, whose remarks concerning Jewish people and Israel sparked backlash in August. El-Sayed sought to distance himself from the controversy, but Stevens has criticized him for not doing enough to reassure Black and Jewish voters who backed her in the primary.

Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers, right, and Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., attend a service at Perfecting Church, Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026, in Detroit. Jose Juarez/AP hide caption

After tomorrow's elections, Trump may choose to bomb Iran again — an option he has discussed with Israel. The U.S.' partners in the Gulf are on edge and bracing for potential conflict. Qatar has been actively leading negotiations with Iran over the past 72 hours to prevent further fighting.

The Supreme Court will hear arguments tomorrow in a case between the Catholic Church and Colorado's taxpayer-funded pre-K programs. The case questions whether religious schools can refuse admission to children of gay and trans parents, which would violate a state law against discrimination. For decades, the Supreme Court upheld the separation of church and state. But in the past 10 years, the court's conservative majority has increasingly shifted focus to the First Amendment's protection of religious freedom. This shift complicates Colorado's inclusive pre-K initiative aimed at ensuring that virtually all 4-year-olds in the state get a pre-K education. To meet its goal, the state included religious schools in its program, as long as they comply with state laws prohibiting discrimination on the basis of race, religion, sexual orientation or gender identity.

Getty Images Getty Images hide caption

"Your Turn" is a special series from NPR's Allison Aubrey, exploring how to navigate your way through midlife.

Burnout can be a challenge during midlife. As work and home obligations take up more of your focus, burnout can slowly sap your sense of joy and wonder in everyday life. Psychiatrist Judith Joseph says there's a term for this: anhedonia. It's the inability or reduced capacity to experience pleasure from things that are normally enjoyable. Joseph says it can accompany what she calls "high-functioning depression," and she describes it as depression's "silent sister." Here's what the research shows about high-functioning depression:

Want to know more? Read more about the Five V's, sign up for the Your Turn newsletter and listen to the Your Turn podcast for tools and inspiring stories that blend science and wisdom to help you move forward to what's next.

by Tamara Keith, senior political correspondent

People arrive at a polling location during early voting in the midterm election, in Atlanta, Georgia, on October 13, 2026. Photo by Erik S. Lesser/AFP via Getty Images hide caption

At this stage in the midterms, all that's left is the voting and the waiting. On election night, I'll be in Studio 31 at NPR headquarters with browser tabs full of spreadsheets, watching the results roll in and sharing context with NPR listeners.

One of those spreadsheets lists all the congressional districts that have been redrawn since 2024 as part of a mid-decade redistricting push by President Trump. Facing down the historical precedent that the president's party usually loses seats in the midterms, the president pressured Republican-led states to create more sure-thing GOP districts.

But headed into voting, the results in two-thirds of those districts are very much up in the air. In some cases, Democrats are favored. These are places Trump would have won by 10 points just two years ago.

Last month, I saw that the president had a campaign rally scheduled in Greenville, N.C. But national Republicans essentially stopped running ads for Michael Whatley — Trump's handpicked nominee — and diverted resources to states with more competitive races. So, why was the president holding another rally? I reached out to a few sources in the state.

What I learned is that the real reason for the president's trip was almost certainly to help the Republican candidate in eastern North Carolina's first congressional district. It is now one of the most hotly contested and expensive House races in the country, despite new district lines that should have made it an easy Republican pick-up.

Two days of driving through this very large district, one Trump rally, two bags of gummy candy and a lot of coffee later, I was back in the office digging into my spreadsheet of congressional districts. NC-01 isn't an isolated case. A majority of districts redrawn to be a firewall for a Republican majority have turned out to be far more competitive than expected.

So, Tuesday night (and beyond), I'll be filling in the wins and losses to see how this gambit turned out. In the meantime, read more from me about how Trump is spending his final days on the campaign trail. And, you can listen to everything you need to know about the midterms on Up First: The Sunday Story.

Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., appears at a news conference at the U.S. Capitol on September 18, 2025. Murphy's office says he was hospitalized this weekend with a stroke. Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images/Getty Images North America hide caption

This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

articles.title: Hundreds evacuate city during temporary ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine
articles.body:
The ceasefire in a Russian-occupied Ukrainian city has ended. The ceasefire, which lasted several days, allowed hundreds of residents to evacuate.

A ceasefire brokered by Pope Leo and Melania Trump in a corner of southern Ukraine has ended. The truce enabled the evacuation of hundreds of residents in a Russian-occupied town, and across the river in the Ukrainian-held city of Kherson, the truce also allowed residents to walk the streets without being targeted by Russian drones. NPR's Joanna Kakissis traveled there this weekend and is on the line from Kyiv. Good morning, Joanna.

JOANNA KAKISSIS, BYLINE: Good morning, Leila.

FADEL: OK, so what was Kherson like?

KAKISSIS: Well, Leila, tunnels of heavy-duty nets cover nearly every street and many of the buildings in Kherson, if you can imagine that. These nets help protect residents from drones because for the last couple of years, Russian soldiers have used FPV, or first-person view drones strapped with explosives, to actually hunt and kill civilians in Kherson. So Russian troops are also about a mile away across a river. They also drop a lot of guided air bombs into the city.

Now, this is a city I first visited in late 2022, right after Ukrainian forces freed Kherson from Russian occupation. Last time I was there was about a year ago. It's a lovely city filled with parks, but, you know, Russian forces have destroyed so many buildings there, and people never left their homes while I was there last time without drone detectors and sometimes even body armor.

FADEL: So how much has changed since you were last there, especially given there was a ceasefire this weekend?

KAKISSIS: Well, Leila, the locals were not wearing body armor this time, and the city did show signs of normal life.

KAKISSIS: We saw people strolling outside with their kids, stocking up on groceries, having coffee in the sun. And at one very busy cafe, we met two best friends, Anna Hersomenko (ph) and Olena Soboleva (ph). They are 21 years old, and here's Olena.

OLENA SOBOLEVA: There is no drones. There is no explosions. It is like a feeling that no one wants to kill you.

KAKISSIS: And Anna told us she took the opportunity to walk to a salon.

ANNA HERSOMENKO: Last two days, I did my nails. Paint my nail. Yeah.

HERSOMENKO: Yes. Thank you a million. Really, it's definitely a lot of people now walking around. A lot of cars.

KAKISSIS: Now, these two friends, Leila, live on the same street, but they only see each other in person about once a month because it's usually so dangerous to walk outside.

FADEL: Wow. So a little bit of a respite for them. So Kherson relaxed a little during the ceasefire, as you pointed out. This truce, though, was negotiated to help a town across the river. What happened there?

KAKISSIS: Well, yeah, Russia and Ukraine agreed to the ceasefire to help the town of Oleshky. This town is occupied by Russian forces, which mined the land around it. Trucks delivering food and medicine could not get in for several months. Some residents in Oleshky were eating boiled weeds to survive. Now, during the ceasefire, hundreds of residents were evacuated from the town, and many went to northern Ukraine to meet their families.

FADEL: Now, the truce ended Sunday night. So does that mean back to war for everyone?

KAKISSIS: Well, I should note that this was a successful truce because it lasted several days and no violations were reported. But, you know, everyone we spoke to in Kherson was already really nervous as the deadline for the truce's end approached.

UNIDENTIFIED MUSICAL ARTIST: (Playing accordion).

KAKISSIS: We met oncology nurse Olena Yehorova (ph) at a bus stop. What you're hearing is a gray-haired musician playing the accordion at that bus stop. Olena kept looking up at the sky for drones while we were talking.

OLENA YEHOROVA: (Speaking Ukrainian).

KAKISSIS: And she's saying, "I'm so anxious because I just cannot trust the Russians." And she also said that she is bracing herself for new attacks now that the truce is over.

FADEL: That's NPR's Joanna Kakissis in Kyiv. Thank you so much for your reporting.

articles.title: UN's peacekeeping mission in disputed Western Sahara ends after 35 years
articles.body:
FILE - A Sahrawi refugee boy stands in the shadow in the Boujdour refugee camp, Oct. 11, 2021. Bernat Armangue/AP hide caption

CASABLANCA, Morocco — The U.N.'s long-running peacekeeping mission for the disputed Western Sahara ceased operations Sunday after 35 years, as a result of a U.S.-Russia standoff at U.N. headquarters over the territory's future.

The end of the mission raises concerns about stability in the region. Rich in minerals and fisheries, Western Sahara is a vast desert territory roughly the size of Colorado along Africa's northwestern Atlantic coast. Once ruled by Spain, it is claimed by both Morocco and the pro-independence Polisario Front.

"This 1 November 2026 marks the start of the liquidation period," Stéphane Dujarric, spokesperson for the U.N. secretary general, said in a statement. "A smaller team reporting to the United Nations' Department of Operational Support will oversee the orderly transportation of assets belonging to troop-contributing countries to their respective nations, and the appropriate disposal of equipment belonging to the United Nations.''

The mission had been repeatedly extended since it was established in 1991. In the U.N. Security Council on Friday, Russia vetoed a draft U.S. resolution that would have supported Morocco's demand for sovereignty over Western Sahara and ended the peacekeeping mission next year.

Then a rival Russian resolution to extend the mission was voted down. The disagreement led to an abrupt end of the force's mandate.

Morocco's royal palace welcomed the non-renewal of the mission. It called it an "instrument to internationalize the dispute.''

The Polisario Front, backed by Algeria, called it "an unacceptable decision.'' The Algerian foreign ministry said it profoundly regrets the non-renewal of the mandate and criticized what it called the ''excessive bias'' of the U.S. draft resolution.

The U.N. classifies Western Sahara as a "non-self-governing territory," while critics of Morocco's control describe it as Africa's last colony. Morocco administers nearly all of the disputed territory, except for a narrow strip known as the "free zone" that lies east of a Moroccan-built sand wall.

After Morocco annexed it in 1975, the dispute escalated into an armed conflict that lasted more than 15 years and claimed more than 16,000 lives on both sides, according to the French Senate.

Bringing Western Sahara under its full sovereignty has been a central objective of Morocco's foreign policy for decades. Rabat, which has secured the backing of a growing number of Western capitals, including Washington, Paris and London, refers to the territory as its southern provinces. The dispute has become a defining feature of Morocco's diplomacy, with the kingdom often measuring its relations with other countries by their position on the issue.

The Polisario Front seeks independence for the territory, which it considers the homeland of the Indigenous Sahrawi people. Operating from refugee camps in the Algerian city of Tindouf, the movement aims to establish an independent Sahrawi Republic. Mainly backed by Algeria, Russia and South Africa, the Polisario has seen its international support dwindle in recent years.

A U.N.-brokered cease-fire took effect in 1991. The agreement also paved the way for the creation of the U.N. Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara, known as MINURSO.

The settlement plan provided for a referendum on self-determination, with independence among the options. But the vote never materialized. Morocco wanted the voter list to include Sahrawis living in the territory it controls, while the Polisario objected, arguing that their inclusion would tilt the outcome toward integration with Morocco. The movement insisted on using Spain's colonial census to determine voter eligibility.

Twenty MINURSO personnel lost their lives in the mission. The U.N. force was authorized to have 534 personnel, and its 2026-2027 budget was more than $62 million. The top military contributors to the force were Egypt, Ghana and Pakistan.

As the mission ends, the U.N. secretary-general ''calls upon all parties to respect and promote the rights of the people of Western Sahara,'' Dujarric said, and "remains concerned about the security situation throughout the Territory and the risk of escalation of hostilities. He calls on all concerned to exercise maximum restraint."

The Polisario withdrew from the ceasefire in 2020 after clashes and the territory has since remained the scene of tensions and low-intensity hostilities, the U.N. said last month.

Western Sahara is the major flashpoint in the rivalry between regional heavyweights Morocco and Algeria. Algiers, which arms, funds and hosts the Polisario Front, sees full Moroccan sovereignty over the territory as a major diplomatic defeat. The two countries severed diplomatic relations in 2021, and the end of the mission risks further straining ties and fueling an arms race.

articles.title: Initial results suggest Iliana Yotova wins runoff to become Bulgaria's 1st elected female president
articles.body:
SOFIA, Bulgaria (AP) — Acting President Iliana Yotova is the apparent winner of Bulgaria's presidential runoff, initial results of the vote count on Sunday showed, as former interim Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov conceded defeat.

According to the count by several polling agencies, Yotova received 58% of the vote. If confirmed by official results, she would become Bulgaria's first elected female head of state.

Gyurov, backed by reformist pro-Western opposition parties, is said to be trailing at around 38%.

Gyurov conceded defeat saying that "this is how the Bulgarian citizens have voted," and added that the results had to be accepted as they stood.

Official results were not expected before Monday.

The vote was the first major test for Prime Minister Rumen Radev's Moscow-friendly Progressive Bulgaria party, which endorsed Yotova. In April's parliamentary vote, the party won 131 of the 240 seats in Parliament, securing an outright majority.

Observers note that a victory for Yotova will keep the presidency in the hands of the governing majority. Such a concentration of power could prevent the effective maintenance of checks and balances on policy decisions by institutions, they say.

Yotova, 62, took over the presidency in January, when Radev stepped down to run for parliament, and was seeking her own elected mandate. She's expected to continue Radev's policy of keeping Bulgaria on its European path, while also supporting better relations with Russia and the lifting of sanctions.

After casting her vote on Sunday, Yotova said she voted for a Bulgaria that makes its own decisions and maintains a strong voice on the international stage.

"I voted for national consensus through dialogue, for institutions that work for citizens, for a strong state with its own foreign policy in a strong Europe," she told reporters.

The Balkan country joined NATO in 2004 and the European Union in 2007. While there is a broad consensus among the parties in parliament on the country's pro-Western path, widespread pro-Russia sentiment based on traditional historical and cultural ties with Russia has divided society, particularly since the start of Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Both Yotova and Radev have called for a diplomatic solution to end the war in Ukraine but remain evasive about possible Russian involvement in drone attacks in the Black Sea region.

During a television debate between the two presidential contenders, Yotova advocated for a settlement involving both Ukraine and Russia, saying that "peace could come only through negotiations." She also proposed a security meeting involving all six Black Sea countries to sign a moratorium on hostilities.

Bulgaria's presidency is primarily ceremonial. Although the head of state has no executive powers, and all major policies must be approved by parliament, direct election gives the president greater political authority. The president leads the armed forces and can veto legislation, signs international treaties and appoints ambassadors.

Presidents in Bulgaria are elected for a five-year term and can serve no more than two terms.

articles.title: WATCH: Zelenskyy confirms Ukraine hacked back after Russia's cyberattack of its emergency alert system
articles.body:
Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed that his country retaliated against Russia by hacking its emergency alert system.

"We only respond on their attacks," Zelenskyy said in an interview with PBS News' Amna Nawaz.

The cyberattack, the Ukrainian leader said, was a response to Russia seemingly hacking Ukraine's emergency alert system, which notifies residents of imminent threats.

"They attacked our system," he said. "It was a cyberattack."

Ukrainian authorities said on Sunday that users received false warnings of an imminent nuclear threat on their emergency alert mobile app. The alert system was suspended but is now back up and running.

SUPPORT PBS NEWS: Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass

"When it was very clear … that it's their personal attack against our people, civilians," Zelenskyy said. "Of course, we responded."

Russian authorities on Monday said hackers gained access to their emergency mobile app and sent fake emergency alerts.

Here are other key takeaways from his interview with PBS News.

When Nawaz asked Zelenskyy to describe his relationship with President Donald Trump in one word, Zelenskyy paused.

Trump has previously described Zelenskyy as "not a good guy," and has said he shouldn't be the Ukrainian president and doesn't want an end to the war.

WATCH: Ukraine less reliant on U.S. as Trump-Zelenskyy rift deepens, former ambassador says

Following the release of an American imprisoned in Russia, U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff described Putin as a "humanitarian." Putin has been indicted for war crimes by the International Criminal Court.

WATCH: American imprisoned by Russia released as Witkoff meets and praises Putin

"Sometimes we need to be pragmatic in this war," Zelenskyy said. "Who is an enemy? Who began this war? Putin. Don't find good words to describe him. I'm not sure that it will be helpful."

Zelenskyy also criticized Trump's deal with Russia to import tons of Russian diesel to the U.S.

"If you are really about money, business and pragmatism, so don't speak that it will have influence on the price in the United States," Zelenskyy said. "No, it's not true, it doesn't work."

WATCH: Ukraine disputes Trump's claim of energy ceasefire as Russian diesel deal draws fire

Experts say it's unlikely the deal will reduce global diesel prices in the near future.

The Ukrainian president told Nawaz the pragmatic thing to do is to support Ukraine.

"We have to support Ukraine," he said. "Because it has to be strong, because otherwise Putin will go further to Europe and to the different parts of NATO countries."

Zelenskyy said he has asked Trump several times to reduce limits to Ukraine's use of Starshield, a military-grade version of Starlink satellite internet service. The system is funded by the Pentagon and operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX.

Starshield, which is a key component of Ukraine's military communications network, has geographic restrictions. It can't be used to carry out attacks inside Russia. It can act defensively and in the Russian occupied territories of Ukraine.

Zelenskyy said if given the opportunity, Ukraine would use the system to identify and attack missile launch sites inside Russia. He said Ukraine would not use Starshield to carry out massive attacks on Russia or energy sites due to the likelihood of civilian casualties.

Lifting Starshield limits would mean Russia wouldn't "have opportunity to use each day ballistic missiles against us," Zelenskyy said. "Because we will block their launches."

The Ukrainian president said Trump seemed open to the reduction of limits.

"He said that he will try. It doesn't depend on him," Zelenskyy said. "He said that it depends mostly on SpaceX. He said that he's supportive, and I was very thankful."

In mid-October, Starshield was partially disabled. The details of what happened are unclear.

WATCH: How Starlink disruptions affected Ukraine's battlefield operations

Musk said limits to Starshield's speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and Trump. Trump has said he didn't order the restrictions and doubted that Musk was to blame for the disruption.

Asked who he thought was to blame for the disruption, Zelenskyy said he's unsure whether Musk can act alone.

"I'm not sure that he can do it with Starshield because it's military. It's government version," Zelenskyy said. "I'm not sure that he could do it personally alone without any representatives from American government."

Asked whether he believes Musk supports Ukraine and wants it to win the war, Zelenskyy said "I don't know."

He said he wanted to speak with Musk following the Starshield disruptions but "they didn't connect with us."

See more of our interview with Zelenskyy on Monday's PBS News Hour.

Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue.

articles.title: A brief ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine opens a perilous escape window from Kherson's riverside kill zone
articles.body:
KOZATSKE, Ukraine (AP) — A white towel on her gate and a white rag in her hand were Ukrainian Nataliia Diadiuk's only ways to tell Russian drone operators she is a civilian. When a brief ceasefire kicked in on Oct. 27, she had a moment of respite.

The 53-year-old is one of a handful of residents left in Kozatske, a riverside village located in the kill zone of Ukraine's Kherson region less than 2 kilometers (1.2 miles) from a Russian-controlled area.

"I really want silence," Diadiuk said, fighting back tears as she stood on an empty street lined with abandoned houses. "And I want to see the people who left, all of them. People left for both sides."

Diadiuk's life has been reduced to basic survival: rainwater to drink, firewood gathered around town for heat, a radio she tries to tune in to for news, and the remnants of humanitarian aid that had not reached her in two years until the brief ceasefire that ended Sunday night just days after it began. Going out means dodging every kind of weapon, including mines scattered everywhere. The neighbors she mentions are more often the dead than the few still living nearby.

A team from The Associated Press gained rare access to a so-called red zone to see firsthand what life in the kill zone looks like, a visit made possible only because of a brief, localized ceasefire tied to the humanitarian aid mission in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky.

People walk next to damaged buildings, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in the frontline city of Kherson, Ukraine, Oct. 28, 2026. Photo by Reuters stringer

Oleshky has drawn the world's attention, but civilians are trapped in many more places on both sides of the front line. During the mission, Ukrainian regional officials, police, the Ukrainian Red Cross Society and volunteers, with the facilitation of civil-military cooperation specialists, used the rare window of time to reach people on their side of the river, some of them cut off for nearly two years.

In all, 180 people were evacuated from riverside communities and the city of Kherson, including 23 children, the regional administration said. About 140,000 people remain in the Ukrainian-held part of the Kherson region.

Before the war, the whole region, now nearly 70% under Russian control, had about 1 million residents. The riverside is designated a red zone, the highest level of military danger. With the ceasefire over, residents will again face drones, artillery, glide bombs and airdropped mines. Still, many refuse to leave. Some cannot afford to start over, and others will not abandon the places where they grew up.

On the road to Diadiuk's village, burned-out cars sit abandoned where they were hit, alongside wrecked ground robots that Ukrainians try sending down roads too dangerous for people. A relic of peacetime still stands on that road: "Thank you for keeping the roadside clean."

In the village, many houses are reduced to burned walls. Glide bombs have left craters, and the tail fins of shells stick out of the asphalt like flowers. Mines dropped from drones lie everywhere, some petal-shaped, others improvised and wrapped in foil or plastic, so every step must be taken with care. Thick vegetation swallows the ruins of empty houses.

What Diadiuk finds hardest to bear is the howling of the dogs left behind in the houses, surviving much as she is. "Even for the sake of these, I can't leave them," she says, pointing to two thin dogs that never stray far from her. But she shares what little food she has with other dogs as well.

A woman walks on a street covered with an anti-drone net, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in the frontline city of Kherson, Ukraine Oct. 30, 2026. Photo by Nina Liashonok/ Reuters

Isolated and forced to fight for survival every day, she has lost track of time. "I turn on my phone only to see what day it is," she says. She charges it with solar panels.

Diadiuk collects rainwater, strains it through gauze, treats it with chlorine and boils it. "The water here is more or less all right," she says. "There are a lot of dead lying in the houses, so it's good water only in a manner of speaking."

The village's ordeal began in the first days of Russia's full-scale invasion, when it was occupied. After Ukrainian forces liberated it, Kozatske gradually came under siege by drones as the war turned increasingly technological.

"Before, I'd just open the door and walk out," said Oleksii Shavokin, 54, who lives a little farther down the street. "Now I open it a crack, stick my ear out and listen to the sky."

His house burned down in early 2023 after a mortar attack, he said, but he patched it up and stays on there. He lives off old humanitarian aid and eggs from the hens he still keeps. "I ration my food so it lasts. I'm used to it," he said. "Now I eat once a day, in the evening, and that's quite enough." He has lost 30 kilograms (66 pounds) from a weight of close to 100 kilograms (220 pounds).

Many of the people he knew were killed by strikes, and others left. He decided to stay.

"I value life, but where's the guarantee a car won't hit me somewhere else?" Shavokin said. "Wherever it's written for you, that's where you'll lose your life, or go on living. And still, I hope this all ends soon."

Many residents who stay do not know where they would go and fear they would be left to fend for themselves, said Oleh Tarabaka, head of the Nova Kakhovka city military administration. He was part of the team that tried to persuade Diadiuk and Shavokin to leave.

But it is difficult, he said. Many have lived there their whole lives and fear that once they leave, they will have nothing to live on. Not everyone has someone to go to. Some have no relatives.

"If there hadn't been a period of quiet, we simply wouldn't have gotten people out," Tarabaka said. "We wouldn't have been able to drive in here."

What residents are living through goes beyond survival, Tarabaka said, adding that perhaps no word has yet been invented to describe it.

Municipality workers wearing helmets drive under anti-drone nets during a regional ceasefire, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in Kherson, Ukraine October 28, 2026. Photo by Thomas Peter/ Reuters

Some, however, can be persuaded to leave. That was the case for Yevhen and his mother, Antonina, who declined to give their last names for security reasons.

One of the military officials turned to Yevhen. "Just make the right decision, the decision of a man and a son," a Ukrainian soldier from the 42nd brigade who was part of the evacuation group told him.

All the way through her bombed-out town, Antonina wailed and wept, not wanting to leave. Her cries echoed through the empty streets.

The temporary truce allowed the Red Cross to evacuate far more people than usual from Kherson city. Normally, every route and every stage must be planned around the constant threat of drones and other weapons.

"Right now, some streets and places in Kherson are a kill zone too. It's simply impossible to slip through there. The risk is very, very high," said Mykola Taranenko, commander of the Ukrainian Red Cross Society's rapid response team in the Kherson region.

His team usually evacuates about 10 people a week, but during the ceasefire week, it took out 32.

Among those evacuated were Volodymyr and Kateryna Yakuba, both 77, who divorced more than 20 years ago but left the city together. Their daughter arranged the evacuation, and they are going to stay with her in Odesa.

"We need to get out before the cold sets in," Kateryna said, adding about the ceasefire: "I don't know how we would have gotten out otherwise."

"It's scary to leave home," her voice trembled. "You don't know if you'll come back, or if there will be anything to come back to."

Associated Press journalists Vasilisa Stepanenko and Evgeniy Maloletka contributed to this report.

articles.title: Iran's delegation has left negotiations in Qatar after a tense weekend. Here's where things stand
articles.body:
JERUSALEM (AP) — The Middle East is bracing for a possible return to all-out war amid concerns that the United States and Israel could strike Iran shortly after Tuesday's U.S. midterm elections.

A regional official briefed on the talks said an Iranian delegation left Qatar on Sunday after negotiations aimed at reaching a deal to end the war. A draft proposal has been circulated for feedback, and a follow-up meeting is under discussion. The official spoke on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the talks.

Iran has expanded its threats but says it is awaiting the latest U.S. response. The latest proposal Iran has publicly discussed would fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz to shipping within two days if Washington meets several conditions, including lifting its blockade of Iranian ports.

Here's where things currently stand.

U.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday evening told reporters he and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had a "very good" call on Saturday. He said they discussed Iran but gave no details.

Even before Netanyahu and his bloc of allies lost their majority in parliament in last week's election, there were growing fears that Netanyahu was pushing for new strikes against Iran in an effort to stay in power in an emergency government during renewed war. Since last Tuesday's election, the prime minister has publicly commented only on the vote.

There was no word from Netanyahu and his office on the latest call with Trump, who has continued to alternate between public comments about pursuing talks with Iran and threats to strike it hard.

"The standoff in the Gulf between the U.S. and Iran is really between Qatar and Israel," Andreas Krieg, a professor at King's College London, said on X. "Qatar is tirelessly working on a diplomatic offramp with the region's backing while Israel is looking for military ways to throw the region under the bus."

The Islamic Republic has stepped up its public messaging during the uncertainty, saying it is ready for both diplomacy and renewed fighting.
