The new supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, met with Iran's military chiefs and said the response to "any kind and level of threat" from the U.S. or Israel should be immediate and without "geographic limits," and urged an expansion of the list of potential targets.

Khamenei still has not been seen publicly since the opening strikes by Israel and the U.S. on Feb. 28 killed his father, the previous supreme leader.

Iran's security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, warned on X that any attack would bring "devastating blows on the aggressor using new weapons."

In an interview with state television, Rezaei said "the tone has completely changed" from the U.S. and called it a "very good sign." He gave no details about the letter he received from U.S. Vice President JD Vance, which Iran acknowledged last week, and said he had not responded.

Rezaei also said no decision had been made to change Iran's nuclear doctrine, though some Iranians had questioned whether it should change if the country were attacked again. Tehran has insisted its nuclear program is peaceful.

Washington seeks to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon and wants to address the issue in any new talks. Iran wants to discuss it later.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, who was on a one-day visit to neighboring Turkmenistan on Monday, has said the final outcome depends on U.S. answers to the "Iranian questions."

More attacks on commercial ships were reported on the Strait of Hormuz during October, in the busiest month for reported assaults since March, during the war's opening weeks.

The mood was grim at the Manama Dialogue, an annual security summit in Bahrain organized by the International Institute for Strategic Studies.

United Arab Emirates presidential adviser Anwar Gargash told attendees that "the rules of logic" show the U.S. and Iranian stances are far apart, and "if these positions are not bridged, then we have to worry about the worst."

Gulf nations have spent billions of dollars to boost their defense capabilities since the war began. Egypt's Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty told the gathering in Bahrain that the next escalation "will be more dangerous, more destructive, and it will lead to nowhere."

Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova described reports of possible new strikes against Iran as "alarming."

Meanwhile, China will send a special envoy to Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia in early to mid-November, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told reporters Monday. Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi also met with Ali Bagheri Kani, deputy secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council.

"The Middle East Gulf region should not become an arena for great-power rivalry and geopolitical conflict," Chinese President Xi Jinping told Oman's sultan, according to a readout from China's Foreign Ministry. China and Oman called for a return to dialogue.

Victoria Eastwood in Cairo, Kanis Leung in Hong Kong and Katie Marie Davies in London contributed to this report.

Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue.

articles.title: Ukraine and Russia both report fake emergency alerts after cyberattacks target apps as limited ceasefire ends
articles.body:
KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Authorities in Ukraine and Russia said their emergency alert mobile apps had been targeted by cyberattacks, with users in Ukraine receiving false warnings of an imminent nuclear threat.

It was not clear if the attacks late Sunday were related. Ukraine said its service, which residents rely on to seek safety amid daily Russian missile and drone strikes, was up and running again after being suspended due to the attack.

WATCH: Inside a Ukrainian city hit by Russian drones during the Starlink disruption

Russian authorities said Monday that hackers had sent fake emergency alerts after gaining access to the Russian Emergency Situations Ministry's mobile app, and that efforts were ongoing to restore the app's functionality.

A Russian Telegram channel said a hacking group, Hitcore, had claimed responsibility for the breach of the Ukrainian system, but that could not be independently verified. Any affiliations or other details surrounding the identities or motivations of the purported hackers were unclear.

The alerts received by Ukrainians — making false claims of high radiation levels, a chemical threat and public disturbances in Kyiv — were written in English with spelling and grammatical errors as well as in a mix of Russian and Ukrainian.

One of the messages, written in Russian, said: "Hi! There will be a nuclear threat across Ukraine. Do not worry, the Oreshnik is incoming," a reference to a Russian intermediate-range ballistic missile.

In a Telegram post late Sunday following the breach, Ukraine's air raid alert channel said "unauthorized parties" had interfered with the app's operation and warned users not to click on links in "suspicious notifications."

Ukraine's state-run Center for Countering Disinformation urged users to monitor other emergency channels on social media and rely on physical alerts while the cyberattack was being addressed.

Yurii Ihnat, a spokesman for Ukraine's air force command, told Ukraine's private 1+1 television that the cyberattack had no impact on Ukraine's security and defense operations because the app is separate from military command systems.

In a statement, Russia's Emergency Ministry said that hackers had used its mobile app to send a false alert across 33 of Russia's 89 regions at approximately 2:45 a.m. Moscow time (11:45 p.m. GMT). It did not name who it believed carried out the attack.

The ministry said that the digital vulnerability exploited by the attackers had been identified and that "necessary measures" were being taken to prevent a similar breach. It also reassured Russians that the wider public alert system was working normally through SMS messages, media broadcasts and municipal sirens and loudspeakers.

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said that all of Russia's state agencies were under the constant threat of cyberattacks, including a growing number that use artificial intelligence.

"All government bodies must take steps to improve the cybersecurity of our digital resources," Peskov said.

Ukrainian authorities in the war-divided Kherson region reported multiple Russian drone attacks early Monday, hours after a humanitarian ceasefire expired.

The regional administration said a 62-year-old woman and a 73-year-old man were hospitalized with blast injuries in the city of Kherson, across the Dnipro River from Russian-occupied territory.

The localized ceasefire, which began on Oct. 27, ended at midnight at the start of Monday. The brief pause in fighting was part of a humanitarian aid and evacuation mission in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, and marked the most significant truce between Kyiv and Moscow since Russia's full-scale invasion began nearly five years ago.

Speaking to reporters in Kyiv on Monday, Ukraine's ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said the oldest person evacuated to Ukrainian territory during the mission was 94 years old, and added that 104 pets, including four parrots, were also rescued.

Lubinets, who was Ukraine's lead civilian negotiator for the mission, said he hoped the localized ceasefire and evacuation would act as a "pilot model" for other missions, and could "add to the momentum" of three-way negotiations between Ukrainian, Russian and U.S. officials expected this month.

He said Ukraine hoped to make future aid deliveries to residents who chose to stay in Oleshky, and that the delivery mechanism was still being worked out. He described the involvement of U.S. first lady Melania Trump, who helped broker the limited truce, as critical.

"Without the American representation, we could not even imagine such cooperation because many bodies, including military and intelligence, were involved in this combined effort," he said.

Lubinets described the mission as exhausting and "very complicated."

"We crossed into the territory of the Russian Federation and had to remain alert at all times," he said. "We are dog-tired."

An estimated 2,000 civilians were in Oleshky when the temporary truce took effect. They could evacuate to territory controlled by either Ukraine or Russia, or remain in the city with replenished food and medical supplies. Exact evacuation totals were withheld to protect those who stayed.

Ukraine's general staff said Monday that Russia's military had bolstered its drone defenses and replenished ammunition supplies in the area during the ceasefire.

Elsewhere in Ukraine, emergency services reported that drone strikes injured 12 people in the eastern Kharkiv region and damaged a refrigeration facility, greenhouses and residential buildings.

Five people were also reported injured in the Black Sea port city of Odesa, where a warehouse was targeted and homes were damaged.

Russia's Ministry of Defense said Monday that it shot down 212 Ukrainian drones overnight, while the head of Russia's Samara region, Gov. Vyacheslav Fedorishchev, said in a statement that local air defenses were repelling an aerial attack, but did not give further details.

Independent Russian media outlets later reported that Ukrainian drones had targeted one of Europe's largest oil transport hubs in Samara.

Katie Marie Davies contributed to this report from Manchester, England.

Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue.

articles.title: Supreme Court rejects Trump administration’s bid to set aside 20K California ballots
articles.body:
by Zach Schonfeld 11/02/26 05:55 PM ET

The Supreme Court on Monday quickly rejected the Trump administration’s effort to force California officials to set aside 20,000 ballots it claims belong to likely noncitizens and must be investigated.

The court’s one-sentence order contained no explanation and had no noted dissents.

California and immigration rights groups question the veracity of the administration’s list and say its lawsuit is an attempt to disenfranchise legal voters. The administration raced its claims to the Supreme Court earlier on Monday after California persuaded lower courts that the administration has no legal right to push the state to comply.

The administration warned that the clock was running out. All sides agree that ballots can’t be separated once they’re processed, and election officials have already received hundreds of thousands of mail ballots ahead of polls opening on Tuesday.

“The only way to preserve the district court’s ability to grant relief to the United States after a full merits proceeding, therefore, is to segregate the challenged ballots now. That remedy would not cause any undue hardship to California,” Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote to the court.

The court rejected the bid within hours and without ordering California to file a response.

articles.title: Forecasts of midterm blue wave put Trump’s legacy on line
articles.body:
by Julia Manchester 11/02/26 05:23 PM ET

President Trump’s political capital is on the line ahead of the midterm elections as a potential blue wave threatens his final two years in office.

Trump has crisscrossed the country, holding 28 in-person campaign rallies in addition to a series of tele-rallies. The president has made stops in Republican strongholds like Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas and even Alaska in an effort to keep the states firmly in the red column. He’s also visited a number of deep-red states like Mississippi and South Carolina, where polls show closer than expected races.

While Trump has argued his rallies have boosted Republican incumbents and candidates in the states, recent polling suggests otherwise.

A New York Times/Siena poll released the day before Election Day showed Democrats with leads in Senate races in Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas and Alaska.

Trump’s heavy political investment in the states means he could end up shouldering the blame for a potential blue wave, which could impact the GOP beyond Election Day.

Republicans warn that a blue wave would be detrimental to the last two years of the Trump administration, and by extension, his legacy.

“It impacts his ability to drive policy over the next two years, or if a Supreme Court nomination comes up, or fill in the blank in terms of even Cabinet turnover,” said one Republican strategist, speaking on condition of anonymity. “All of that too will help shape his legacy, and it’s how people remember you at the end that guides you into the history books.”

In a statement to The Hill on Monday, the Republican National Committee (RNC) warned that Democrats would “obstruct” Trump’s agenda and that their “disastrous economic policies” would drive jobs overseas.

“The president knows what’s at stake this cycle, which is why he’s barnstormed the country to encourage our voters to support Republican candidates that will advance his agenda and deliver for the American people,” said RNC spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre.

But during an election eve speech at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, Trump did not appear entirely focused on the elections that could impact the trajectory of his last two years in office.

The president spent the first 22 minutes of his 37-minute address — largely viewed as a closing message before the midterms — talking about his administration’s efforts to repair the Reflecting Pool. Trump showed off a number of pre-renovation pictures of the pool and at one point invited Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to the podium to give brief remarks.

Trump also touted his numerous beautification projects and lower crime in the nation’s capital.

Republican operative Rob Stutzman called Trump’s speech “another Captain Queeg moment,” a reference to a character from Herman Wouk’s 1951 novel “The Caine Mutiny” who is considered an unstable and incompetent commander.

A second Republican strategist said, “What the utter f— was that?” when asked for their reaction to Trump’s speech at the Reflecting Pool.

“Republicans were hoping that he would have some sort of a closing message, some sort of American message with it, with a wonderful backdrop that could maybe be of help in the closing hours here,” the unnamed GOP strategist said. “As we Republicans are losing touch with the public, it looked like he was losing touch with reality.”

One national Republican operative noted the speech was “not surprising” considering Trump’s communication style but expressed frustration with the closing message.

“This perfectly encapsulates his messaging throughout this entire campaign cycle, but it’s deeply frustrating when we need to be laser-focused on turning out our low propensity voters tomorrow,” the operative said.

A third Republican strategist defended the speech, arguing the Reflecting Pool was “a hook” for Trump to be able to talk about issues like crime and immigration.

“It’s one of these things that wherever you get the opportunity to speak to a national audience, you’re going to talk about the midterms even if you have to start with something else,” the strategist said.

Trump did take some time during his speech Monday to urge Republicans to turn out on Election Day.

“If the people that voted for me and voted in the last election where we had such a great victory, if they go out and vote, just a good portion of them, we will win in a landslide,” the president said.

“Now, that doesn’t happen because usually whoever the sitting president is — Republican or Democrat, good or bad, good president, great president, bad president — for some reason the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms.”

“We gave this a very strong shot,” he added.

Much of the GOP’s strategy has hinged on turning out its low-propensity base as much as possible, arguably a tall order for any political party in a nonpresidential election. Republicans hoped to defy that trend by dispatching Trump on the campaign trail, urging voters to “pretend” like he is on the ballot.

“The amount of rallies he did shows he ‘believes’ that he’s on the ballot tomorrow,” said Dan Eberhart, a Republican donor. “He worked hard, and he’s right: Tomorrow’s outcome is a reflection on him.”

In a statement to The Hill, White House spokesperson Davis Ingle referred to Trump as the GOP’s “best messenger” and “unmatched motivator” who is “committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress.”

But some Republicans are unsure whether that tactic will ultimately work.

“So far from what we’ve seen, those rallies have not done what they were meant to do,” said the first unnamed Republican strategist.

Democrats have been heartened by signs of early turnout in key battlegrounds, but Republicans argue that a large share of their voters tend to vote in person on Election Day.

“They’re banking on these Republicans and the folks that he’s trying to rally to show up tomorrow, and Republicans historically and should do exceedingly well tomorrow,” the first Republican strategist said. “But the fact is, they still underperformed in places like Texas and in Florida in the early vote.”

According to data released by Texas’s secretary of State, 7.7 million voters in the Lone Star State voted early.

Meanwhile in Florida, registered Republicans led registered Democrats in early voting by just a little more than 200,000 voters. By comparison, in 2022, registered Republicans led Democrats in early voting by just a little less than 500,000 voters.

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) on Sunday sounded the alarm over low turnout in the state, which has become known as a nerve center for Republican politics.

“If people stay home, you could end up seeing results that you’re going to be wondering what happened. That’s just the reality,” DeSantis said at a campaign event.

“The reality is gas is higher, and that’s not good. Some of these Republicans act like it’s no big deal. I disagree with that. It is a big deal to people,” the Florida governor continued.

articles.title: Vladimir Putin’s Nov. 3 panic
articles.body:
by Rep. George Whitesides (D-Calif.), opinion contributor 11/02/26 05:00 PM ET

President Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin are reading the same polling data. On Nov. 3, Republicans look set to suffer a heavy defeat in the midterm elections — a result that will almost certainly hand the House of Representatives back to the Democrats, put the Senate in play, and break the White House’s stranglehold over Ukraine policy. The window to finalize a Moscow-skewed settlement is rapidly closing.

That political calculus explains the sudden, strong-armed campaign from Washington and Moscow to bully Kyiv into concessions. Knowing their political leverage is about to expire, Trump and Putin are racing to lock Ukraine into a bad deal before a newly elected, pro-Ukraine Congress arrives in January to stop them.

Look at the sheer brazenness of the terms Washington is shoving across the table at Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. Faced with record-high American diesel prices ahead of Election Day — in large part due to his war in Iran — Trump has opted to blame Ukraine instead. On Oct. 9, Trump struck a deal with Putin to bring sanctioned Russian diesel to American and global markets, while demanding that Kyiv halt its highly-effective long-range drone strikes on the Russian refineries that produce and distribute the diesel.

This deal exposes a reality that the Kremlin has desperately tried to hide: Putin is hurting badly and Kyiv’s drone campaign is working. In recent months, Putin has acknowledged Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy infrastructure has created problems for the country. Kyiv’s campaign has knocked out so much Russian refining capacity that Moscow is desperate to protect what is left.

Putin is unable to stop the drones with his own air defenses, which have proven capable of reaching even Moscow. So, he has enlisted the American president to act as a shield for Russia’s energy sector, single-handedly giving the Kremlin a fresh revenue stream in the midst of a war.

When Zelensky resisted, the administration escalated to battlefield coercion. U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner warned Ukrainian officials that the United States’ critical intelligence sharing could be cut off if Ukraine kept hitting Russian oil refineries. Moving the administration’s approach from threats to action, the U.S. may have withheld early warnings of incoming Russian ballistic missiles. Those strikes killed six Ukrainians and knocked out power to 600,000 people.

Simultaneously, reports indicate the White House then demanded that Pete Hegseth’s Defense Department impose speed restrictions on the military-grade Starshield terminals used by the Ukrainian armed forces, cutting off data links whenever a terminal moves above 100 miles per hour — a change that would hobble Ukraine’s high-speed interceptor and strike drones in the middle of active combat.

The financial squeeze is just as blatant. Witkoff and Kushner have been pressing European capitals to transfer billions in frozen Russian central-bank assets into a Washington-run mechanism to “revive peace talks.” Fortunately, European leaders have rejected the pitch out of hand. Handing that money back to the Kremlin would bail out Russia’s overheating war economy while stripping Europe of the financial reserves it needs to bankroll Ukraine’s defense independently of Washington.

The timing of this three-pronged assault is obvious. Even a Democratic takeover of the House alone — let alone a sweep that includes the Senate — will upend this coercion campaign. Already, a bipartisan group of senators, including Republicans like Sens. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) and John Cornyn (R-Texas), is demanding that Trump rescind the Russian diesel deal. If Democrats take control in January, they will have the budgetary leverage and investigative power to lock in intelligence sharing by statute, force the Pentagon to restore full Starshield access, pass multi-year military aid, and keep Russian sovereign assets frozen.

For Putin, who is grappling with double-digit interest rates and acute labor shortages at home, another two years of attritional war against a fully funded Ukraine is a prospect he may not survive. He desperately needs an end to refinery strikes, restored oil revenues, and a crippled Ukrainian military before the American voter strips Trump of his ability to deliver them.

This pressure campaign will fail, because Ukrainians are not going to trade away their survival to rescue Trump and Putin from their respective political calendars. Tragically, however, it has already cost Ukrainian lives, and it will cost scores more as Russian missiles hit cities denied early warnings and power grids fail in the autumn cold.

Kyiv and its European allies need to hold their nerve through the end of the year. The sheer desperation of this squeeze proves that time is no longer on Moscow’s side. Strong leaders do not scramble to beat a voting deadline. Ukraine’s task is to weather the extortion, keep the drones flying toward Russia’s refineries, make sure Europe keeps the frozen Russian assets under lock and key, and wait for January.

George Whitesides represents California’s 27th District in Congress and is a member of the Armed Services Committee.

articles.title: Zelensky warns Russia could exploit US midterms to launch massive attack
articles.body:
by Mira Bhakta 11/02/26 04:35 PM ET

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky warned Russia could use Tuesday’s midterm elections in the U.S. to launch a massive attack against Ukraine.

“We have intel that Russia is preparing a new massive attack on our country – primarily targeting energy and logistics,” he wrote in a statement on social media. “The assumption is basically that tomorrow the world will be watching the American midterms, and what is happening here in Ukraine, along with our difficulties with air defense and Patriot missiles, will be overlooked.”

He renewed his calls for the U.S. and other countries to make Russia “feel that terror is no good,” adding “we must not play games with Russia’s oil or gas revenue.”

“We must put pressure on Russia in such a way that it has no alternative but to end this war. America can do this,” he concluded.

The statement appeared alongside a video of Zelensky describing recent Russian attacks on a humanitarian site in Ukraine that reportedly killed 34 people, with some victims still stuck under the rubble.

He added that air raid sirens were playing in Kyiv as the city braces for potential missile fire.

This comes after first lady Melania Trump announced a localized ceasefire between the European countries in and around Oleshky — a town occupied by Russia since its invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Ukrainian officials accused Russia of using the ceasefire to bring in new troops, strengthen its military positions, add in more antidrone defenses on roads and send more ammunition to the area, according to multiple outlets.

The ceasefire ended on Sunday, with the first lady calling it a “success,” touting on social media that it enabled “the evacuation of nearly 800 people.”

Three-way peace negotiations between the U.S., Ukraine and Russia are slated for later this month in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates.

articles.title: Reflecting Pool dominates Trump’s closing midterm speech
articles.body:
by Mallory Wilson 11/02/26 04:19 PM ET

President Trump’s closing speech a day before the midterm elections focused on the reopening of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and other changes around Washington, D.C.

Trump in remarks at the Reflecting Pool announced its reopening. He showed pictures of what was replaced and said it should be a project that “unites all Americans.”

“Today, I’m thrilled to announce the official opening of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool,” he said.

He said they were considering renaming it the Trump Reflecting Pool but then said he was joking.

The pool has been fenced off for months after algae blooms and slits in the lining plagued the original renovation that Trump wanted.

The president didn’t touch on the midterm elections until roughly 20 minutes into his speech, focusing mostly on the pool repairs and other efforts to beautify D.C., such as fixing fountains, removing graffiti and cutting down on crime.

“As you know, this is the last day before the midterm elections, the most important midterm I believe in our lifetime,” he said. “The Democrat Party has nominated the most extreme and dangerous slate of candidates in American history. These are the most dangerous candidates ever put up.”

He touted his administration’s achievements and hit on several candidates, such as Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, repeating claims about the nominee’s ties to the Muslim Brotherhood. Trump also touched on Alaska Senate candidate Dan J. Sullivan, who is running against incumbent GOP Sen. Dan S. Sullivan.

“We’ve achieved more in less than two years than any administration in American history, and I’ve kept every single promise I made, except far more,” he said. “I’ve actually kept far more promises than I made. We’ve done much more than I promised, and we have the most secure border in American history.”

He repeated his promise of giving American adults a $5,000 check if Republicans win the midterms.

He noted that he has traveled extensively the last few weeks to hold rallies, saying they were “full of love.”

“America is ready to go,” he said. “They’re ready to vote. I hope they’re ready to do the right thing.”

Trump said Republicans gave this election cycle “a very strong shot.”

“For some reason, the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms, but we gave this a very strong shot,” he said.

Trump spoke briefly about not allowing Iran to have a nuclear weapon before bringing his speech back to the Reflecting Pool.

articles.title: Trump, Hegseth underwater on approval from military members, veterans: Poll
articles.body:
by Ryan J. Karlin 11/02/26 04:09 PM ET

President Trump and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth are underwater in their approval ratings with veterans and military members, according to a poll conducted by Common Defense.

In a survey of 731 active-duty service members, veterans and military families, 67 percent of respondents said they believe military decisions under Trump are being made for political gain. About 50 percent said they disapprove of Trump and Hegseth.

“Right now, nearly 8-in-10 veterans and military families say they’re being left behind, and active-duty troops are telling us that politicization is pushing them toward the exit. That’s not a talking point; it’s a readiness crisis,” said Jose Vasquez, U.S. Army veteran and executive director of Common Defense.

Fifty-three percent of respondents said they want to separate from the military sooner because of politicization, while 45 percent said policy changes or uncertainty under Trump made them want to exit sooner.

Still, 47 percent of respondents said the Republican Party does a better job at communicating with the military. The poll’s sample consisted of 47 percent Republicans and 35 percent Democrats.

Common Defense found 67 percent of respondents felt decisions that affect service members were being made for political gain and not mission readiness.

Hegseth has moved to reform the Pentagon through changes to readiness standards that often regard culture war issues and the implementation of a “warrior ethos.”

“Veterans know what real leadership looks like: you take care of the people under your command and you keep politics out of the mission,” Vasquez said.

Almost three-fourths of respondents expressed their disapproval of Congress. Forty-eight percent of active-duty respondents said they want the U.S. to pull out of Iran, while 55 percent want Congress to investigate the “deployments and troops’ health, safety, and welfare” during Operation Epic Fury in the Middle East.

Vasquez said military voters will consider candidates based on “what they’ve actually done for those who serve” and not on how emphatically they speak about supporting the military.

Common Defense reached respondents online and said the sample “skews older, whiter, more male, and more Republican.” The poll, taken in September and released in October, has a 4-point margin of error.

articles.title: Trump touts oil price drop on day before election
articles.body:
by Rachel Frazin 11/02/26 04:01 PM ET

President Trump on Monday touted a new drop in oil prices during his closing pitch to voters ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections.

International benchmark Brent crude was trading at $104 Monday afternoon, down from $112 earlier in the day. U.S. benchmark WTI was trading at about $96 per barrel, down from nearly $103.

The price drop came amid some signs of positivity in talks with Iran. Tehran offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz if the U.S. agreed to meet certain conditions, but it is unclear if the U.S. will meet those conditions. There has also been talk in Washington of new strikes on Iran after the midterm elections.

The war has periodically seen closures of the Strait of Hormuz, a key oil shipping lane, as well as higher costs to transport oil even when ships have been allowed to pass through. Damage to oil infrastructure in that conflict and the Russia-Ukraine conflict have also put upward pressure on prices.

“Oil today is down $10,” Trump said Monday while delivering his closing midterm remarks at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in Washington.

“It’s going to go down a lot further because we’re winning with Iran, easily winning,” he added.

Trump claimed that the decline was “the biggest drop in oil in history.”

Recent history has seen larger drops; during the COVID-19 pandemic, oil prices on one day briefly sank to about negative $38 per barrel, falling by far more than $10.

If Monday’s drop is sustained, it could be good news for prices at the pump in the days and weeks ahead, but it can also take time for changes in the price of oil to reflect in gasoline and diesel.

Voters’ discontent with these prices is expected to be a major factor in the election. As of Monday, the average U.S. gasoline price was around $4.17 per gallon, up $1.13 from the same time last year, according to AAA.

articles.title: Iran offers to open Strait of Hormuz on several conditions
articles.body:
by Filip Timotija 11/02/26 03:13 PM ET

Iran offered to open the Strait of Hormuz on several conditions during negotiations, as President Trump has warned he is open to authorizing major combat operations against Tehran after the November midterm elections.

Iranian officials are demanding that the U.S. government lift sanctions and release billions of dollars in frozen Iranian assets — requests that Washington is unlikely to accept as diplomatic talks in the Middle East continue.

“If Iran’s legitimate demands are accepted and implemented, it would be possible to put the entire plan into operation within two days, restore security to the Strait of Hormuz and initiate the negotiation process,” Esmail Baghaei, spokesperson for the Iranian Foreign Ministry, told reporters on Monday, according to multiple outlets.

“⁠The realization of this depends entirely on Washington’s will and decision,” Baghaei said.

Iran effectively closed down the Strait of Hormuz, through which around 20 percent of the world’s oil transits daily, following the U.S. and Israeli military strikes against Tehran in late February, a closure that has ratcheted up energy prices.

The conditions are not significantly different from Iran’s position throughout the conflict, but they come as Trump has signaled increased openness to greenlighting strikes.

“The only reason why I’m not finished with Iran is I want to be nice. I want to try and save all those lives if I can,” the president said Saturday at a rally in Iowa. “But at some point we’re going to have to give them the hammer.”

Baghaei’s remarks come days after an Iranian delegation traveled to Doha as part of an effort by mediators, led by Qatar, to revive talks in hopes of staving off another cycle of military conflict.

Vice President Vance sent a letter to Iranian security official Mohsen Rezaei via Qatari mediators last week to revive peace negotiations. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said in a recent interview that it was a “positive step.”

“If Washington’s goal in sending this letter is to stir up discord, it would be yet another mistake to add to its previous ones,” Araghchi told Al Jazeera on Saturday.

articles.title: Adam Hamilton responds to Trump’s ‘perverted pastor’ remarks in Kansas
articles.body:
by Ryan J. Karlin 11/02/26 02:26 PM ET

Kansas Democratic Senate candidate Adam Hamilton said it was “pathetic” for President Trump to call him a “perverted pastor” at a Sunday rally in support of Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.).

“I think it’s sad, it’s pathetic to be calling a pastor a pervert and all the things that he’s been saying,” Hamilton told NewsNation’s Mills Hayes on Monday.

Hamilton said he took Trump’s Sunday insults, which echoed attacks the president made against Hamilton at another October rally, as an “honor.” The Democrat added he is praying for both Trump and Marshall.

Hamilton is locked in a tight race that could make him the first Democrat to represent Kansas in the upper chamber in nearly a century.

“I’ll just say, it doesn’t bother me,” Hamilton added of Trump’s remark. “I feel like that says more about him than it says about me.”

Hamilton said Trump — who hit Hamilton over his support for transgender rights — held the rally two days before Election Day to boost the Republican in a race most did not expect to be competitive just a few months ago.

The president originally canceled the rally but ended up appearing anyway after forcefully pushing back on reporters questioning his motive for the cancellation.

“He’s come here at the end of a long day, and he’s come here desperately trying to save my opponent, Roger Marshall, and I don’t think that’s going to happen,” Hamilton said.

Hamilton has consistently portrayed himself as a centrist as he tries to win in a state Trump carried by more than 16 points two years ago. Despite the conflict, Hamilton said he will work with the president on anything that would benefit Kansans.

“Anything the president wants to do that’s good for the people of Kansas, I will be his best partner here,” Hamilton said.

Hamilton, the longtime pastor for one of the largest United Methodist churches in the nation, said there is no need to be squeamish over his ties to the church and that he believes the separation of church and state is “very important.” A supporter of same-sex marriage and abortion rights, Hamilton also addressed concerns from Christians about his views on the issues.

“There’s room for people to have differences of opinion on things,” Hamilton said. “If you’re not in favor of same-sex marriage, then be who you are. But do it lovingly.”

As for his chances of winning, Hamilton said he is “cautiously optimistic.”

“I do think we have a really good chance to win on election night,” the pastor said. “It’s going to be fun.”

articles.title: Mamdani threatens to sue Trump administration over alleged ICE use of New York City property
articles.body:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) on Monday threatened to sue the Trump administration over Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) alleged use of city property.

In a letter addressed to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, acting ICE Director David Venturella and ICE New York field office Director Kenneth Genalo, Mamdani states that he is “deeply troubled by recent reports” of ICE officers “using property owned by the City of New York to stage enforcement operations.”

“This use of City property in furtherance of federal immigration enforcement is unauthorized and is therefore illegal, endangers City residents, and sows fear among those who seek to access City property,” the mayor said in his letter.

“If your agents continue any unauthorized use of these lots, New York City will take legal action to prevent this unlawful commandeering of City property,” Mamdani added.

Mamdani, one of the more prominent progressive figures in the Democratic Party, has pushed for the abolition of ICE.

In mid-October, Mamdani and other New York Democratic leaders pushed for the city’s private parking lot owners to bar ICE from their properties.

“In solidarity with immigrant New Yorkers and in our shared commitment to the City we love, we ask that you do not rent, lend or otherwise make your property available to ICE as a staging area for its enforcement operations,” the mayor wrote in a letter to owners and operators of these properties.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) were among more than 100 elected officials who signed on to Mamdani’s earlier letter.

The Hill has reached out to the Department of Homeland Security for comment.

articles.title: The 119th Congress did more by making government do less
articles.body:
by Rep. Lisa McClain (R-Mich.), opinion contributor 11/02/26 01:30 PM ET

Washington has a peculiar definition of progress. A new program is an accomplishment. A new regulation is action. A new federal office means somebody is finally doing something. That is why some of the most important work Republicans did this Congress involved undoing that so-called “progress.”

For decades, Washington accumulated authority one seemingly reasonable decision at a time. Congress delegated power to an agency full of faceless bureaucrats. The agency wrote a rule. The rule became another permit to obtain, expense to absorb, or decision somebody in Washington had already made for you.

Government grows quietly that way. Freedom disappears just as quietly. House Republicans of the 119th Congress came to Washington with the idea that the most consequential thing government can do is return freedom to the American people. Yes, we passed over 900 pieces of legislation this Congress, the second most in U.S. history, but that matters much less than what changed once the votes were cast.

House Republicans have overturned 23 federal rules through the Congressional Review Act, the most in history and more successful repeals than every previous Congress combined. In one session, we have turned a little-used oversight law into one of Washington’s most powerful tools for permanently returning authority from federal regulators to the people they regulate.

Washington is accustomed to ratchets that turn in one direction. Government expands, the bureaucracy adjusts, and everyone learns to live with the new baseline. We turned the ratchet backward.

Democrats would have let the 2017 tax cuts expire and taken more money out of Americans’ pockets. We made them permanent, cut taxes on tips and overtime, delivered new relief for seniors, and restored incentives to invest and build in America.

Americans have already claimed more than $82 billion in individual tax relief. Over the decade, the tax changes we enacted are projected to give $4.6 trillion back to families and businesses, and the laws enacted cut projected federal spending by roughly $1.1 trillion, meaning Washington will take less of Americans’ money.

People take bigger chances when they know more of the reward will still belong to them. That is how opportunity compounds and how countries grow. But opportunity can only flourish where freedom is protected by order and the rules still mean something.

A limited government is not a weak government. It does a smaller number of things, and it does the essential ones well. It must defend the country, enforce the law, protect basic rights, and establish rules that allow a free society to function.

Securing a nation’s borders is among the most basic responsibilities that government has. Democrats chose to dismantle our border and turn lawlessness into policy. Republicans flipped the script and have not allowed a single illegal immigrant to be released into the country in 16 months.

This Congress put the philosophy of limited government into practice across the economy. We gave small businesses tax certainty to hire and invest. We cleared regulatory barriers so manufacturers can expand, unleashed more American energy, and made it easier to build.

None of these policies determines what Americans must do with their lives. They expand what Americans are free to do for themselves.

The alternative is government by permission slip. Washington chooses which industries deserve to grow, which products people may buy, which energy sources are acceptable, and how much of a worker’s success belongs to somebody else. There needs to be a line between the power government is granted by the people, and the freedom Americans deserve to keep.

That is the foundation the 119th Congress has spent two years laying.

A foundation is not glamorous. Nobody walks through a finished house admiring the concrete underneath it, but everything built above depends on whether the foundation is strong.

Tax certainty. Regulatory relief. A secure border. American energy. Lower crime. More room to work, build and invest. These are not the finished house. They are what makes everything that comes next possible.

I don’t call the 119th Congress the most successful because of the paper it produced. I say it because we changed the direction of the country. Washington has enough monuments to what government can build. We spent this Congress creating room for what Americans can build instead.

The government does not know what your life should look like. Neither do I, and that’s precisely the point — you do.

Lisa McClain is chairwoman of the House Republican Conference.

articles.title: Ukraine: Russia used ceasefire in occupied town to strengthen positions
articles.body:
by Ellen Mitchell 11/02/26 11:59 AM ET

Ukraine is accusing Russia of using a localized ceasefire agreement for the border city of Oleshky, brokered by first lady Melania Trump, to shore up its military positions around the city.

The truce for the Russian-occupied town located in southern Ukraine began on Tuesday and ended late Sunday, and it was meant to allow for the delivery of critical aid and evacuate residents. Around 2,000 people were reportedly trapped in the city because of fighting, including a large elderly population.

While there were no reported violations of the localized ceasefire, Ukraine’s military on Monday said Moscow had used the humanitarian pause to bring in new troops, strengthen its military positions, add in more anti-drone defenses on roads and send more ammunition to the area, according to multiple outlets.

Russia has held Oleshky since Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

The first lady characterized Oleshky as a “front-line war city on the brink of disaster” in a press release announcing the ceasefire agreement late last month.

Russia and Ukraine have pointed fingers at one another for the humanitarian crisis in the city, where explosive mines and drone attacks in the region kept residents from being able to escape as food, medicine and clean water all but disappeared.

The Kremlin accused Ukraine of repeatedly attacking Oleshky, effectively placing a blockade on the city, while Kyiv said Moscow on numerous occasions rejected temporary ceasefire proposals, stole aid packages and downed drones carrying supplies for civilians.

Despite the traded accusations, Trump on Sunday declared the ceasefire had been a “success” with nearly 800 people evacuated.

“On behalf of America, I commend Russia and Ukraine for their leadership and cooperation surrounding the Oleshky ceasefire,” she said in a statement posted to social media. “I hope Oleshky serves as a foundation for lasting peace between both nations.”

But the war between Russia and Ukraine continues to rage, with Russian forces over the weekend hitting energy infrastructure in four regions and cutting off power for hundreds of thousands of homes, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.

Three-way peace negotiations between the U.S., Ukraine and Russia are set for later this month in Abu Dhabi as President Trump has looked to jump-start talks largely abandoned by Washington following the start of the the U.S.-Israeli war in Iran on Feb. 28.

articles.title: Trump administration brings California ballot fight to Supreme Court
articles.body:
by Zach Schonfeld 11/02/26 11:45 AM ET

The Trump administration on Monday brought its demand that California separate 20,000 mail ballots it says belong to likely noncitizens to the Supreme Court, thrusting the justices back into the center of the midterm campaign one day before Election Day.

Lower courts have ruled the list isn’t credible and the Trump administration has no authority to force the state to verify those voters’ citizenship, saying it would cause chaos if officials were to oblige.

“That doomsday prediction ignores that segregating ballots is a routine remedy when the lawfulness of ballots is questioned,” Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote to the Supreme Court.

The fight over the 20,000 California ballots has rapidly escalated as Election Day approaches, as all sides agree they can’t be segregated once they’re processed. Hundreds of thousands of ballots have already been returned across the state, court filings show.

“If the United States is correct, and the individuals it has identified (or even some of those individuals) turn out to be aliens who are unlawfully voting in California, then the United States will suffer irreparable harm from the commingling of their ballots with lawful votes,” Sauer wrote.

Democrats and immigration groups have questioned the list’s veracity and warned the lawsuit is laying the groundwork to disenfranchise voters.

California says it’s not feasible to verify voters’ citizenship so late in the election cycle, and the state criticized the administration for refusing to say who supplied the list.

Lower courts have sided with the state as the Trump administration has raced for a judicial intervention. As it continues appealing, the administration has also sent subpoenas to local election officials and announced criminal charges against alleged noncitizens who’ve tried to register to vote.

The battle reached the Supreme Court after the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit sided against the administration in a 2-1 vote on Friday, saying segregating the ballots would have “potentially catastrophic effects on the entire system.”

The Trump administration’s Supreme Court appeal heads to Justice Elena Kagan, who by default handles emergency matters arising from California. Kagan has not yet announced a deadline for California to respond. She could act on the request alone or refer it to the full court for a vote.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta (D) said he had “strong reason” to believe his office would win again.

“This latest move reeks of desperation and is another attempt to undermine our elections and trample on the rule of law,” Bonta said in a statement. “If the U.S. Supreme Court calls for a response, we will be ready to defend the fundamental right to vote and push back against this lawlessness.”

“My message to Californians is simple: Election Day is tomorrow, but don’t wait until then to vote. If you haven’t cast your ballot yet, make a plan to do so as soon as possible. We’ll keep handling the legal fight in court,” Bonta continued.

articles.title: The Trump era is over
articles.body:
by John Kenneth White, opinion contributor 11/02/26 11:30 AM ET

When the history of the 2026 midterm elections is written, the most remembered political advertisement will be Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy’s (R) commercial starring the mother of his opponent, Dr. Amy Acton (D).

Acton was called a “liar” by her mother, who fled the state along with her abusive husband after he was charged with raping Acton, his stepdaughter. Removed from her home by the state of Ohio, Acton had not seen her mother since 1978.

Ramaswamy’s advertisement generated an immediate political backlash. Ohio’s Republican governor, Mike DeWine, urged Ramaswamy to take it off the air. Local businesses canceled events featuring the beleaguered Republican candidate. And the Cleveland Plain Dealer endorsed Acton, saying that Ramaswamy had “crossed a line.”

But President Trump and JD Vance doubled down in backing Ramaswamy. Trump said that if a candidate’s mother called her daughter a liar, that was political “gold.” Vance complained that Republicans should “stop whining” about Ramaswamy’s tactics, adding, “Politics is a tough business.” After spending $1 million, the Ramaswamy campaign took the controversial ad off the air.

But something bigger than the misadventures of one Republican candidate is at work here. In Kansas, a pastor has a chance to win a Senate seat Democrats have not won since 1932. And in Texas, a state senator and seminarian, has consistently run ahead in the polls, giving Democrats a chance to win a U.S. Senate seat in a state where the party has not won one since 1988.

Some have said that only Trump could have gotten away with running an ad like Ramaswamy’s. After all, when Trump first appeared on the political scene many of his devoted followers admired him for rejecting “political correctness” and saying things other conventional politicians would not.

But this is wrong. Today, the stench of political death has repelled even Trump’s most devoted followers. On the campaign trail, Trump speaks to arenas filled with empty seats. And in the words of Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), those who show up are subjected to two hours of “senile babbling.”

Even a dozen Catholic bishops who were filmed praying over Trump distanced themselves from him. Milwaukee Archbishop Jeffrey S. Grob called the meeting a mistake and apologized for “the pain I caused.” Denver Archbishop James R. Golka said it “was never my intention” for the encounter to be seen as an endorsement.

Americans are profoundly dissatisfied with Trump’s performance, including high gas and grocery prices, the killing of innocent citizens on urban streets, the mass deportation of migrants who have raised families in the U.S. and are a vital engine of economic growth and starting a war with Iran. This runs contrary to Trump’s 2024 promises to bring down costs, deport only migrant criminals and never start another foreign war.

The sense of betrayal is so pervasive that Trump’s job approval ratings have fallen to historic lows.

Rather than solving the problems that concern Americans most, Trump is building a ballroom and an arch, littering the White House with gold and defacing the Reflecting Pool on the National Mall. Barack Obama likened Trump’s gold-littered White House to Saddam Hussein’s opening a Cheesecake Factory.

The path forward to addressing the problems Trump has created is unclear. Some want to deal with the healthcare crisis by creating a Medicare for All option. Potential job losses caused by artificial intelligence and how to regulate it are issues where most agree something must be done, but the solutions are unclear. Dealing with inadequate housing and covering the cost of childcare involve differing approaches. And the Iran War is akin to an unsolvable puzzle where a lasting peace deal might be impossible.

But what is clear is that Americans are demanding an end to the anything-goes rhetoric and want leaders they can admire. Two past presidents — one a Democrat, the other a Republican — set examples that resonate today.

After the stench of Watergate, Jimmy Carter promised a government that was “as competent, as compassionate, as good” as the American people.

Carter’s successor, Ronald Reagan, was also widely admired. New York’s Democratic governor, Mario Cuomo, once said of Reagan, “By his personal conduct when he’s shot, when he’s told he has cancer, when he goes to Normandy — the way he’s deported himself has been a moral instruction to my children.”

Baron de Montesquieu once argued that virtue is “the spring which sets the republican government in motion.” This year, the competitive races run by Democrats Adam Hamilton in Kansas and James Talarico in Texas are signs of an emerging new era where partisanship is cast aside in favor of virtuous leaders who set a high moral example and are role models the rest of us can admire.

The springs of government may be back in motion, but the Trump Era is over. Cause of death: political suicide.

John Kenneth White is a professor emeritus at The Catholic University of America who writes on Substack. His latest book, coauthored with Matthew R. Kerbel, is titled “Democracy on the Edge: The Trump Elections and the Future of American Politics.”

articles.title: Trump says aides have ‘concept’ of Canada trade deal
articles.body:
President Trump said Sunday his administration and Canadian officials are close to reaching a deal to end their months-long trade dispute.

“We have the concept of a very good deal with Canada,” Trump told reporters in Iowa, adding the two sides are “very close” to reaching an agreement.

The president noted he spoke to Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Saturday, saying the deal they discussed would be “great for our farmers, great for our country” and “fine” for Canada.

“Part of the agreement is that our farmers will have to pay no tariffs,” Trump said.

The U.S. and Canada have traded tariffs on each other’s goods since late August, when Trump’s 50 percent levies on $27.6 billion worth of Canadian pr’oducts took effect.

Carney matched those tariffs in September, and Trump later banned American businesses from importing nearly $1 billion worth of Canadian dairy products, motor vehicles and many alcoholic beverages.

The president has also threatened to increase import taxes to 50 percent on Canadian cars, trucks, auto parts and steel starting on Jan. 1.

Carney said Sunday he had a “good conversation” with Trump on the “future” of trade between the two countries.

“This builds on our recent constructive discussions on the outlines of a mutually beneficial trade deal that would create jobs for our workers, boost affordability for families, and fully respect Canada’s languages, culture, and sovereignty,” the Canadian leader wrote on social platform X.

Carney added he and Trump’s teams “will now be working in the coming weeks to deliver that outcome.”

Trump also said Sunday the construction of the Keystone Pipeline expansion will be part of a trade agreement, noting Canada will pay for the project.

“We’re going to give them the route, and it’s largely been determined,” the president added.

The Biden administration revoked a federal permit for the Keystone XL project, which would expand the established pipeline between Western Canada and Texas. TC Energy canceled the expansion project in 2021.

Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said the project would benefit American farmers and ranchers in the form of lower diesel prices. Diesel costs nearly $6.30 per gallon as of Monday, per AAA.

articles.title: The GOP struggles to find a message beyond Trump ahead of elections
articles.body:
by Juan Williams, opinion contributor 11/02/26 09:30 AM ET

As voters head to the polls tomorrow, let’s stop and look at the best messages to voters coming from Republicans.

“Bankruptcies are up, suicides are up but nonetheless [our hope is that President Trump]…can take us to victory here,” Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) told Bloomberg TV last week.

To be fair to Marshall, several Republicans in the 2026 midterms have made similar appeals to voters.

Their best message is that any voter who supported Trump for president should close their eyes, hold their noses and remain loyal to Trump and vote for his supporters in Congress despite bad outcomes.

Unfortunately, that GOP message is facing a high bar. An NPR/PBS Marist poll shows 44 percent of registered voters plan to vote out of opposition to Trump. They oppose corruption, high prices for gas and groceries and another “never-ending” war in the Middle East?

Even with a big bankroll for advertising, the GOP candidates have not found a compelling closing argument beyond blind loyalty to Trump.

What can a GOP candidate say about corruption when the president is making billions on crypto currencies? What is there to say when the bill for his son’s wedding reception is picked up by a Russian oligarch?

Republicans currently in Congress conspicuously closed their eyes to that corruption. They also acquiesced to his economic policies and handling of foreign affairs.

They thought it was smart politics.

Given Trump’s grip on their party they feared losing a GOP primary to a rival endorsed by Trump if dared to defy Trump’s policies.

But in a general election every Republican congressional candidate bears the weight of a president with low approval ratings. He is in negative territory with voters on corruption, on the economy, on inflation, and the war.

That’s why the best message to midterm voters from Republicans has been to try to get voters to look away from Trump. They prefer to lash Democrats as radicals, extremists, and elitists who lack Christian faith, patriotism and family values.

That kind of Republican messaging got a boost from riots in France. The candidates stirred fear of unrest in the U.S. if Democrats win control of Congress.

And then there is a culture war message.

In Iowa, one Republican’s ad featured a narrator who accused his Democratic opponent of being “just plain dangerous to kids” by “voting to let grown men in girl’s lockers rooms,” to accommodate transgender student athletes.

That one backfired when the narrator was found to have a rap sheet that included a 2017 incident where she pled guilty to a count of child endangerment while she was driving intoxicated.

As for concern over the negative impact of Trump’s economic policies, the best they can do is issue repeated statements of “strong concern.”

This is Sen. Susan Collins’ (R-Maine) message in her bid for reelection.

In a recent debate, she boasted about securing limits on Trump’s tariffs on Canadian road salt for Mainers.

That left her open to a strong comeback from her Democrat opponent, Troy Jackson. Noting the high price of food, Jackson won applause on social media for saying Mainers “can’t eat road salt.”

The last resort for Republicans in the 2026 midterms has been to advertise that Trump will appear at a rally for them. They hope the sight of the president will excite voters and increase GOP turnout.

Trump has tried several messages at those rallies including a promise to send $5,000 to each voter if the GOP retains control of the House and Senate.

But that appeal, apart from looking like an attempt to buy votes and being a likely violation of federal bribery laws, never gained traction.

Last week, Trump jokingly invited his supporters to his private club in Palm Beach, Mar-a-Lago.

“The problem is that for $5,000, the most you’ll be able to buy is a hamburger and maybe a small dessert,” he said. “I’m not even sure you could buy that. No, don’t go there. That’s not a good place if you’re price conscious.”

I’m sure that joke is of great comfort to Marshall’s constituents in rural Kansas who are facing farm bankruptcy amid rising rates of suicide.

Trump’s pitch of dollars for votes led to a return volley from former President Obama.

Stumping for Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El Sayed, Obama said Trump’s gold-plated decor of the White House looked like “Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.”

MAGA spinmeisters tried to cast this as a culture war attack on working-class Cheesecake Factory patrons. Obama later noted that Trump did not protest being likened to an Iraqi dictator.

Trump’s messaging notably failed to revive GOP support on social media.

“What Trump stood for, some of it turned out to not be real,” said Joe Rogan, a top podcaster who previously spoke favorably of Trump. “Like one of [Trump’s 2024 promises] was the no wars. Well, look, we’re at war with Iran. So that wasn’t real.”

Political prognosticator Charlie Cook recently said this election looks less like a “blue wave” than the result of a “red undertow.”

In other words, the Republicans never surfaced an effective message, leaving Democrats sailing toward victory.

Juan Williams is senior political analyst for Fox News Channel and a prize-winning civil rights historian. He is the author of the new book “New Prize for These Eyes: The Rise of America’s Second Civil Rights Movement.“

articles.title: Trump disapproval hits record 60 percent in new survey
articles.body:
by Ryan Mancini 11/02/26 09:29 AM ET

A new poll shows President Trump’s disapproval rating reached a record high on Sunday, less than 48 hours before Election Day.

The NBC News poll found that 60 percent of respondents did not approve of Trump’s job performance, a new high across both of his terms as president. His approval rating hit 40 percent.

The outlet’s pollsters saw that roughly 3 in 4 voters were dissatisfied with the state of the economy and almost two-thirds called for a change from Trump’s direction on the economy, with 50 percent calling for “a great deal” of change, also a record high according to NBC News’s polling data.

There was a narrow divide between the 51 percent of respondents who said they were dissatisfied with their personal financial situation versus the 49 percent who said they were satisfied. This marked another first for NBC News polling in the 30 years it has asked respondents about their personal financial situations, even with a 56 percent to 44 percent gap when respondents were asked during the 2009 Great Recession.

Sixty-four percent of respondents, including one-third of Trump voters, said he has fallen short of their expectations, while 34 percent said he has met expectations, according to the poll.

Democratic pollster Jeff Horwitt of Hart Research Associates, who conducted the survey with Republican pollster Bill McInturff of Public Opinion Strategies, told NBC News that Trump’s presidency “can be summarized as the promise of two years ago and the peril of two days from now.”

Horwitt emphasized Trump’s 2024 campaign pledge to lower costs and tackle inflation, but voters have grown concerned over high prices driven up by the Iran war.

In the poll, 53 percent of Republican respondents were not satisfied with the state of the economy, and 37 percent said the GOP has not met Trump’s promises. Forty-six percent of non-MAGA Republicans overall said they disapprove of Trump’s handling of the presidency, and 20 percent said they prefer to see Democrats control Congress after the midterms.

The president holds a 93 percent approval rating among respondents who identify themselves as MAGA voters.

Democrats appear poised to take control of the House following Tuesday’s midterms. The Hill’s election partner Decision Desk HQ estimated Monday that Democrats have an 84 percent chance of winning the House and a 64 percent probability they’ll take the Senate.

Trump warned in a “Pod Force One” interview set to air on Monday that he will be “Mr. Veto” if Democrats win control of Congress.

The NBC News survey was conducted Oct. 28-30 and included 1,000 respondents with a margin of error of 3.1 percentage points.

articles.title: Reject the oath-breakers and election-deniers on the ballot tomorrow
articles.body:
by William S. Becker, opinion contributor 11/02/26 08:00 AM ET

Around 250 million Americans are eligible to vote in tomorrow’s midterm elections. By the end of last week, more than 34 million already had. And all the while, President Trump and his allies are doing all they can to meddle in the process.

Voters will find that hundreds of candidates on this year’s ballots are undermining confidence in elections, despite repeated findings that the electoral process is fair. Many participated in Trump’s plot to overturn the 2020 election. Others have simply bought into his persistent but entirely unsubstantiated claims of election fraud. Either way, voters should reject them.

No responsibility of citizenship is more important than choosing who represents us in government. In democracies, it is a sacred secular ritual. It gives every eligible citizen a measure of political power, including the ability to stand against tyranny and corruption, influence how tax dollars are spent, and help shape the country’s future.

Fair elections allow power to transfer peacefully from one set of leaders to the next. Scholars call this a “rare and recent practice” among nations. Its upkeep is one reason every public official in the U.S. must swear to protect and defend the Constitution.

Trump has taken that oath twice, but he has repeatedly violated it as president. He is now openly engaged in a conspiracy to erode voter confidence in elections and interfere with the ability of states to run them honestly. His interference is unpatriotic, unethical and unconstitutional.

Trump has engaged the U.S. Departments of Justice and Homeland Security in this effort. They are not acting alone. According to an Oct. 5 analysis by the nonpartisan States United Democracy Center, voters will find the names of 197 election deniers across 43 states on their midterm ballots. The center defines election denial as candidates who helped spread Trump’s persistent lies about the 2020 election, refused to certify the results on Jan. 6, 2021, or tried to overturn former President Joe Biden’s victory.

States United counts 163 congressional races with election deniers on the ballot. That is significant, because those elected to the House or Senate will participate in certifying the 2028 presidential election, the process that Trump and his co-conspirators tried to sabotage in 2021 by appointing false electors and inciting the riot that delayed Congress’s validation of Joe Biden’s lawful victory.

At least 33 other deniers across 21 states are running for statewide offices, States United says, hoping to become governors, attorneys general or secretaries of state, the chief election officers in most states.

Three Republican gubernatorial candidates on tomorrow’s ballots are departing members of Congress that the center has identified as election deniers: Reps. Andy Biggs (R-Ariz.), Byron Donalds (R-Fla), and Tom Tiffany (R-Wis). They voted to sustain objections to valid electoral votes during the 2021 certification process.

These candidates should be defeated because their involvement affronts the democratic process. Study after study has concluded that claims of significant election irregularities, such as voter fraud, are baseless.

“American elections are quite well-run,” states the American Bar Association. “[E]fforts to cast doubt on their security and accuracy pose a grave systemic threat to our form of government.”

Interestingly, some legal scholars argue the Constitution disqualifies members of the denial movement from holding any public office. Section 3 of the 14th Amendment says that any federal or state official who swears to uphold the Constitution (all public officials are obligated to do so) and then participates in or supports a rebellion against it should be disqualified from serving in office again.

But in 2024, the U.S. Supreme Court muddied the waters on how to enforce this. In a 5-4 ruling, the court said only Congress can disqualify federal officials for rebellion. The Constitution doesn’t say that.

Although Trump won’t be on tomorrow’s ballots, voters can hold him accountable by rejecting the midterm candidates who participated in denying the 2020 election outcome and who continue supporting his efforts to rig the electoral process, intimidate state election officials, destroy public confidence in voting, and interfere with states’ constitutional election duties.

Facts are facts. The moneychangers, snake-oil salesmen, charlatans, crooks, capitulators, collaborators and cowards have taken over the temples of democracy. They plan to stay. Tomorrow, we must begin kicking them out.

William S. Becker is co-editor of and a contributor to “Democracy Unchained: How to Rebuild Government for the People,” and a contributor to “Democracy in a Hotter Time.” He previously served as a senior official in the Wisconsin Department of Justice. He is currently executive director of the Presidential Climate Action Project.

articles.title: Trump plans to deliver closing message at Reflecting Pool
articles.body:
President Trump will make his final pitch to voters Monday ahead of Election Day at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, using the Washington landmark to tout his administration’s beautification projects in the nation’s capital.

Trump’s remarks will focus on the agenda he and Republican lawmakers have advanced since the start of his second term, a source familiar told NewsNation. The president is also expected to promote his expensive and controversial restoration projects, including the pool’s expensive renovation that had a list of issues.

The White House confirmed the event Sunday, hours after Trump floated the possibility while speaking to reporters in Iowa.

“We might hold it tomorrow or something,” the president said, adding that an appearance at the landmark would “show how beautiful it is.”

The expected speech marks an unconventional end to Trump’s midterm campaign blitz, with the president opting to spend the final day before the election in Washington instead of rallying in a battleground state to boost GOP voter turnout.

Trump has held more than 25 rallies over the past month in an effort to help Republicans maintain control of the House and Senate amid a record-low approval rating and voter frustration over the war in Iran, rising energy prices and the economy.

The decision to visit the Reflecting Pool for the speech also puts renewed attention on a renovation project that has been plagued by delays, ballooning costs and legal controversies over alleged vandalism.

The pool’s renovation is part of Trump’s broader push to reshape the nation’s capital during his second term. His administration also demolished the White House’s East Wing to make room for a new ballroom, transformed the Rose Garden into a patio and pursued other construction projects around the federal district.

articles.title: Exit exams out, mediocrity in: The decline and fall of US graduation standards
articles.body:
by Daniel Buck, opinion contributor 11/02/26 07:30 AM ET

Last month, the New York State Education Department announced that it intends to nix the Regents Exam as a graduation requirement in the Empire State.

The policy change received widespread condemnation. Former Gov. George Pataki (R) ripped the move as “incredibly stupid.” The Wall Street Journal editorial board criticized it as “as one more sorry milestone on America’s educational march to mediocrity.”

They’re right to heap scorn on the change. It’s entirely appropriate to test and ensure that graduates leave high school with basic competencies in reading, writing, and math. Receiving less opprobrium, but equally deserving of it, is what will replace the exam itself.

Education Commissioner Betty Rosa has explained that instead of relying on the Regents, the state is building a “graduation system grounded in New York’s Portrait of a Graduate,” a program wherein students can demonstrate their learning through performance-based assessments and portfolios. Instead of simply passing a basic competency test, the Portrait of a Graduate requires that students demonstrate their ability to be a “critical thinker” and “global citizen” through “multiple measures.”

Such banalities are superficially appealing — after all, who would oppose critical thinking? But the ability to think critically relies upon rudimentary academic skills of the kind the Regents Exam tested. No student can meaningfully analyze current events without basic factual knowledge of history or the ability to read paragraphs and comprehend them.

These portraits replace with vague aspirations the concrete, measurable, academic benchmarks that allow for higher-level cognitive functions. Consequently, students are likely to develop neither.

New York is actually late to this trend. In the mid-2000s, 27 states required high school exit exams. That number is now down to just six. Concurrently, 26 states have adopted some variation of “Portrait of a Graduate,” so we have evidence of what these shifts mean in practice.

A 2024 report by the ed-tech nonprofit Digital Promise analyzed more than 60 graduate portraits from districts. It devised a model for districts to follow that it says incorporates 90 percent of the specific competencies that appear across their sample. These include an ability to “care for and contribute to society” and “communicate in all media and modalities.”

In their report, they include models of what such a Portrait might look like in practice. For example, Digital Promise recommends middle school students demonstrate their problem-solving abilities through spaghetti tower challenges.

Another performance task that the ed-tech lauds comes by way of Howard-Suamico, Wisconsin, where students demonstrate “collaboration” by crafting tri-fold posters about potential gluten-free Taco trucks. Even the student model includes basic errors — get your taco with “sweat corn.”

I was once a teacher. I don’t fault students for letting a typo slip through here or there. I have seen plenty of last-minute projects cobbled together the night before. But when such work is set forth as the ideal, it makes the whole effort look like a method to justify seemingly everything except academics.

Battelle for Kids, one of the main organizations behind the trend toward measurements such as “Portraits of a Graduate,” sets forth as an exemplar a student presentation analyzing Tupac and Lil Wayne lyrics from Affton School District in Missouri. It holds up as another example a collage of political posters on gun control and abortion rights in Winston-Salem, N.C.

In other words, by adopting poorly defined and unmeasurable goals, schools can use almost any activity to demonstrate preferred competencies. Running in parallel, schools can then also explain away academic failure. Sure, the students may not be able to add fractions, and they can’t name the three branches of government, but fortunately we have abolished all the tools we once had to measure such failures.

We can measure whether students can multiply and whether certain instructional practices helped them do it. But how do we measure global citizenship and determine if any one activity or another fosters it? We can’t, and so anything goes. Oh well — at least they can all conspicuously “embrace diversity!”

Most everyone hopes that schools will foster some competencies, such as perseverance or problem-solving. But they are situated to do so best when they emphasize traditional academics.

How can a school foster grit? Maintain demanding academic gauntlets. How can schools create self-discipline? Set behavioral standards and hold students to them. How can schools enable critical thinking? Provide them the knowledge of history, science, literature, grammar, and the arts that become the tools of critical thought.

Students become thoughtful, self-controlled citizens by wrestling with worthy subject matter, not through kitschy activities where they make posters about how kindness is cool.

Getting rid of the Regents Exams was a mistake, but what they are replacing it with might be even worse.

Daniel Buck is a research fellow and the director of the Conservative Education Reform Network at the American Enterprise Institute.

articles.title: Democrats squabbling over how to contain Trump after Election Day
articles.body:
by Alexander Bolton 11/02/26 06:00 AM ET

Democrats are expecting to win big on Election Day, but disagreements are already erupting among them over how aggressively to target President Trump for what they say are abuses of power and corruption.

Democratic lawmakers and strategists are divided over whether to push another impeachment against Trump.

Senators and leaders in the House are generally opposed to advancing a third impeachment of Trump that has virtually no chance of picking up 67 votes in the Senate — the number of votes needed to convict.

A senior Senate Democratic aide warned there is little “appetite” for holding a third Trump impeachment trial in the Senate, after previous impeachment efforts in 2020 and 2021 failed to impact Trump politically.

Democrats agree there need to be investigations of Trump and his allies next year to hold them to account, but there is little consensus over what to prioritize, according to Democratic strategists and aides.

But some senior lawmakers are warning that the party can’t get so wrapped up in tracking down the misdeeds of the president and the administration that they get pulled into too many directions or lose sight of addressing high prices and ending the war in Iran — two of the top issues of this year’s election.

“I don’t think we can ignore it,” said Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) of the need to investigate alleged corruption in the Trump administration.

“More than 90 percent of voters think that government has been corrupted. We just have to be thoughtful and strategic about where investigative work goes and not allow that to distract us from solving fairly immediate cost problems that American families feel,” he said.

Whitehouse would become chair of the powerful Senate Judiciary Committee if Democrats win control of the Senate.
