To keep their hoped-for new House majority — and possible Senate majority — from getting sucked into solely partisan battles with Trump over what has already transpired, Democratic leaders in Congress are mapping out positive agendas for the first 100 hours, the first 100 days and the first year of their new majorities, according to sources familiar with internal discussions.

Yet the desire among Democratic lawmakers to inflict retribution on Trump is strong.

Some want to delve further into the Jeffrey Epstein sex-trafficking scandal to probe whether the Justice Department violated the Epstein Files Transparency Act by withholding or improperly redacting documents.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), who would return to the role of majority leader if Democrats capture the Senate, created a special Senate working group in February to plumb Epstein-related information held back from the public by the Trump Justice Department.

“We are demanding that the Department of Justice and the FBI preserve records on what transpired behind the scenes. We want to know who was involved in the decision to hide the truth,” he declared.

Other Democrats want to prioritize investigations of the Defense Department and the awarding of lucrative contracts linked to Donald Trump Jr.

Sens. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), Andy Kim (D-N.J.) and Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) sent a letter to Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth earlier this year demanding information about decisions at the Pentagon to give loans and contracts to companies “associated with the president’s son” that may have had “conflicts of interest.”

Some Democrats are pushing for investigations into the Trump family’s massive investments in the crypto industry; the president’s pardon of Binance founder and former CEO Changpeng Zhao, who pleaded guilty to violating money laundering law; and whether crypto investments provided an avenue for foreign interests to influence the president.

“We’re going to have to do voluminous oversight work because there is rampant corruption in this administration, and we need to get to the bottom of it,” said Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.).

Some Democrats want to investigate Trump’s pardon record more closely and scrutinize donations that wealthy individuals and families made in hopes of receiving clemency.

The New York Times reported that Alina Habba Mildon, one of Trump’s former lawyers, earned $50 million to help secure a pardon for the member of a wealthy Venezuelan family, among other duties.

A Democratic strategist and former House leadership aide said Democratic leaders are looking at a wide array of issues to investigate when they take back the Speaker’s gavel in January.

“Everything from corporate America and their ties to the Trump administration, Epstein, immigration,” said the strategist, noting that Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), who would take over as chair of the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, has been outspoken about investigating conditions at Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention facilities and immigration enforcement activities more generally.

“They’re going to spend their time looking at a variety of issues,” the strategist added, noting Democrats are “running on affordability and corruption” in the midterm election.

The House-aligned Democratic strategist said there’s little desire among House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries’s (N.Y.) leadership team to move toward another impeachment proceeding, even though there are rank-and-file members in the Democratic caucus who want to.

“I’ll tell you right now that I have not heard about impeachment, not for Trump,” the source said.

The strategist said Democratic leaders instead are eyeing a lower-key strategy to hamstring the Trump administration by tying up Cabinet and other senior officials in oversight hearings.

“That’s what they’re elected to do, to constrain Trump and to ensure that they try to get some of their agenda passed and signed into law,” the strategist said.

Beyond investigations, Democrats are threatening to make it much tougher for Trump to make appointments to the federal judiciary and the executive branch if they win control of the Senate.

And they’ve threatened to cut off funding for the war with Iran if Trump doesn’t bring the conflict to a swift conclusion.

Sen. Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii), who is set to become the next Senate Democratic whip, has warned that getting bipartisan majorities to vote for bills to authorize and fund the Pentagon will be “extremely difficult” if the war drags on.

Some Democrats, however, argue that Trump still needs to face accountability for trying to overturn the results of the 2020 presidential election or for mishandling classified documents and conspiring to obstruct justice related to those documents after leaving office in 2021.

“Donald Trump’s alleged crimes still have not been given justice. There’s been no justice yet for these alleged crimes, which are just so deeply serious, and were stopped midway in the criminal justice process,” said Blumenthal, a member of the Senate Judiciary Committee.

“I still feel there needs to be some reckoning,” he said.

Blumenthal would be poised to take over as chair of the Senate’s Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations if Democrats win control of the Senate this week.

Other Democrats say they want to investigate what they say has been a “corrupt relationship” between the Trump administration and wealthy special interests over the past 20 months.

Murphy says he wants to know more about “an $8 million donation made by R.J. Reynolds to the administration that resulted one week later in flavored vapes being made legal for kids.”

“We should get to the bottom of the corrupt relationship that exists between corporations in this country and the Trump administration,” he said.

articles.title: Newsom on possible Democratic ‘tsunami’ on Election Day: ‘That’s a word I haven’t used lightly’
articles.body:
by Ryan Mancini 11/01/26 09:09 PM ET

California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) on Sunday said there’s a chance there could be a massive Democratic victory, or a “blue tsunami,” on Election Day, and that there is momentum behind the party to reclaim one or both chambers of Congress.

“It could be that blue tsunami, but you make that legitimate and obvious point,” Newsom said on “Decision Desk ’26: Midterm Preview,” hosted by 2WAY in collaboration with The Hill and NewsNation, to moderator and journalist Mark Halperin. “The margins in those Senate races suggest that, obviously, maybe it won’t be on that side of the aisle, as well.”

“We’re all going to be experts in hindsight. It will all be obvious –– what’s happened –– in 48 hours. But I just –– that tsunami. That’s a word I haven’t used lightly and it’s a word that I’m sharing privately and publicly,” he told Halperin and his co-hosts for the evening, Democratic strategist Kevin Walling and conservative commentator Larry O’Connor.

The governor added, “I just feel it everywhere I’ve been. These things seem to be teed up despite the headwinds of today in Michigan,” referring to Rep. Haley Stevens’s (D-Mich.) endorsement of Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers.

Rep. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.), who is up for reelection on Tuesday, appeared after Newsom and dismissed any chances of a “tsunami.” He said there was a “frustration” at the state and national levels against Democrats.

“People are feeling the pain,” he said. “I listened to Gavin Newsom. It’s as if he hasn’t been in elected office for 30 years though. California and New York are two of the most expensive states anywhere in the country because of the policy decisions that they make.”

“And so I don’t think the blue tsunami, as Gavin Newsom predicts, is going to be reaching New York in terms of my congressional seat,” Lawler later added.

Polling shows that Democrats are primed to likely win the House on Tuesday. The Hill’s election partner Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) projects an 83-percent probability that Democrats will win the House. They will need at least three seats to win a majority.

Democrats must flip four Republican-held seats to win the Senate. DDHQ estimates that they have a 62-percent chance to bring the Senate under Democratic control.

Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) on Sunday said there will be “debate” within the GOP about the MAGA movement should they suffer losses in the midterms. He cited “Ronald Reagan principles” as something the party has backed away from during President Trump’s two administrations.

“I think the Republican Party, I think America yearns for those principles. … And I surely would like to see a debate, and I know I want to be a part of it,” he said on CNN.

Trump, who has seen his approval ratings plummet across several polls over his handling on the economy and the Iran war, has called on Republicans to “pretend” as though he is on the ballot to increase voter turnout, which is generally lower in midterm cycles.

articles.title: Iran’s Supreme Court upholds death sentence for a fruit seller arrested in connection with nationwide protests
articles.body:
Editor's note: This story was translated from the original VOA Persian article.

A U.S.-based rights organization says that Iran's Supreme Court has upheld the death sentence against a fruit seller convicted in connection with anti-government protests earlier this year.

The Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA), the media arm of the Human Rights Activists in Iran, reported Monday that the court reached the decision in the case against Arman Marefati.

The group also said that two female protesters arrested in connection with the protests have been sentenced to a combined 44 years in prison.

Marefati was convicted in March 2026 by an Islamic revolutionary court in Tehran on charges alleging participation in activities against national security, entering religious sites with the intent to destroy them, and participating in the burning of a mosque and a religious seminary.

He has been transferred to from Greater Tehran Prison to Qezel Hesar Prison in Karaj in June where political and death-row prisoners are held.

His two co-defendants in the case, Mehrdad Mohammadiania and Ashkan Maleki, were executed in June after they were convicted of allegedly cooperating with Israel and hostile governments, creating insecurity and public fear, destroying and setting fire to public property, and participation in activities against national security.

Rights group Amnesty International said the executions were carried out without advance notice to their families or lawyers.

Marefati who is believed to be 38 years old, is originally from Saqqez County and lived in Tehran when he was arrested during nationwide protests in January 2026. He worked at a fruit and vegetable market, HRANA reported.

U.S. President Donald Trump, in early September accused Iranian officials of crimes against humanity over the regime's repression, killing, and execution of protesters and called for them to be brought to justice.

The U.S. State Department in its 2026 Human Rights report has also condemned issuance of death sentences against protesters and government opponents on security-related charges, including capital charges known locally as Moharebeh and cooperation with foreign countries.

Thousands of Iranians participated in protests that began late last year and continued into this year over economic hardships, including a sharp devaluation of the country’s currency. From the outset, however, demonstrators called for the overthrow of the Islamic Republic.

President Trump told world leaders on September that Iran had killed 72,000 of its citizens this year.

Iran has claimed the number of deaths related to the protests to be at 3,038; however, a recent U.N. fact-finding mission concluded that true figures are "significantly" higher than the government reported.

Human rights organizations have repeatedly accused the Iranian authorities of using torture, prolonged solitary confinement and other forms of coercion to extract confessions from detainees, which are then used as evidence in prosecutions, including cases carrying the death penalty.Rights groups have also raised concerns that defendants are subjected to unfair trials based on forced confessions and vague or politically motivated national security charges, as well as allegations they say are fabricated or unsupported by credible evidence.Amnesty International and other rights organizations have documented cases in which defendants were denied meaningful access to lawyers and due process, raising concerns about the reliability of convictions and the use of the death penalty against protesters and government opponents.

articles.title: ICBL: North Korea’s reported mine-laying could be world’s largest since 2001
articles.body:
Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Korean article.

South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff told members of the National Assembly’s intelligence and defense committee last month that North Korea has laid an estimated 960,000 land mines in the Demilitarized Zone since 2024.

South Korean media, citing lawmakers’ offices, reported that the military had presented the estimate to the National Assembly in late October.

VOA reached out to the International Campaign to Ban Landmines for a response to the news, but the ICBL said it could not independently verify the figure or explain how it was calculated.

The ICBL did tell VOA that if the 960-thousand mine figure is accurate, it would be one of the "largest uses of antipersonnel mines anywhere in the world..."

But it's not the largest. In Russia’s war in Ukraine, international experts estimate Russia has laid more than 2 million land mines since 2022, according to the U.S. State Department.

The ICBL did say that North Korean landmines can float into waterways beyond the Demilitarized Zone, threatening civilians and soldiers with injuries likely to cost them a limb.

The ICBL notably shared the 1997 Nobel Peace Prize with Jody Williams for efforts to ban and clear antipersonnel mines.

Separately, South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff concluded on October 5 that North Korean antipersonnel mines deliberately planted on the South Korean-controlled side of the DMZ caused the September 21 explosions that injured three South Korean troops.

Citing a joint investigation with United Nations Command and forensic testing, the military said those mines had been planted rather than washed into the area.

North Korea rejected responsibility for planting the mines. In an October 25 letter to the U.N. Security Council president, Pyongyang called the incident a South Korean fabrication intended to obstruct its border fortifications and evade blame for worsening tensions.

articles.title: US lawmaker calls on Beijing to release all political prisoners
articles.body:
Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Mandarin article.

Representative John Moolenaar, the chairman of the U.S. House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party is calling on Beijing to release all political prisoners in China.

October 30 marks the International Day of Political Prisoners, a day that originated in the Soviet Union era and observed by a global coalition of rights groups to show solidarity with political prisoners worldwide.

"The tragic cases of Joshua Wong, Jimmy Lai, Dr. Youlin Chen, Min Zin, Pastor Gao Quanfu, Dr. Gulshan Abbas, and countless others exemplify how the CCP will use arbitrary detainment, wrongful detention, and collective punishment for political leverage and to silence those who fight for freedom and liberty," the Michigan Republican said in a statement on Friday.

Joshua Wong is a prominent Hong Kong pro-democracy activist, and Jimmy Lai is the founder of the now-closed Apple Daily. Both are serving sentences under the National Security Law imposed by Beijing. Lai is serving a 20-year sentence, while Wong, already jailed for subversion, faces additional prison time after pleading guilty to a foreign collusion charge.

Youlin Chen is a U.S. citizen and Boston-based seismologist who was detained in November 2024 and charged with espionage in May 2025. He is still awaiting trial. Min Zin is a Burmese American scholar who was detained in June after traveling to China for an academic conference. He is being held on suspicion of espionage, but it's not clear if he's been charged with any crime. The U.S. State Department says both men are being wrongfully detained.

Pastor Gao Quanfu is the jailed leader of an unregistered house church called the Light of Zion Church in Xi'an. He was detained in May of 2025 on charges of fraud along with his wife and is awaiting trial. Dr. Gulshan Abbas, a retired Uyghur physician, is serving a 20-year sentence on terrorism-related charges, imposed in 2019.

"This is a day to honor the courage and bravery of all the dissidents who have stood up to the CCP’s authoritarian rule and are unjustly imprisoned," Moolenaar noted in his statement Friday. "We must make sure the world does not forget that China has jailed these people for believing in freedom and democracy, and I again call on the CCP to release all of its political prisoners."

“We must make sure the world does not forget that China has jailed these people for believing in freedom and democracy, and I again call on the CCP to release all of its political prisoners," he said.

The U.S. House Select Committee on China was established in January of 2023. The committee is tasked with investigating and providing policy recommendations regarding the strategic competition between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party.

Also on Friday, the Congressional-Executive Commission on China (CECC) posted its most updated Chinese political prisoner database on X.

According to the independent government agency, as of Friday, the database, which the commission says captures “only a fraction of the actual number of detentions,” has documented 11,486 cases of political and religious prisoners in China, including 2,613 cases of active detention.

“On the International Day of Political Prisoners, all those imprisoned for speaking the truth, defending human rights, and peacefully exercising their fundamental freedoms should be remembered,” the CECC said.

articles.title: Human rights group: at least 69 political prisoners in Russian custody have died since February 2022
articles.body:
Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Russian article.

A Russian human rights group says at least 69 people subjected to political persecution have died in Russia or Russian-occupied territory since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022.

Speaking on the eve of Russia's Day of Remembrance for Victims of Political Repression, Sergei Davidis, head of the "Political Prisoners. Memorial" human rights project, said the most common cause of death was from illness and lack of medical care.

According to Davidis, the team has been compiling lists of political prisoners and monitoring political repression since 2008: 81 people whose imprisonment was politically motivated died during that time. "Of those," Davidis said, "69 died after the start of the full-scale war. The increase is enormous."

While Russian officials have not commented on this specific report, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, as recently as September, has denied reports that Russia holds political prisoners.

Davidis said since the war began, the numbers have increased substantially.

"When we began monitoring the situation, there were about 30 people on our list. Today, the number of political prisoners exceeded 1,800," he said.

He also said repression has become more severe.

"When we first began monitoring the situation, torture was not as widespread as it is now, for example, in cases involving Ukrainian citizens," Davidis said.

The longtime human rights advocate said deaths from illness and the denial or delayed provision of medical care have become a systemic problem. The report also states that "increasing numbers of young people, including minors, are being subjected to politically motivated imprisonment."

Davidis said political repression in Russia is not some isolated phenomenon carried out by judges or individual security officers.

"The brutality of this repression and the absence of any leniency toward prisoners are deliberate state policies, not simply individual abuses by officials," he said. "Those directly involved in the deaths of specific political prisoners bear responsibility and must be held accountable."

articles.title: US military reveals a clear image of China’s secretive spaceplane
articles.body:
Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Mandarin article.

The U.S. military has released a clear image showing China's secretive reusable spaceplane docked with a satellite in orbit.

The 2024 photo image appears in the latest edition of Challenges to Security in Space published recently by the U.S. Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA). The unclassified report assesses “adversary threats” in space, detailing space-related goals and activities of China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea.

The image was taken by Vantor (formerly Maxar), a private U.S. satellite and space intelligence firm. It shows an unmanned Chinese spaceplane rendezvousing with a satellite. The satellite has its solar panels deployed, and the spaceplane payload bay doors are open.

The DIA included the image in a section of the report which discusses reusable space launch vehicles (R-SLVs).

The report notes that the United States is currently the only nation with an operational R-SLV program, while China is seeking to become the second one.

The report says that in addition to working on reusable space rockets, Beijing is also developing spaceplanes, which offer similar reusability with enhanced maneuverability.

"China has two primary spaceplane models according to the report: the Shenlong and Tengyun," which translate to "Divine Dragon," and "Cloud Rider," respectively.

The report, released Oct. 26, describes three Chinese spaceplane missions. The first, in 2020, lasted two days. The second, launched in August 2022, spent 276 days in orbit, and the third, launched in December 2023, spent 268 days in orbit. More recently, Chinese state media reported a fourth launch in February.

The DIA report does not specify whether the spaceplane is a Shenlong or a Tengyun. Past Chinese official media reports about these missions only vaguely alluded to “a reusable experimental spacecraft”. However, it is widely believed that the spaceplane, which is vertically launched by a Long March rocket, is the reusable, uncrewed spaceplane Shenlong. The Tengyun which uses the newer horizontal launch technologies as described by Chinese official accounts, is at a more experimental stage.

Some observers have compared the Shenlong to the X-37B, an autonomous and reusable uncrewed spaceplane developed by Boeing for the U.S. Space Force.

David Shedd, former acting director of the DIA, told VOA the spaceplane image is “big news."

“DIA’s published picture is a striking image as it underscores that China is actively looking to both enhance its offensive and defensive posture in space,” he said in an emailed statement.

“These advances by the PRC (People's Republic of China) in space remind us that the U.S. must continue to actively work to counter the significant and advancement of Chinese capabilities in space that could and actually will threaten America's satellite constellations in both the defense and commercial arena," Shedd told VOA.

“Malign efforts” of China, Russia, Iran and North Korea

In its report, the DIA, an agency under the U.S. Department of War, outlines various threats in space that endanger the defense of the United States and its allies.

The report named China and three other countries which “have exhibited behaviors that often run counter to a safe, secure, and sustainable space domain”.

"China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea are developing, testing, deploying, and using space capabilities in a way that threatens the security of all space systems and their associated space benefits,” the report states.

The report further notes that "the malign efforts" of China, Russia, and what it terms "emerging space powers" Iran and North Korea have extended beyond the development of new technologies into the diplomatic and economic arenas.

The Chinese government has not specifically responded to the new DIA report. Beijing has claimed that China opposes weaponization of outer space.

Spearheaded by Beijing and Moscow, the United Nations passed two resolutions in December 2025 ostensibly aimed at preventing arms race and forbidding first placement of weapons in outer space. The DIA report described these as “unverifiable international space treaties and commitments”, which have not stopped the “dangerous or ambiguous behavior on-orbit” by China and Russia.

The U.S. Defense Intelligence Agency first released its Challenges to Security in Space report in early 2019 and issued an update in 2022. This year’s report marks the third edition.

VOA Mandarin’s Yu-wen Cheng contributed to this report.
